<example number="1">
    <heading level="4">Example 1</heading>
    <paragraph>Simplify the expressions:</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>$${({3x^{2}})}{({4x^{3}})}$$</item>
      <item>$$\frac{16^{5 \slash 4}}{16^{1 \slash 2}}$$</item>
      <item>$${(6^{2 \slash 3})}^{3}$$</item>
      <item>$${(x^{3}y^{- 2})}^{- 2}$$</item>
      <item>$$\left( \frac{y^{3 \slash 2}}{x^{1 \slash 4}} \right)^{- 2}$$</item>
    </list>
    <heading level="4">Solution</heading>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>$${(3x^{2})(4x^{3}) = 12x^{2 + 3} = 12x^{5}} {{Law}1}$$</item>
      <item>$${\frac{16^{5 \slash 4}}{16^{1 \slash 2}} = 16^{5 \slash 4 - 1 \slash 2} = 16^{3 \slash 4} = {(\sqrt[4]{16})}^{3} = 2^{3} = 8} {{Law}2}$$</item>
      <item>$${{(6^{2 \slash 3})}^{3} = 6^{(2 \slash 3)(3)} = 6^{2} = 36} {{Law}3}$$</item>
      <item>$${{(x^{3}y^{- 2})}^{- 2} = {(x^{3})}^{- 2}{(y^{- 2})}^{- 2} = x^{(3)( - 2)}y^{( - 2)( - 2)} = x^{- 6}y^{4} = \frac{y^{4}}{x^{6}}} {{Law}4}$$</item>
      <item>$${\left( \frac{y^{3 \slash 2}}{x^{1 \slash 4}} \right)^{- 2} = \frac{y^{(3 \slash 2)( - 2)}}{x^{(1 \slash 4)( - 2)}} = \frac{y^{- 3}}{x^{- 1 \slash 2}} = \frac{x^{1 \slash 2}}{y^{3}}} {{Law}5}$$</item>
    </list>
  </example>

      <item>$$\sqrt[4]{16x^{4}y^{8}}$$</item>
      <item>$$\sqrt{12m^{3}n} \cdot \sqrt{3m^{5}n}$$</item>

      <item>$$\frac{\sqrt[3]{- 27x^{6}}}{\sqrt[3]{8y^{3}}} = \frac{{( - 27x^{6})}^{1 \slash 3}}{{(8y^{3})}^{1 \slash 3}} = \frac{- 27^{1 \slash 3}x^{2}}{8^{1 \slash 3}y} = - \frac{3x^{2}}{2y}$$</item>

    <paragraph>Rationalize the numerator of the expression $$\frac{3\sqrt{x}}{2x}$$ .</paragraph>
    <heading level="4">Solution</heading>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{3\sqrt{x}}{2x} = \frac{3\sqrt{x}}{2x} \cdot \frac{\sqrt{x}}{\sqrt{x}} = \frac{3\sqrt{x^{2}}}{2x\sqrt{x}} = \frac{3x}{2x\sqrt{x}} = \frac{3}{2\sqrt{x}}$$</paragraph>

body_xml:
<example number="7">
    <heading level="4">Example 7</heading>
    <paragraph>Perform the indicated operations:</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>$$(x^{2} + 1)(3x^{2} + 10x + 3)$$</item>
      <item>$$x\left( {300 - \frac{1}{4}x - \frac{1}{8}y} \right) + y\left( {240 - \frac{1}{8}x - \frac{3}{8}y} \right)$$</item>
      <item>$$(e^{t} + e^{- t})e^{t} - e^{t}(e^{t} - e^{- t})$$</item>
    </list>
    <heading level="4">Solution</heading>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>$$\begin{array}{l} {{(x^{2} + 1)(3x^{2} + 10x + 3)} = {x^{2}(3x^{2} + 10x + 3) + 1(3x^{2} + 10x + 3)}} \\ {\phantom{(x^{2} + 1)(3x^{2} + 10x + 3)} = {3x^{4} + 10x^{3} + 3x^{2} + 3x^{2} + 10x + 3}} \\ {\phantom{(x^{2} + 1)(3x^{2} + 10x + 3)} = {3x^{4} + 10x^{3} + 6x^{2} + 10x + 3}} \end{array}$$</item>
      <item>$$\begin{array}{l} {x\left( {300 - \frac{1}{4}x - \frac{1}{8}y} \right) + y\left( {240 - \frac{1}{8}x - \frac{3}{8}y} \right)} \\ { = 300x - \frac{1}{4}x^{2} - \frac{1}{8}xy + 240y - \frac{1}{8}xy - \frac{3}{8}y^{2}} \\ { = - \frac{1}{4}x^{2} - \frac{3}{8}y^{2} - \frac{1}{4}xy + 300x + 240y} \end{array}$$</item>
      <item>$$\begin{array}{l} {{(e^{t} + e^{- t})e^{t} - e^{t}(e^{t} - e^{- t})} = {e^{2t} + e^{0} - e^{2t} + e^{0}}} \\ {\phantom{(e^{t} + e^{- t})e^{t} - e^{t}(e^{t} - e^{- t})} = {e^{2t} - e^{2t} + e^{0} + e^{0}}} \\ {\phantom{(e^{t} + e^{- t})e^{t} - e^{t}(e^{t} - e^{- t})} = {1 + 1} { \text{Recall that} e^{0} = 1.}} \\ {\phantom{(e^{t} + e^{- t})e^{t} - e^{t}(e^{t} - e^{- t})} = 2} \end{array}$$</item>
    </list>
  </example>

<example number="8">
    <heading level="4">Example 8</heading>
    <paragraph>Factor out the greatest common factor in each expression:</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>$$- 3t^{2} + 3t$$</item>
      <item>$$2x^{3 \slash 2} - 3x^{1 \slash 2}$$</item>
      <item>$$2ye^{xy^{2}} + 2xy^{3}e^{xy^{2}}$$</item>
      <item>$$4x{(x + 1)}^{1 \slash 2} - 2x^{2}\left( \frac{1}{2} \right){(x + 1)}^{- 1 \slash 2}$$</item>
    </list>
    <heading level="4">Solution</heading>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>$$- 3t^{2} + 3t = - 3t(t - 1)$$</item>
      <item>$$2x^{3 \slash 2} - 3x^{1 \slash 2} = x^{1 \slash 2}(2x - 3)$$</item>
      <item>$$2ye^{xy^{2}} + 2xy^{3}e^{xy^{2}} = 2ye^{xy^{2}}(1 + xy^{2})$$</item>
      <item>$$\begin{array}{l} {4x{(x + 1)}^{1 \slash 2} - 2x^{2}\left( \frac{1}{2} \right){(x + 1)}^{- 1 \slash 2} = 4x{(x + 1)}^{1 \slash 2} - x^{2}{(x + 1)}^{- 1 \slash 2}} \\ { = x{(x + 1)}^{- 1 \slash 2}\lbrack 4{(x + 1)}^{1 \slash 2}{(x + 1)}^{1 \slash 2} - x\rbrack} \\ { = x{(x + 1)}^{- 1 \slash 2}\lbrack 4(x + 1) - x\rbrack} \\ { = x{(x + 1)}^{- 1 \slash 2}(4x + 4 - x) = x{(x + 1)}^{- 1 \slash 2}(3x + 4)} \end{array}$$ Here, we select $${(x + 1)}^{- 1 \slash 2}$$ as the greatest common factor because it is the highest power of $$(x + 1)$$ in each algebraic term. In particular, observe that $${(x + 1)}^{- 1 \slash 2}{(x + 1)}^{1 \slash 2}{(x + 1)}^{1 \slash 2} = {(x + 1)}^{- 1 \slash 2 + 1 \slash 2 + 1 \slash 2} = {(x + 1)}^{1 \slash 2}$$</item>
    </list>
  </example>

<example number="9">
    <heading level="4">Example 9</heading>
    <paragraph>Factor:</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>$$2ax + 2ay + bx + by$$</item>
      <item>$$3x\sqrt{y} - 4 - 2\sqrt{y} + 6x$$</item>
    </list>
    <heading level="4">Solution</heading>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>First, factor the common term $$2a$$ from the first two terms and the common term $$b$$ from the last two terms. Thus, $$2\mathit{ax} + 2\mathit{ay} + \mathit{bx} + \mathit{by} = 2a(x + y) + b(x + y)$$ Since $$(x + y)$$ is common to both terms of the polynomial, we may factor it out. Hence $$2a(x + y) + b(x + y) = (2a + b)(x + y)$$</item>
      <item>$$\begin{array}{l} {{3x\sqrt{y} - 4 - 2\sqrt{y} + 6x} = {3x\sqrt{y} - 2\sqrt{y} + 6x - 4 \text{Rearrange terms.} }} \\ {\phantom{3x\sqrt{y} - 4 - 2\sqrt{y} + 6x} = {\sqrt{y}(3x - 2) + 2(3x - 2)} \text{Factor out common factors.} } \\ {\phantom{3x\sqrt{y} - 4 - 2\sqrt{y} + 6x} = {(3x - 2)(\sqrt{y} + 2)}} \end{array}$$</item>
    </list>
  </example>

snippet: Example 10: Example 10 Factor: 3x^{2} + 4x - 4 3x^{2} - 6x - 24 - 3t^{2} + 192t + 195 Solution Using trial and error, we find that the correct factorization is 3x^{2} + 4x - 4 = (3x - 2)(x + 2) Since each term has the common factor 3 , we...
body_xml:
<example number="10">
    <heading level="4">Example 10</heading>
    <paragraph>Factor:</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>$$3x^{2} + 4x - 4$$</item>
      <item>$$3x^{2} - 6x - 24$$</item>
      <item>$$- 3t^{2} + 192t + 195$$</item>
    </list>
    <heading level="4">Solution</heading>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>Using trial and error, we find that the correct factorization is $$3x^{2} + 4x - 4 = (3x - 2)(x + 2)$$</item>
      <item>Since each term has the common factor $$3$$ , we have $$3x^{2} - 6x - 24 = 3(x^{2} - 2x - 8)$$ Using the trial-and-error method of factorization, we find that $$x^{2} - 2x - 8 = (x - 4)(x + 2)$$ Thus, we have $$3x^{2} - 6x - 24 = 3(x - 4)(x + 2)$$</item>
      <item>Since each term has the common factor $$- 3$$ , we have $$- 3t^{2} + 192t + 195 = - 3(t^{2} - 64t - 65)$$ Using the trial-and-error method of factorization, we find that $$(t^{2} - 64t - 65) = (t - 65)(t + 1)$$ Therefore, $$- 3t^{2} + 192t + 195 = - 3(t - 65)(t + 1)$$</item>
    </list>
  </example>

body_xml:
<example number="11">
    <heading level="4">Example 11</heading>
    <paragraph>Solve each of the following quadratic equations:</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>$$2x^{2} + 5x - 12 = 0$$</item>
      <item>$$x^{2} = - 3x + 8$$</item>
    </list>
    <heading level="4">Solution</heading>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>The equation is in standard form, with $$a = 2$$ , $$b = 5$$ , and $$c = - 12$$ . Using the quadratic formula, we find $$\begin{array}{l} {x = {\frac{- b \pm \sqrt{b^{2} - 4ac}}{2a} = \frac{- 5 \pm \sqrt{5^{2} - 4(2)( - 12)}}{2(2)}}} \\ {\phantom{x} = {\frac{- 5 \pm \sqrt{121}}{4} = \frac{- 5 \pm 11}{4}}} \\ {\phantom{x} = {- 4 {or} \frac{3}{2}}} \end{array}$$ This equation can also be solved by factoring. Thus, $$2x^{2} + 5x - 12 = (2x - 3)(x + 4) = 0$$ from which we see that the desired roots are $$x = \frac{3}{2}$$ or $$x = - 4$$ , as obtained earlier.</item>
      <item>We first rewrite the given equation in the standard form $$x^{2} + 3x - 8 = 0$$ , from which we see that $$a = 1$$ , $$b = 3$$ , and $$c = - 8$$ . Using the quadratic formula, we find $$\begin{array}{l} {x = {\frac{- b \pm \sqrt{b^{2} - 4ac}}{2a} = \frac{- 3 \pm \sqrt{3^{2} - 4(1)( - 8)}}{2(1)}}} \\ {\phantom{x} = \frac{- 3 \pm \sqrt{41}}{2}} \end{array}$$ That is, the solutions are $$\frac{- 3 + \sqrt{41}}{2} \approx 1.7$$ and $$\frac{- 3 - \sqrt{41}}{2} \approx - 4.7$$ In this case, the quadratic formula proves quite handy!</item>
    </list>
  </example>

<example number="1">
    <heading level="4">Example 1</heading>
    <paragraph>Simplify the following expressions:</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>$$\frac{x^{2} + 2x - 3}{x^{2} + 4x + 3}$$</item>
      <item>$$\frac{{(x^{2} + 1)}^{2}( - 2) + (2x)(2)(x^{2} + 1)(2x)}{{(x^{2} + 1)}^{4}}$$</item>

    </list>

<example number="3">
    <heading level="4">Example 3</heading>
    <paragraph>Simplify:</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>$$\frac{2x}{x^{2} + 1} + \frac{6(3x^{2})}{x^{3} + 2}$$</item>
      <item>$$\frac{1}{x + h} - \frac{1}{x}$$</item>

      <item>$$\begin{array}{l} {{\frac{1}{x + h} - \frac{1}{x}} = \frac{x - (x + h)}{x(x + h)} {{LCD} = x(x + h)}} \\ {\phantom{\frac{1}{x + h} - \frac{1}{x}} = \frac{x - x - h}{x(x + h)} \text{Remove parentheses.} } \\ {\phantom{\frac{1}{x + h} - \frac{1}{x}} = \frac{- h}{x(x + h)} \text{Combine like terms.} } \end{array}$$</item>
    </list>
  </example>

<example number="4">
    <heading level="4">Example 4</heading>

      <item>$$\begin{array}{l} {\frac{x^{- 1} + y^{- 1}}{x^{- 2} - y^{- 2}} = {\frac{\frac{1}{x} + \frac{1}{y}}{\frac{1}{x^{2}} - \frac{1}{y^{2}}} = \frac{\frac{y + x}{\mathit{xy}}}{\frac{y^{2} - x^{2}}{x^{2}y^{2}}}} {x^{- n} = \frac{1}{x^{n}}}} \\ {\phantom{\frac{x^{- 1} + y^{- 1}}{x^{- 2} - y^{- 2}}} = {\frac{y + x}{\mathit{xy}} \cdot \frac{x^{2}y^{2}}{y^{2} - x^{2}} = \frac{y + x}{\mathit{xy}} \cdot \frac{x^{2}y^{2}}{(y + x)(y - x)}}} \\ {\phantom{\frac{x^{- 1} + y^{- 1}}{x^{- 2} - y^{- 2}}} = \frac{\mathit{xy}}{y - x}} \end{array}$$</item>
    </list>
  </example>

snippet: Example 9: Example 9 Solve the inequality x^{2} + 2x - 8 < 0 . Solution Observe that x^{2} + 2x - 8 = (x + 4)(x - 2) , so the given inequality is equivalent to the inequality (x + 4)(x - 2) < 0 . Since the product of two real numbers is...
body_xml: Example 9 Solve the inequality $$x^{2} + 2x - 8 < 0$$ . Solution Observe that $$x^{2} + 2x - 8 = (x + 4)(x - 2)$$ , so the given inequality is equivalent to the inequality $$(x + 4)(x - 2) < 0$$ . Since the product of two real numbers is negative if and only if the two numbers have opposite signs, we solve the inequality $$(x + 4)(x - 2) < 0$$ by studying the signs of the two factors $$x + 4$$ and $$x - 2$$ . Now, $$x + 4 > 0$$ when $$x > - 4$$ , and $$x + 4 < 0$$ when $$x < - 4$$ . Similarly, $$x - 2 > 0$$ when $$x > 2$$ , and $$x - 2 < 0$$ when $$x < 2$$ . These results are summarized graphically in Figure 2. From Figure 2, we see that the two factors $$x + 4$$ and $$x - 2$$ have opposite signs when and only when $$x$$ lies strictly between $$- 4$$ and $$2$$ . Therefore, the required solution is the interval $$( - 4,2)$$ .

body_xml: Example 10 Solve the inequality $$\frac{x + 1}{x - 1} \geq 0$$ . Solution The quotient $$(x + 1) \slash (x - 1)$$ is strictly positive if and only if both the numerator and the denominator have the same sign. The signs of $$x + 1$$ and $$x - 1$$ are shown in Figure 3. From Figure 3, we see that $$x + 1$$ and $$x - 1$$ have the same sign if $$x < - 1$$ or $$x > 1$$ . The quotient $$(x + 1) \slash (x - 1)$$ is equal to zero if $$x = - 1$$ . Therefore, the required solution is the set of all $$x$$ in the intervals $$( - \infty, - 1\rbrack$$ and $$(1,\infty)$$ .

body_xml: Example 13 Solve the inequalities $$\left| x \middle| \leq 5 \right.$$ and $$\left| x \middle| \geq 5 \right.$$ . Solution First, we consider the inequality $$\left| x \middle| \leq 5 \right.$$ . If $$x \geq 0$$ , then $$\left| x \middle| = x \right.$$ , so $$\left| x \middle| \leq 5 \right.$$ implies $$x \leq 5$$ in this case. On the other hand, if $$x < 0$$ , then $$\left| x \middle| = - x \right.$$ , so $$\left| x \middle| \leq 5 \right.$$ implies $$- x \leq 5$$ or $$x \geq - 5$$ . Thus, $$\left| x \middle| \leq 5 \right.$$ means $$- 5 \leq x \leq 5$$ (Figure 5a). To obtain an alternative solution, observe that $$|x|$$ is the distance from the point $$x$$ to zero, so the inequality $$\left| x \middle| \leq 5 \right.$$ implies immediately that $$- 5 \leq x \leq 5$$ . Next, the inequality $$\left| x \middle| \geq 5 \right.$$ states that the distance from $$x$$ to zero is greater than or equal to $$5$$ . This observation yields the result $$x \geq 5$$ or $$x \leq - 5$$ (Figure 5b).

Determine whether $$L_{1}$$ and $$L_{2}$$ are parallel. title: Example 12
snippet: Example 12: Example 12 Sketch the straight line represented by the equation 3x - 4y - 12 = 0 Does the point \left( 2, - \frac{3}{2} \right) lie on L ? Does the point (1, - 2) lie on L ? Solution Since every straight line is uniquely...
body_xml:
<example number="12">
    <heading level="4">Example 12</heading>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>Sketch the straight line represented by the equation $$3x - 4y - 12 = 0$$</item>
      <item>Does the point $$\left( 2, - \frac{3}{2} \right)$$ lie on $$L$$ ?</item>
      <item>Does the point $$(1, - 2)$$ lie on $$L$$ ?</item>
    </list>
    <heading level="4">Solution</heading>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>Since every straight line is uniquely determined by two distinct points, we need find only two such points through which the line passes in order to sketch it. For convenience, let’s compute the $$x$$ - and $$y$$ -intercepts. Setting $$y = 0$$ , we find $$x = 4$$ ; thus, the $$x$$ -intercept is $$4$$ . Setting $$x = 0$$ gives $$y = - 3$$ , and the $$y$$ -intercept is $$- 3$$ . A sketch of the line appears in Figure 32. Figure 32 Details Two points and a line passing through them are graphed on the x y coordinate plane. The line with a positive slope enters the third quadrant, passes through the point (0, negative 3) on the vertical axis, cuts across the fourth quadrant, and crosses the horizontal axis at (4, 0), and continues into the first quadrant. To sketch $$3x - 4y - 12 = 0$$ , first find the $$x$$ -intercept, $$4$$ , and the $$y$$ -intercept, $$- 3$$ .</item>
      <item>Substituting $$x = 2$$ and $$y = - \frac{3}{2}$$ into the left-hand side of the equation $$3x - 4y - 12 = 0$$ found in part (a), we obtain $$3(2) - 4\left( {- \frac{3}{2}} \right) - 12 = 6 + 6 - 12 = 0$$ This shows that the equation is satisfied, and we conclude that the point $$\left( {2, - \frac{3}{2}} \right)$$ does indeed lie on $$L$$ .</item>
      <item>Substituting $$x = 1$$ and $$y = - 2$$ into the given equation, we obtain $$3(1) - 4( - 2) - 12 = 3 + 8 - 12 = - 1$$ which is not equal to zero, the number on the right-hand side of the equation. This shows that the point $$(1, - 2)$$ does not lie on $$L$$ .</item>
    </list>
  </example>

    <paragraph>Let the function $$f$$ be defined by the rule $$f(x) = {2x}^{2} - x + 1$$ . Find:</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">

title: Example 3
snippet: Example 3: Example 3 Find the domain of each function. f(x) = \sqrt{x - 1} f(x) = \frac{1}{x^{2} - 4} f(x) = x^{2} + 3 Solution Since the square root of a negative number is not a real number, it is necessary that x - 1 \geq 0 . The...
body_xml:
<example number="3">
    <heading level="4">Example 3</heading>
    <paragraph>Find the domain of each function.</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>$$f(x) = \sqrt{x - 1}$$</item>
      <item>$$f(x) = \frac{1}{x^{2} - 4}$$</item>
      <item>$$f(x) = x^{2} + 3$$</item>
    </list>
    <heading level="4">Solution</heading>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>Since the square root of a negative number is not a real number, it is necessary that $$x - 1 \geq 0$$ . The inequality is satisfied by the set of real numbers $$x \geq 1$$ . Thus, the domain of $$f$$ is the interval $$\lbrack 1,\infty)$$ .</item>
      <item>The only restriction on $$x$$ is that $$x^{2} - 4$$ be different from zero, since division by zero is not allowed. But $$(x^{2} - 4) = (x + 2)(x - 2) = 0$$ if $$x = - 2$$ or $$x = 2$$ . Thus, the domain of $$f$$ in this case consists of the intervals $$( - \infty, - 2)$$ , $$( - 2,2)$$ , and $$(2,\infty)$$ .</item>
      <item>Here, any real number satisfies the equation, so the domain of $$f$$ is the set of all real numbers.</item>
    </list>
  </example>

body_xml: Example 5 The graph of a function $$f$$ is shown in Figure 5. What is the value of $$f(3)$$ ? The value of $$f(5)$$ ? What is the height or depth of the point $$\left( 3,f{(3))} \right.$$ from the $$x$$ -axis? The point $$\left( 5,f(5) \right)$$ from the $$x$$ -axis? What is the domain of $$f$$ ? The range of $$f$$ ? Solution From the graph of $$f$$ , we see that $$y = - 2$$ when $$x = 3$$ , and we conclude that $$f(3) = - 2$$ . Similarly, we see that $$f(5) = 3$$ . Since the point $$(3, - 2)$$ lies below the $$x$$ -axis, we see that the depth of the point $$\left( 3,f(3) \right)$$ is $$- f(3) = - ( - 2) = 2$$ units below the $$x$$ -axis. The point $$\left( 5,f(5) \right)$$ lies above the $$x$$ -axis and is located at a height of $$f(5)$$ , or $$3$$ units above the $$x$$ -axis. Observe that $$x$$ may take on all values between $$x = - 1$$ and $$x = 7$$ , inclusive, so the domain of $$f$$ is $$\lbrack - 1,7\rbrack$$ . Next, observe that as $$x$$ takes on all values in the domain of $$f$$ , $$f(x)$$ takes on all values between $$- 2$$ and $$7$$ , inclusive. (You can easily see this by running your index finger along the $$x$$ -axis from $$x = - 1$$ to $$x = 7$$ and observing the corresponding values assumed by the $$y$$ -coordinate of each point of the graph of $$f$$ .) Therefore, the range of $$f$$ is $$\lbrack - 2,7\rbrack$$ .

title: Example 6
snippet: Example 6: Example 6 Sketch the graph of the function defined by the equation y = x^{2} + 1 . What is the range of f ? Solution The domain of the function is the set of all real numbers. By assigning several values to the variable x and...
body_xml:
Example 6 Sketch the graph of the function defined by the equation $$y = x^{2} + 1$$ . What is the range of $$f$$ ? Solution The domain of the function is the set of all real numbers. By assigning several values to the variable $$x$$ and computing the corresponding values for $$y$$ , we obtain the following solutions to the equation $$y = x^{2} + 1$$ : x −3 −2 −1 0 1 2 3 y 10 5 2 1 2 5 10
By plotting these points and then connecting them with a smooth curve, we obtain the graph of $$y = f(x)$$ , which is a parabola (Figure 6). To determine the range of $$f$$ , we observe that $$x^{2} \geq 0$$ if $$x$$ is any real number, and so $$x^{2} + 1 \geq 1$$ for all real numbers $$x$$ . We conclude that the range of $$f$$ is $$\lbrack 1,\infty)$$ . The graph of $$f$$ confirms this result visually.

body_xml:
Example 7 Sketch the graph of the function $$f$$ defined by $$f(x) = \{\begin{array}{lr} {- x} & {{if}x < 0} \\ \sqrt{x} & {{if}x \geq 0} \end{array}$$ Solution The function $$f$$ is defined in a piecewise fashion on the set of all real numbers. In the subdomain $$( - \infty,0)$$ , the rule for $$f$$ is given by $$f(x) = - x$$ . The equation $$y = - x$$ is a linear equation in the slope-intercept form (with slope $$- 1$$ and intercept $$0$$ ). Therefore, the graph of $$f$$ corresponding to the subdomain $$( - \infty,0)$$ is the half-line shown in Figure 7. Next, in the subdomain $$\lbrack 0,\infty)$$ , the rule for $$f$$ is given by $$f(x) = \sqrt{x}$$ . The values of $$f(x)$$ corresponding to $$x = 0$$ , $$1$$ , $$2$$ , $$3$$ , and $$4$$ are shown in the following table: x 0 1 2 3 4 f ( x ) 0 1 $$\sqrt{2}$$ $$\sqrt{3}$$ 2
Using these values, we sketch the graph of the function $$f$$ as shown in Figure 7.

title: The Sum, Difference, Product, and Quotient of Functions

snippet: The Sum, Difference, Product, and Quotient of Functions: The Sum, Difference, Product, and Quotient of Functions Let f and g be functions with domains A and B , respectively. Then the sum f + g , difference f - g , and product \mathit{fg}...
body_xml:
<note type="theorem" source_type="The Sum, Difference, Product, and Quotient of Functions" title="The Sum, Difference, Product, and Quotient of Functions">
    <heading level="4">The Sum, Difference, Product, and Quotient of Functions</heading>
    <paragraph>Let $$f$$ and $$g$$ be functions with domains $$A$$ and $$B$$ , respectively. Then the sum $$f + g$$ , difference $$f - g$$ , and product $$\mathit{fg}$$ of $$f$$ and $$g$$ are functions with domain $$A \cap B$$ * and rule given by</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} {(f + g)(x)} & = & {{f(x) + g(x)} {Sum}} \\ {(f - g)(x)} & = & {{f(x) - g(x)} {Difference}} \\ {\left( \mathit{fg} \right)(x)} & = & {f(x)g(x) {Product}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>$$A \cap B$$ is read “ $$A$$ intersected with $$B$$ ” and denotes the set of all points common to both $$A$$ and $$B$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The quotient $$f \slash g$$ of $$f$$ and $$g$$ has domain $$A \cap B$$ excluding all numbers $$x$$ such that $$g(x) = 0$$ and rule given by</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\left( \frac{f}{g} \right)(x) = \frac{f(x)}{g(x)} {Quotient}$$</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Example 1
snippet: Example 1: Example 1 Let f(x) = \sqrt{x + 1} and g(x) = 2x + 1 . Find the sum s , the difference d , the product p , and the quotient q of the functions f and g . Solution Since the domain of f is A = \lbrack - 1,\infty) and the domain of...
body_xml:
<example number="1">
    <heading level="4">Example 1</heading>
    <paragraph>Let $$f(x) = \sqrt{x + 1}$$ and $$g(x) = 2x + 1$$ . Find the sum $$s$$ , the difference $$d$$ , the product $$p$$ , and the quotient $$q$$ of the functions $$f$$ and $$g$$ .</paragraph>
    <heading level="4">Solution</heading>
    <paragraph>Since the domain of $$f$$ is $$A = \lbrack - 1,\infty)$$ and the domain of $$g$$ is $$B = ( - \infty,\infty)$$ , we see that the domain of $$s$$ , $$d$$ , and $$p$$ is $$A \cap B = \lbrack - 1,\infty)$$ . The rules follow.</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{lll} {s(x)} & = & {(f + g)(x) = f(x) + g(x) = \sqrt{x + 1} + 2x + 1} \\ {d(x)} & = & {(f - g)(x) = f(x) - g(x) = \sqrt{x + 1} - (2x + 1) = \sqrt{x + 1} - 2x - 1} \\ {p(x)} & = & {\left( \mathit{fg} \right)(x) = f(x)g(x) = \sqrt{x + 1}(2x + 1) = (2x + 1)\sqrt{x + 1}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The rule for the quotient function $$q$$ is</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$q(x) = \left( \frac{f}{g} \right)(x) = \frac{f(x)}{g(x)} = \frac{\sqrt{x + 1}}{2x + 1}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Its domain is $$\lbrack - 1,\infty)$$ together with the restriction $$x \neq - \frac{1}{2}$$ . We denote this by $$\left\lbrack - 1, - \frac{1}{2} \right) \cup \left( - \frac{1}{2},\infty \right)$$ .</paragraph>
  </example>

title: The Composition of Two Functions
snippet: The Composition of Two Functions: The Composition of Two Functions Let f and g be functions. Then the composition of g and f is the function g \circ f defined by (g \circ f)(x) = g\left( f(x) \right) The domain of g \circ f is the set of...

<note type="theorem" source_type="The Composition of Two Functions" title="The Composition of Two Functions">
    <heading level="4">The Composition of Two Functions</heading>
    <paragraph>Let $$f$$ and $$g$$ be functions. Then the composition of $$g$$ and $$f$$ is the function $$g \circ f$$ defined by</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$(g \circ f)(x) = g\left( f(x) \right)$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The domain of $$g \circ f$$ is the set of all $$x$$ in the domain of $$f$$ such that $$f(x)$$ lies in the domain of $$g$$ .</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Example 4
snippet: Example 4: Example 4 Let f(x) = x^{2} - 1 and g(x) = \sqrt{x} + 1 . Find: The rule for the composite function g \circ f . The rule for the composite function f \circ g . Solution To find the rule for the composite function g \circ f ,...
body_xml:
<example number="4">
    <heading level="4">Example 4</heading>
    <paragraph>Let $$f(x) = x^{2} - 1$$ and $$g(x) = \sqrt{x} + 1$$ . Find:</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>The rule for the composite function $$g \circ f$$ .</item>
      <item>The rule for the composite function $$f \circ g$$ .</item>
    </list>
    <heading level="4">Solution</heading>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>To find the rule for the composite function $$g \circ f$$ , evaluate the function $$g$$ at $$f(x)$$ . We obtain $$(g \circ f)(x) = g(f(x)) = \sqrt{f(x)} + 1 = \sqrt{x^{2} - 1} + 1$$</item>
      <item>To find the rule for the composite function $$f \circ g$$ , evaluate the function $$f$$ at $$g(x)$$ . Thus, $$\begin{array}{l} {(f \circ g){(x) = f(g(x)) = \left( g(x) \right)^{2} - 1 = \left( \sqrt{x} + 1 \right)^{2} - 1}} \\ {\phantom{(f \circ g)(x)} = x + 2\sqrt{x} + 1 - 1 = x + 2\sqrt{x}} \end{array}$$</item>
    </list>
  </example>

title: Portfolio Todd Kodet
snippet: Portfolio Todd Kodet: Portfolio Todd Kodet Title Senior Vice-President of Supply Institution Earthbound Farm Earthbound Farm is America’s largest grower of organic produce, offering more than 100 varieties of organic salads, vegetables,...
body_xml: Portfolio Todd Kodet Title Senior Vice-President of Supply Institution Earthbound Farm Earthbound Farm is America’s largest grower of organic produce, offering more than $$100$$ varieties of organic salads, vegetables, fruits, and herbs on $$34,000$$ crop acres. As Senior Vice-President of Supply, I am responsible for getting our products into and out of Earthbound Farm. A major part of my work is scheduling plantings for upcoming seasons, matching projected supply to projected demand for any given day and season. I use applied mathematics in every step of my planning to create models for predicting supply and demand. After the sales department provides me with information about projected demand, I take their estimates, along with historical data for expected yields, to determine how much of each organic product we need to plant. There are several factors that I have to think about when I make these determinations. For example, I not only have to consider gross yield per acre of farmland, but also have to calculate average trimming waste per acre, to arrive at net pounds needed per customer. Some of the other variables I consider are the amount of organic land available, the location of the farms, seasonal information (because days to maturity for each of our crops varies greatly depending on the weather), and historical information relating to weeds, pests, and diseases. I emphasize the importance of understanding the mathematics that drives our business plans when I work with my team to analyze the reports they have generated. They need to recognize when the information they have gathered does not make sense so that they can spot errors that could skew our projections. With a sound understanding of mathematics, we are able to create more accurate predictions to help us meet our company’s goals.

body_xml: Example 3 Evaluate the limit of the following functions as $$x$$ approaches the indicated point. $$f(x) = \{\begin{aligned} {- 1} & { {if}x < 0} \\ 1 & { {if}x \geq 0} \end{aligned}$$ ; $$x = 0$$ $$g(x) = \frac{1}{x^{2}}$$ ; $$x = 0$$ Solution The graphs of the functions $$f$$ and $$g$$ are shown in Figure 31. Referring to Figure 31a, we see that no matter how close $$x$$ is to zero, $$f(x)$$ takes on the values $$1$$ or $$- 1$$ , depending on whether $$x$$ is positive or negative. Thus, there is no single real number $$L$$ that $$f(x)$$ approaches as $$x$$ approaches zero. We conclude that the limit of $$f(x)$$ does not exist as $$x$$ approaches zero. Referring to Figure 31b, we see that as $$x$$ approaches zero (from either side), $$g(x)$$ increases without bound and thus does not approach any specific real number. We conclude, accordingly, that the limit of $$g(x)$$ does not exist as $$x$$ approaches zero.

title: Theorem 1. Properties of Limits
snippet: Theorem 1. Properties of Limits: Theorem 1. Properties of Limits Suppose \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}f(x) = L and \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}g(x) = M Then \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}\left\lbrack {f(x)} \right\rbrack^{r} =...
body_xml:
<note type="theorem" source_type="Theorem 1. Properties of Limits" title="Theorem 1. Properties of Limits">
    <heading level="4">Theorem 1. Properties of Limits</heading>
    <paragraph>Suppose</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}f(x) = L$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>and</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}g(x) = M$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Then</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}\left\lbrack {f(x)} \right\rbrack^{r} = {\lbrack{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}f(x)}\rbrack}^{r} = L^{r} {r, \text{a positive constant} }$$</item>
      <item>$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}cf(x) = c\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}f(x) = cL {c, \text{a real number} }$$</item>
      <item>$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}\left\lbrack {f(x) \pm g(x)} \right\rbrack = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}f(x) \pm \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}g(x) = L \pm M$$</item>
      <item>$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}\left\lbrack {f(x)g(x)} \right\rbrack = {\lbrack{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}f(x)}\rbrack}{\lbrack{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}g(x)}\rbrack} = LM$$</item>
      <item>$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}\frac{f(x)}{g(x)} = \frac{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}f(x)}{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}g(x)} = \frac{L}{M} { \text{Provided that} M \neq 0}$$</item>
    </list>
  </note>

snippet: Example 4: Example 4 Use Theorem 1 to evaluate the following limits. \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 2}x^{3} \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 4}5x^{3 \slash 2} \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1}{({5x^{4} - 2})} \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 3}2x^{3}\sqrt{x^{2} +...
body_xml:
<example number="4">
    <heading level="4">Example 4</heading>
    <paragraph>Use Theorem 1 to evaluate the following limits.</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 2}x^{3}$$</item>
      <item>$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 4}5x^{3 \slash 2}$$</item>
      <item>$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1}{({5x^{4} - 2})}$$</item>
      <item>$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 3}2x^{3}\sqrt{x^{2} + 7}$$</item>
      <item>$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 2}\frac{2x^{2} + 1}{x + 1}$$</item>
    </list>
    <heading level="4">Solution</heading>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>$$\begin{array}{l} {\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 2}x^{3} = {\lbrack{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 2}x}\rbrack}^{3} { \text{Property} 1}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 2}x^{3}} = 2^{3} = 8 {\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 2}x = 2}} \end{array}$$</item>
      <item>$$\begin{array}{l} {\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 4}5x^{3 \slash 2} = 5{\lbrack{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 4}x^{3 \slash 2}}\rbrack} { \text{Property} 2}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 2}5x^{3 \slash 2}} = 5(4)^{3 \slash 2} = 40 { \text{Property} 1}} \end{array}$$</item>
      <item>$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1}{({5x^{4} - 2})} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1}5x^{4} - \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1}2 { \text{Property} 3}$$ To evaluate $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1}2$$ , observe that the constant function $$g(x) = 2$$ has value $$2$$ for all values of $$x$$ . Therefore, $$g(x)$$ must approach the limit $$2$$ as $$x$$ approaches $$1$$ (or any other point for that matter!). Therefore, $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1}{({5x^{4} - 2})} = 5(1)^{4} - 2 = 3$$</item>
      <item>$$\begin{array}{l} {\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 3}2x^{3}\sqrt{x^{2} + 7} = 2\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 3}x^{3}\sqrt{x^{2} + 7} { \text{Property} 2}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1}2x^{3}\sqrt{x^{2} + 7}} = 2\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 3}x^{3}\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 3}\sqrt{x^{2} + 7} { \text{Property} 4}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1}2x^{3}\sqrt{x^{2} + 7}} = 2(3)^{3}\sqrt{3^{2} + 7} {{Properties}1{and}3}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1}2x^{3}\sqrt{x^{2} + 7}} = 2(27)\sqrt{16} = 216} \end{array}$$</item>
      <item>$$\begin{array}{l} {\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 2}\frac{2x^{2} + 1}{x + 1} = \frac{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 2}\left( {2x^{2} + 1} \right)}{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 2}\left( {x + 1} \right)} { \text{Property} 5}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 2}\frac{2x^{2} + 1}{x + 1}} = \frac{2(2)^{2} + 1}{2 + 1} = \frac{9}{3} = 3} \end{array}$$</item>
    </list>
  </example>

title: Example 5
snippet: Example 5: Example 5 Evaluate: \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 2}\frac{4{({x^{2} - 4})}}{x - 2} Solution Since both the numerator and the denominator of this expression approach zero as x approaches 2 , we have the indeterminate form 0 \slash 0...
body_xml: Example 5 Evaluate: $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 2}\frac{4{({x^{2} - 4})}}{x - 2}$$ Solution Since both the numerator and the denominator of this expression approach zero as $$x$$ approaches $$2$$ , we have the indeterminate form $$0 \slash 0$$ . We rewrite $$\frac{4{({x^{2} - 4})}}{x - 2} = \frac{4\left( {x - 2} \right)\left( {x + 2} \right)}{\left( {x - 2} \right)}$$ which, upon cancellation of the common factors, is equivalent to $$4(x + 2)$$ , provided that $$x \neq 2$$ . Next, we replace $$4(x^{2} - 4) \slash (x - 2)$$ with $$4(x + 2)$$ and find that $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 2}\frac{4{({x^{2} - 4})}}{x - 2} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 2}4\left( {x + 2} \right) = 16$$ The graphs of the functions $$f(x) = \frac{4{({x^{2} - 4})}}{x - 2}$$ and $$g(x) = 4(x + 2)$$ are shown in Figure 32. Observe that the graphs are identical except when $$x = 2$$ . The function $$g$$ is defined for all values of $$x$$ and, in particular, its value at $$x = 2$$ is $$g(2) = 4(2 + 2) = 16$$ . Thus, the point $$(2,16)$$ is on the graph of $$g$$ . However, the function $$f$$ is not defined at $$x = 2$$ . Since $$f(x) = g(x)$$ for all values of $$x$$ except $$x = 2$$ , it follows that the graph of $$f$$ must look exactly like the graph of $$g$$ , with the exception that the point $$(2,16)$$ is missing from the graph of $$f$$ . This illustrates graphically why we can evaluate the limit of $$f$$ by evaluating the limit of the “equivalent” function $$g$$ .

title: Example 6
snippet: Example 6: Example 6 Evaluate: \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{\sqrt{1 + h} - 1}{h} Solution Letting h approach zero, we obtain the indeterminate form 0 \slash 0 . Next, we rationalize the numerator of the quotient by multiplying both...
body_xml:
<example number="6">
    <heading level="4">Example 6</heading>
    <paragraph>Evaluate:</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{\sqrt{1 + h} - 1}{h}$$</paragraph>
    <heading level="4">Solution</heading>
    <paragraph>Letting $$h$$ approach zero, we obtain the indeterminate form $$0 \slash 0$$ . Next, we rationalize the numerator of the quotient by multiplying both the numerator and the denominator by the expression $$({\sqrt{1 + h} + 1})$$ , obtaining</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {\frac{\sqrt{1 + h} - 1}{h} = \frac{({\sqrt{1 + h} - 1})({\sqrt{1 + h} + 1})}{h{({\sqrt{1 + h} + 1})}} {({\sqrt{a} - \sqrt{b}})({\sqrt{a} + \sqrt{b}}) = a - b}} \\ {\phantom{\frac{\sqrt{1 + h} - 1}{h}} = \frac{1 + h - 1}{h{({\sqrt{1 + h} + 1})}}} \\ {\phantom{\frac{\sqrt{1 + h} - 1}{h}} = \frac{h}{h{({\sqrt{1 + h} + 1})}}} \\ {\phantom{\frac{\sqrt{1 + h} - 1}{h}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1 + h} + 1}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <note type="theorem" source_type="">
      <heading level="4">Algebra</heading>
      <paragraph>See Example 7.</paragraph>
    </note>
    <note type="theorem" source_type="">
      <heading level="4">Algebra</heading>
      <paragraph>The algebra icon is used to indicate that the algebraic computation or problem-solving skill used in the example is reviewed on the referenced page. For instance, in Example 6, if you refer to Example 7, you will find a review of the process of rationalizing an algebraic fraction. This is followed by a worked example in which the numerator of the expression $$\frac{\sqrt{1 + h} - 1}{h}$$ is rationalized.</paragraph>
    </note>
    <paragraph>Therefore,</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{\sqrt{1 + h} - 1}{h} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{1}{\sqrt{1 + h} + 1} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1} + 1} = \frac{1}{2}$$</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Example 8

body_xml: Example 8 Evaluate: $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{x^{2} - x + 3}{2x^{3} + 1}$$ Solution Since the limits of both the numerator and the denominator do not exist as $$x$$ approaches infinity, the property pertaining to the limit of a quotient (Property 5) is not applicable. Let’s divide the numerator and denominator of the rational expression by $$x^{3}$$ , obtaining $$\begin{array}{l} {\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{x^{2} - x + 3}{2x^{3} + 1} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{\frac{1}{x} - \frac{1}{x^{2}} + \frac{3}{x^{3}}}{2 + \frac{1}{x^{3}}}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{x^{2} - x + 3}{2x^{3} + 1}} = \frac{0 - 0 + 0}{2 + 0} = \frac{0}{2}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{x^{2} - x + 3}{2x^{3} + 1}} = 0} \end{array}$$ Use Theorem 2.

title: Example 9

body_xml: Example 9 Let $$f(x) = \frac{3x^{2} + 8x - 4}{2x^{2} + 4x - 5}$$ Compute $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}f(x)$$ if it exists. Solution Again, we see that Property 5 is not applicable. Dividing the numerator and the denominator by $$x^{2}$$ , we obtain $$\begin{array}{l} {\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{3x^{2} + 8x - 4}{2x^{2} + 4x - 5} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{3 + \frac{8}{x} - \frac{4}{x^{2}}}{2 + \frac{4}{x} - \frac{5}{x^{2}}}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{3x^{2} + 8x - 4}{2x^{2} + 4x - 5}} = \frac{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}3 + 8\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{x} - 4\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{x^{2}}}{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}2 + 4\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{x} - 5\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{x^{2}}}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{3x^{2} + 8x - 4}{2x^{2} + 4x - 5}} = \frac{3 + 0 - 0}{2 + 0 - 0}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{3x^{2} + 8x - 4}{2x^{2} + 4x - 5}} = \frac{3}{2}} \end{array}$$ Use Theorem 2.

title: Example 10
snippet: Example 10: Example 10 Let f(x) = \frac{2x^{3} - 3x^{2} + 1}{x^{2} + 2x + 4} and evaluate: \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}f(x) \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - \infty}f(x) Solution Dividing the numerator and the denominator of the rational...
body_xml:
<example number="10">
    <heading level="4">Example 10</heading>
    <paragraph>Let $$f(x) = \frac{2x^{3} - 3x^{2} + 1}{x^{2} + 2x + 4}$$ and evaluate:</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}f(x)$$</item>
      <item>$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - \infty}f(x)$$</item>
    </list>
    <heading level="4">Solution</heading>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>Dividing the numerator and the denominator of the rational expression by $$x^{2}$$ , we obtain $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{2x^{3} - 3x^{2} + 1}{x^{2} + 2x + 4} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{2x - 3 + \frac{1}{x^{2}}}{1 + \frac{2}{x} + \frac{4}{x^{2}}}$$ Since the numerator becomes arbitrarily large, whereas the denominator approaches $$1$$ as $$x$$ approaches infinity, we see that the quotient $$f(x)$$ gets larger and larger as $$x$$ approaches infinity. In other words, the limit does not exist. In this case, we indicate this by writing $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow\infty}\frac{2x^{3} - 3x^{2} + 1}{x^{2} + 2x + 4} = \infty$$</item>
      <item>Once again, dividing both the numerator and the denominator by $$x^{2}$$ , we obtain $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - \infty}\frac{2x^{3} - 3x^{2} + 1}{x^{2} + 2x + 4} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - \infty}\frac{2x - 3 + \frac{1}{x^{2}}}{1 + \frac{2}{x} + \frac{4}{x^{2}}}$$ In this case, the numerator becomes arbitrarily large in magnitude but negative in sign, whereas the denominator approaches $$1$$ as $$x$$ approaches negative infinity. Therefore, the quotient $$f(x)$$ decreases without bound, and the limit does not exist. In this case, we indicate this by writing $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow - \infty}\frac{2x^{3} - 3x^{2} + 1}{x^{2} + 2x + 4} = - \infty$$</item>
    </list>
  </example>

<example number="1">
    <heading level="4">Example 1</heading>
    <paragraph>Let $$f(x) = \frac{x^{3} - 1}{x - 1}$$ .</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>Plot the graph of $$f$$ in the viewing window $$\lbrack - 2,2\rbrack \times \lbrack 0,4\rbrack$$ .</item>
      <item>Use zoom to find $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1} = \frac{x^{3} - 1}{x - 1}$$ .</item>
      <item>Verify your result by evaluating the limit algebraically.</item>
    </list>
    <heading level="4">Solution</heading>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>The graph of $$f$$ in the viewing window $$\lbrack - 2,2\rbrack \times \lbrack 0,4\rbrack$$ is shown in Figure T1a. Figure T1 Details A U shaped curve is graphed on a coordinate plane and a display screen displays data. In the graph labeled a, the horizontal axis ranges from negative 2 to over 2 and the vertical axis ranges from 0 to 4. The curve enters the second quadrant from the top left of the viewing window, slopes downward reaches its lowest peak at the coordinate approximately (negative 0.5, 0.9), bends upward, slopes to the right, crosses the vertical axis at the coordinate (0, 1) to enter the first quadrant and continues to slope upward to the right to exit the first quadrant at the top right of the viewing window. The display screen labeled b reads, Line 1: Plot 1 Plot 2 Plot 3 Line 2: Y_1 = (X^3 minus 1) / (X minus 1) Line 3: \Y_2 = Line 4: \Y_3 = Line 5: \Y_4 = Line 6: \Y_5 = Line 7: \Y_6 = (a) The graph of $$f(x) = {(x^{3} - 1)}/(x - 1)$$ in the viewing window $$\lbrack - 2,2\rbrack \times \lbrack 0,4\rbrack$$ ; (b) the TI-83/84 equation screen</item>
      <item>Using zoom-in repeatedly, we see that the $$y$$ -value approaches $$3$$ as the $$x$$ -value approaches $$1$$ . We conclude, accordingly, that $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1}\frac{x^{3} - 1}{x - 1} = 3$$</item>
      <item>We compute $$\begin{array}{l} {\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1}\frac{x^{3} - 1}{x - 1} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1}\frac{({x - 1})({x^{2} + x + 1})}{x - 1}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1}\frac{x^{3} - 1}{x - 1}} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 1}{({x^{2} + x + 1})} = 3} \end{array}$$</item>
    </list>
  </example>

body_xml: Example 2 Use zoom to find $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0}{\left( {1 + x} \right)}^{1 \slash x}$$ . Solution We first plot the graph of $$f(x) = \left( {1 + x} \right)^{1 \slash x}$$ in a suitable viewing window. Figure T2a shows a plot of $$f$$ in the window $$\lbrack - 1,1\rbrack \times \lbrack 0,4\rbrack$$ . Using zoom-in repeatedly, we see that $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0} = \left( {1 + x} \right)^{1 \slash x} \approx 2.71828$$ The limit of $$f(x) = \left( {1 + x} \right)^{1 \slash x}$$ as $$x$$ approaches zero, denoted by the letter $$e$$ , plays a very important role in the study of mathematics and its applications (see Section 5.6). Thus, $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0}\left( {1 + x} \right)^{1 \slash x} = e$$ where, as we have just seen, $$e \approx 2.71828$$ .

<example number="1">
    <heading level="4">Example 1</heading>
    <paragraph>Let</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$f(x) = \begin{cases} {- x} & { {if}x \leq 0} \\ \sqrt{x} & { {if}x > 0} \end{cases}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>and</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$g(x) = \left\{ \begin{aligned} {- 1} & { {if}x < 0} \\ 1 & { {if}x \geq 0} \end{aligned} \right.$$</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>Show that $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0}f(x)$$ exists by studying the one-sided limits of $$f$$ as $$x$$ approaches $$x = 0$$ .</item>
      <item>Show that $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0}g(x)$$ does not exist.</item>
    </list>
    <heading level="4">Solution</heading>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>For $$x \leq 0$$ , $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{-}}f(x) = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{-}}( - x) = 0$$ and for $$x > 0$$ , we find $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{+}}f(x) = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{+}}\sqrt{x} = 0$$ Thus, $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0}f(x) = 0$$ (Figure 38a).</item>
      <item>We have $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{-}}g(x) = - 1$$ and $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0^{+}}g(x) = 1$$ and since these one-sided limits are not equal, we conclude that $$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0}g(x)$$ does not exist (Figure 38b). body_xml: Example 2 Find the values of $$x$$ for which each function is continuous. $$f(x) = x + 2$$ $$g(x) = \frac{x^{2} - 4}{x - 2}$$ $$h(x) = \begin{cases} {x + 2} & { {if}x \neq 2} \\ 1 & { {if}x = 2} \end{cases}$$ $$F(x) = \left\{ \begin{aligned} {- 1} & { {if}x < 0} \\ 1 & { {if}x \geq 0} \end{aligned} \right.$$ $$G(x) = \left\{ \begin{aligned} \frac{1}{x} & { {if}x > 0} \\ {- 1} & { {if}x \leq 0} \end{aligned} \right.$$ The graph of each function is shown in Figure 41. Solution The function $$f$$ is continuous everywhere because the three conditions for continuity are satisfied for all values of $$x$$ . The function $$g$$ is discontinuous at $$x = 2$$ because $$g$$ is not defined at that number. It is continuous everywhere else. The function $$h$$ is discontinuous at $$x = 2$$ because the third condition for continuity is violated; the limit of $$h(x)$$ as $$x$$ approaches $$2$$ exists and has the value $$4$$ , but this limit is not equal to $$h(2) = 1$$ . It is continuous for all other values of $$x$$ . The function $$F$$ is continuous everywhere except at $$x = 0$$ , where the limit of $$F(x)$$ fails to exist as $$x$$ approaches zero (see Example 3a, Section 2.4). Since the limit of $$G(x)$$ does not exist as $$x$$ approaches zero, we conclude that $$G$$ fails to be continuous at $$x = 0$$ . The function $$G$$ is continuous everywhere else.

<example number="3">
    <heading level="4">Example 3</heading>
    <paragraph>Find the values of $$x$$ for which each function is continuous.</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>$$f(x) = {3x}^{3} + {2x}^{2} - x + 10$$</item>
      <item>$$g(x) = \frac{8x^{10} - 4x + 1}{x^{2} + 1}$$</item>
      <item>$$h(x) = \frac{4x^{3} - 3x^{2} + 1}{x^{2} - 3x + 2}$$</item>
    </list>
    <heading level="4">Solution</heading>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>The function $$f$$ is a polynomial function of degree $$3$$ , so $$f(x)$$ is continuous for all values of $$x$$ .</item>
      <item>The function $$g$$ is a rational function. Observe that the denominator of $$g$$ —namely, $$x^{2} + 1$$ —is never equal to zero. Therefore, we conclude that $$g$$ is continuous for all values of $$x$$ .</item>
      <item>The function $$h$$ is a rational function. In this case, however, the denominator of $$h$$ is equal to zero at $$x = 1$$ and $$x = 2$$ , which can be seen by factoring it. Thus, $$x^{2} - 3x + 2 = (x - 2)(x - 1)$$ We therefore conclude that $$h$$ is continuous everywhere except at $$x = 1$$ and $$x = 2$$ , where it is discontinuous.</item>
    </list>
  </example>

body_xml:
<example number="5">
    <heading level="4">Example 5</heading>
    <paragraph>Let $$f(x) = x^{3} + x + 1$$ .</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>Show that $$f$$ is continuous for all values of $$x$$ .</item>
      <item>Compute $$f( - 1)$$ and $$f(1)$$ , and use the results to deduce that there must be at least one number $$x = c$$ , where $$c$$ lies in the interval $$( - 1,1)$$ and $$f(c) = 0$$ .</item>
    </list>
    <heading level="4">Solution</heading>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>The function $$f$$ is a polynomial function of degree $$3$$ and is therefore continuous everywhere.</item>
      <item>$$f{( - 1)} = {( - 1)}^{3} + {( - 1)} + 1 = - 1$$ and $$f{(1)} = 1^{3} + 1 + 1 = 3$$ Since $$f( - 1)$$ and $$f(1)$$ have opposite signs, Theorem 5 tells us that there must be at least one number $$x = c$$ with $$- 1 < c < 1$$ such that $$f(c) = 0$$ .</item>

title: Example 6
snippet: Example 6: Example 6 Let f(x) = x^{3} + x - 1 . Since f is a polynomial function, it is continuous everywhere. Observe that f(0) = - 1 and f(1) = 1 , so Theorem 5 guarantees the existence of at least one root of the equation f(x) = 0 in...
body_xml:
Example 6 Let $$f(x) = x^{3} + x - 1$$ . Since $$f$$ is a polynomial function, it is continuous everywhere. Observe that $$f(0) = - 1$$ and $$f(1) = 1$$ , so Theorem 5 guarantees the existence of at least one root of the equation $$f(x) = 0$$ in $$(0,1)$$ .* It can be shown that $$f$$ has precisely one zero in $$(0,1)$$ (see Exercise 110, Section 4.1). We can locate the root more precisely by using Theorem 5 once again as follows: Evaluate $$f(x)$$ at the midpoint of $$\lbrack 0,1\rbrack$$ , obtaining $$f(0.5) = - 0.375$$ Because $$f(0.5) < 0$$ and $$f(1) > 0$$ , Theorem 5 now tells us that the root must lie in $$(0.5,1)$$ . Repeat the process: Evaluate $$f(x)$$ at the midpoint of $$\lbrack 0.5,1\rbrack$$ , which is $$\frac{0.5 + 1}{2} = 0.75$$ Thus, $$f(0.75) \approx 0.1719$$ Because $$f(0.5) < 0$$ and $$f(0.75) > 0$$ , Theorem 5 tells us that the root is in $$(0.5,0.75)$$ . This process can be continued. Table 3 summarizes the results of our computations through nine steps. Table 3 Step Root of $$\mathbf{f}\left( \mathbf{x} \right) = 0$$ Lies in 1 (0, 1) 2 (0.5, 1) 3 (0.5, 0.75) 4 (0.625, 0.75) 5 (0.625, 0.6875) 6 (0.65625, 0.6875) 7 (0.671875, 0.6875) 8 (0.6796875, 0.6875) 9 (0.6796875, 0.6835937)
From Table 3, we see that the root is approximately $$0.68$$ , accurate to two decimal places. By continuing the process through a sufficient number of steps, we can obtain as accurate an approximation to the root as we please.

title: Example 2
snippet: Example 2: Example 2 Find the slope of the tangent line to the graph of f(x) = 3x + 5 at any point \left( x,f(x) \right) . Solution The slope of the tangent line at any point on the graph of f is given by the derivative of f at x . To find...
body_xml:
<example number="2">
    <heading level="4">Example 2</heading>
    <paragraph>Find the slope of the tangent line to the graph of $$f(x) = 3x + 5$$ at any point $$\left( x,f(x) \right)$$ .</paragraph>
    <heading level="4">Solution</heading>
    <paragraph>The slope of the tangent line at any point on the graph of $$f$$ is given by the derivative of $$f$$ at $$x$$ . To find the derivative, we use the four-step process:</paragraph>
    <heading level="4">Step 1</heading>
    <paragraph>$$f(x + h) = 3(x + h) + 5 = 3x + 3h + 5$$</paragraph>
    <heading level="4">Step 2</heading>
    <paragraph>$$f(x + h) - f(x) = (3x + 3h + 5) - (3x + 5) = 3h$$</paragraph>
    <heading level="4">Step 3</heading>
    <paragraph>$$\frac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{h} = \frac{3h}{h} = 3$$</paragraph>
    <heading level="4">Step 4</heading>
    <paragraph>$$f^{\prime}(x) = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{h} = \underset{h\rightarrow 0}{\lim 3} = 3$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>We expect this result, since the tangent line to any point on a straight line must coincide with the line itself and therefore must have the same slope as the line. In this case, the graph of $$f$$ is a straight line with slope 3.</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Example 3
snippet: Example 3: Example 3 Let f(x) = x^{2} . Find f^{\prime}(x) . Compute f^{\prime}(2) and interpret your result. Solution To find f^{\prime}(x) , we use the four-step process: Step 1 f(x + h) = (x + h)^{2} = x^{2} + 2xh + h^{2} Step 2 f(x +...
body_xml: Example 3 Let $$f(x) = x^{2}$$ . Find $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ . Compute $$f^{\prime}(2)$$ and interpret your result. Solution To find $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ , we use the four-step process: Step 1 $$f(x + h) = (x + h)^{2} = x^{2} + 2xh + h^{2}$$ Step 2 $$f(x + h) - f(x) = x^{2} + 2xh + h^{2} - x^{2} = 2xh + h^{2} = h(2x + h)$$ Step 3 $$\frac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{h} = \frac{h(2x + h)}{h} = 2x + h$$ Step 4 $$f^{\prime}{(x)} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{f(x + h) - f{(x)}}{h} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}(2x + h) = 2x$$ $$f^{\prime}(2) = 2(2) = 4$$ . This result tells us that the slope of the tangent line to the graph of $$f$$ at the point $$(2,4)$$ is $$4$$ . It also tells us that the function $$f$$ is changing at the rate of $$4$$ units per unit change in $$x$$ at $$x = 2$$ . The graph of $$f$$ and the tangent line at $$(2,4)$$ are shown in Figure 55.

title: Example 4
snippet: Example 4: Example 4 Let f(x) = x^{2} - 4x . Find f^{\prime}(x) . Find the point on the graph of f where the tangent line to the curve is horizontal. Sketch the graph of f and the tangent line to the curve at the point found in part (b)....
body_xml:
<example number="4">
    <heading level="4">Example 4</heading>
    <paragraph>Let $$f(x) = x^{2} - 4x$$ .</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>Find $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ .</item>
      <item>Find the point on the graph of $$f$$ where the tangent line to the curve is horizontal.</item>
      <item>Sketch the graph of $$f$$ and the tangent line to the curve at the point found in part (b).</item>
      <item>What is the rate of change of $$f$$ at this point?</item>
    </list>
    <heading level="4">Solution</heading>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>To find $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ , we use the four-step process: Step 1 $$f\left( {x + h} \right) = \left( {x + h} \right)^{2} - 4\left( {x + h} \right) = x^{2} + 2xh + h^{2} - 4x - 4h$$ Step 2 $$\begin{array}{l} {f\left( {x + h} \right) - f(x) = x^{2} + 2xh + h^{2} - 4x - 4h - {({x^{2} - 4x})}} \\ {\phantom{f\left( {x + h} \right) - f(x)} = 2\mathit{xh} + h^{2} - 4h = h\left( {2x + h - 4} \right)} \end{array}$$ Step 3 $$\frac{f{({x + h})} - f{(x)}}{h} = \frac{h{({2x + h - 4})}}{h} = 2x + h - 4$$ Step 4 $$f^{\prime}{(x)} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{f{({x + h})} - f{(x)}}{h} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}{({2x + h - 4})} = 2x - 4$$</item>
      <item>At a point on the graph of $$f$$ where the tangent line to the curve is horizontal and hence has slope zero, the derivative $$f^{\prime}$$ of $$f$$ is zero. Accordingly, to find such point(s), we set $$f^{\prime}(x) = 0$$ , which gives $$2x - 4 = 0$$ or $$x = 2$$ . The corresponding value of $$y$$ is given by $$y = f(2) = - 4$$ , and the required point is $$(2, - 4)$$ .</item>
      <item>The graph of $$f$$ and the tangent line are shown in Figure 56. Figure 56 Details A curve y = x^2 minus 4 x, an open upward parabola with its vertex at (2, negative 4) and its tangent y = negative 4 are graphed in the x y coordinate plane. The x axis ranges from around negative 1 to about 5 units. The y axis ranges from below negative 5 to over 3 units. The curve enters the second quadrant at around (negative 0.8, 3.5), descends downward to the right,, passes through the origin, descends downward into the fourth quadrant, inflects at (2, negative 4), and rises upward to the right, bulging away from the y axis. The curve then cuts the x axis at (4, 0) and continues rising upward to the right, into the first quadrant. A horizontal line y = negative 4 runs to the right, parallel to the x axis enters the third quadrant, cuts the y axis at the negative 4 mark, touches the curve at (2, negative 4) as it continues into the fourth quadrant. The tangent line to the graph of $$y = x^{2} - 4x$$ at $$\left( {2, - 4} \right)$$ is $$y = - 4$$ .</item>
      <item>The rate of change of $$f$$ at $$x = 2$$ is zero.</item>
    </list>
  </example>

title: Example 5
snippet: Example 5: Example 5 Let f(x) = \frac{1}{x} . Find f^{\prime}(x) . Find the slope of the tangent line T to the graph of f at the point where x = 1 . Find an equation of the tangent line T in part (b). Solution To find f^{\prime}(x) , we...
body_xml:
<example number="5">
    <heading level="4">Example 5</heading>
    <paragraph>Let $$f(x) = \frac{1}{x}$$ .</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>Find $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ .</item>
      <item>Find the slope of the tangent line $$T$$ to the graph of $$f$$ at the point where $$x = 1$$ .</item>
      <item>Find an equation of the tangent line $$T$$ in part (b).</item>
    </list>
    <heading level="4">Solution</heading>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>To find $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ , we use the four-step process: Step 1 $$f\left( {x + h} \right) = \frac{1}{x + h}$$ Step 2 $$f{({x + h})} - f{(x)} = \frac{1}{x + h} - \frac{1}{x} = \frac{x - {({x + h})}}{x{({x + h})}} = - \frac{h}{x{({x + h})}}$$ Algebra See Example 3. Step 3 $$\frac{f{({x + h})} - f{(x)}}{h} = - \frac{h}{x{({x + h})}} \cdot \frac{1}{h} = - \frac{1}{x{({x + h})}}$$ Algebra See Example 3. Step 4 $$f^{\prime}{(x)} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{f{({x + h})} - f{(x)}}{h} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0} - \frac{h}{x{({x + h})}} = - \frac{1}{x^{2}}$$</item>
      <item>The slope of the tangent line $$T$$ to the graph of $$f$$ where $$x = 1$$ is given by $$f^{\prime}(1) = - 1$$ .</item>
      <item>When $$x = 1$$ , $$y = f(1) = 1$$ and $$T$$ is tangent to the graph of $$f$$ at the point $$(1,1)$$ . From part (b), we know that the slope of $$T$$ is $$- 1$$ . Thus, an equation of $$T$$ is $$\begin{array}{rcl} {y - 1} & = & {- 1\left( {x - 1} \right)} \\ y & = & {- x + 2} \end{array}$$ (Figure 57). Figure 57 Details A curve y = 1/x and a line y = negative x + 2 are graphed on the x y coordinate plane. The curve has two parts. One part of the curve is entirely in the third quadrant and enters close to the negative x axis almost parallel to it, veering off the axis at around (negative 4, 0.25), descends to the right bulging towards the origin, continues to descend downward steeply, becoming almost parallel to the negative y axis as it descends downward. The second part of the curve lies entirely in the first quadrant, enters close the to the y axis, almost parallel to it, increasingly veering off the y axis from about (0.2, 4), descends to the right, passing through a low point (1, 1) bulging towards the origin, descends to the right, running almost parallel to the x axis as it proceeds further to the right. The tangent to the curve y = negative x + 2, descends into the second quadrant at around (2.8, 5), slopes downward to the right, cuts the y axis at (0, 3), touches the curve at (1, 1), cuts the x axis at (2, 0) and then proceeds to slope downward into the fourth quadrant. The tangent line to the graph of $$f(x) = 1 \slash x$$ at $$(1,1)$$</item>
    </list>
  </example>

body_xml: Example 9 Figure 61 depicts a portion of the graph of a function. Explain why the function fails to be differentiable at each of the numbers $$x = a,b,c,d,e,f$$ , and $$g$$ . Solution The function fails to be differentiable at $$x = a,b$$ , and $$c$$ because it is discontinuous at each of these numbers. The derivative of the function does not exist at $$x = d,e$$ , and $$f$$ because it has a kink at each point on the graph corresponding to these numbers. Finally, the function is not differentiable at $$x = g$$ because the tangent line is vertical at the corresponding point on the graph.

    <paragraph>Find the derivatives of the following functions:</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>$$f(x) = 4x^{5} + 3x^{4} - 8x^{2} + x + 3$$</item>
      <item>$$g(t) = \frac{t^{2}}{5} + \frac{5}{t^{3}}$$</item>
    </list>
    <heading level="4">Solution</heading>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>$$\begin{array}{l} {f^{\prime}(x) = \frac{d}{dx}(4x^{5} + 3x^{4} - 8x^{2} + x + 3)} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}(x)} = \frac{d}{dx}(4x^{5}) + \frac{d}{dx}(3x^{4}) - \frac{d}{dx}(8x^{2}) + \frac{d}{dx}(x) + \frac{d}{dx}(3)} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}(x)} = 20x^{4} + 12x^{3} - 16x + 1} \end{array}$$</item>
      <item>Here, the independent variable is $$t$$ instead of $$x$$ , so we differentiate with respect to $$t$$ . Thus, $$\begin{array}{l} {g^{\prime}(t) = \frac{d}{dt}\left( \frac{1}{5}t^{2} + 5t^{- 3} \right) { \text{Rewrite} \frac{1}{t^{3}} \text{as} t^{- 3}.}} \\ {\phantom{g^{\prime}(t)} = \frac{2}{5}t - 15t^{- 4} = \frac{2}{5}t - \frac{15}{t^{4}} { \text{Rewrite} t^{- 4} \text{as} \frac{1}{t^{4}}.}} \\ {\phantom{g^{\prime}(t)} = \frac{2t^{5} - 75}{5t^{4}}} \end{array}$$</item>
    </list>
  </example>

body_xml: Example 6 Find the slope and an equation of the tangent line to the graph of $$f(x) = 2x + 1 \slash \sqrt{x}$$ at the point $$(1,3)$$ . Solution The slope of the tangent line at any point on the graph of $$f$$ is given by $$\begin{array}{l} {f^{\prime}(x) = \frac{d}{dx}\left( 2x + \frac{1}{\sqrt{x}} \right)} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}(x)} = \frac{d}{dx}(2x + x^{- 1 \slash 2}) { \text{Rewrite} \frac{1}{\sqrt{x}} \text{as} \frac{1}{x^{1 \slash 2}} = x^{- 1 \slash 2}.}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}(x)} = 2 - \frac{1}{2}x^{- 3 \slash 2} \text{Use the Sum Rule.} } \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}(x)} = 2 - \frac{1}{2x^{3 \slash 2}} { \text{Rewrite} \frac{1}{2}x^{- 3 \slash 2} \text{as} \frac{1}{2x^{3 \slash 2}}.}} \end{array}$$ In particular, the slope of the tangent line to the graph of $$f$$ at $$(1,3)$$ (where $$x = 1$$ ) is $$f^{\prime}(1) = 2 - \frac{1}{2(1^{3 \slash 2})} = 2 - \frac{1}{2} = \frac{3}{2}$$ Using the point-slope form of an equation of a line with slope $$\frac{3}{2}$$ and the point $$\left( {1,3} \right)$$ , we see that an equation of the tangent line is $$y - 3 = \frac{3}{2}(x - 1) {y - y_{1} = m(x - x_{1})}$$ Algebra See Example 5. or, upon simplification, $$y = \frac{3}{2}x + \frac{3}{2}$$ (see Figure 2).

<example number="1">
    <heading level="4">Example 1</heading>
    <paragraph>Let $$y = 3t^{3} + 2\sqrt{t}$$ .</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>Use the numerical derivative operation of a graphing utility to find how fast $$y$$ is changing with respect to $$t$$ when $$t = 1$$ .</item>
      <item>Verify the result of part (a), using the rules of differentiation of this section.</item>
    </list>
    <heading level="4">Solution</heading>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>Let $$f(t) = 3t^{3} + 2\sqrt{t}$$ . Using the numerical derivative operation of a graphing utility, we find that the rate of change of $$y$$ with respect to $$t$$ when $$t = 1$$ is given by $$f^{\prime}(1) = 10$$ (Figure T1). Figure T1 Details A numerical derivative screen reads Line 1: n Deriv ( (3 x carat 3 + 2 x carat .5), x, 1) Line 2: 10.00000313 The TI-83/84 numerical derivative screen for computing $$f^{\prime}(1)$$</item>
      <item>Here, $$f(t) = 3t^{3} + 2t^{1 \slash 2}$$ , and $$f^{\prime}(t) = 9t^{2} + 2\left( \frac{1}{2}t^{- 1 \slash 2} \right) = 9t^{2} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{t}}$$ Using this result, we see that when $$t = 1$$ , $$y$$ is changing at the rate of $$f^{\prime}(1) = 9(1^{2}) + \frac{1}{\sqrt{1}} = 10$$ units per unit change in $$t$$ , as obtained earlier.</item>
    </list>
  </example>

<example number="4">
    <heading level="4">Example 4</heading>

    <paragraph>Finally, observing that $$\left( 2x^{2} + 3 \right)^{3}(3x - 1)^{4}$$ is common to both terms, we can factor and simplify as follows:</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {f^{\prime}(x) = {(2x^{2} + 3)}^{3}{(3x - 1)}^{4}\lbrack 15(2x^{2} + 3) + 16x(3x - 1)\rbrack} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}(x)} = {(2x^{2} + 3)}^{3}{(3x - 1)}^{4}(30x^{2} + 45 + 48x^{2} - 16x)} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}(x)} = {(2x^{2} + 3)}^{3}{(3x - 1)}^{4}(78x^{2} - 16x + 45)} \end{array}$$</paragraph>

    <paragraph>at the point $$\left( 0,\frac{1}{8} \right)$$ .</paragraph>
    <heading level="4">Solution</heading>
    <paragraph>The slope of the tangent line to the graph of $$f$$ at any point $$x$$ is given by $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ . To compute $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ , we use the General Power Rule followed by the Quotient Rule, obtaining</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {f^{\prime}(x) = 3\left( \frac{2x + 1}{3x + 2} \right)^{2}\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left( \frac{2x + 1}{3x + 2} \right)} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}(x)} = 3\left( \frac{2x + 1}{3x + 2} \right)^{2}\left\lbrack \frac{(3x + 2)(2) - (2x + 1)(3)}{(3x + 2)^{2}} \right\rbrack} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}(x)} = 3\left( \frac{2x + 1}{3x + 2} \right)^{2}\left\lbrack \frac{6x + 4 - 6x - 3}{(3x + 2)^{2}} \right\rbrack} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}(x)} = \frac{3(2x + 1)^{2}}{(3x + 2)^{4}} {Combine like terms, and simplify.}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>

body_xml: Example 2 Find the third derivative of the function $$f$$ defined by $$y = x^{2 \slash 3}$$ . What is its domain? Solution We have $$\begin{array}{rcl} y^{\prime} & = & {\frac{2}{3}x^{- 1 \slash 3}} \\ y^{''} & = & {\left( \frac{2}{3} \right)\left( {- \frac{1}{3}} \right)x^{- 4 \slash 3} = - \frac{2}{9}x^{- 4 \slash 3}} \end{array}$$ so the required derivative is $$y^{'''} = \left( - \frac{2}{9} \right)\left( - \frac{4}{3} \right)x^{- 7 \slash 3} = \frac{8}{27}x^{- 7 \slash 3} = \frac{8}{27x^{7 \slash 3}}$$ The common domain of the functions $$f^{\prime}$$ , $$f^{''}$$ , and $$f^{'''}$$ is the set of all real numbers except $$x = 0$$ . The domain of $$y = x^{2 \slash 3}$$ is the set of all real numbers. The graph of the function $$y = x^{2 \slash 3}$$ appears in Figure 15.

<example number="3">
    <heading level="4">Example 3</heading>
    <paragraph>Find the second derivative of the function $$y = \left( 2x^{2} + 3 \right)^{3 \slash 2}$$ .</paragraph>
    <heading level="4">Solution</heading>
    <paragraph>We have, using the General Power Rule,</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$y^{\prime} = \frac{3}{2}{(2x^{2} + 3)}^{1 \slash 2}(4x) = 6x{(2x^{2} + 3)}^{1 \slash 2}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Next, using the Product Rule and then the General Power Rule, we find</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {y^{''} = (6x) \cdot \frac{d}{dx}{(2x^{2} + 3)}^{1 \slash 2} + \left\lbrack \frac{d}{dx}(6x) \right\rbrack{(2x^{2} + 3)}^{1 \slash 2}} \\ {\phantom{y^{''}} = (6x)\left( \frac{1}{2} \right){(2x^{2} + 3)}^{- 1 \slash 2}(4x) + 6{(2x^{2} + 3)}^{1 \slash 2}} \\ {\phantom{y^{''}} = 12x^{2}{(2x^{2} + 3)}^{- 1 \slash 2} + 6{(2x^{2} + 3)}^{1 \slash 2}} \\ {\phantom{y^{''}} = 6{(2x^{2} + 3)}^{- 1 \slash 2}\lbrack 2x^{2} + (2x^{2} + 3)\rbrack { \text{Factor out} 6{(2x^{2} + 3)}^{- 1 \slash 2}.}} \\ {\phantom{y^{''}} = \frac{6(4x^{2} + 3)}{\sqrt{2x^{2} + 3}}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <note type="theorem" source_type="">
      <heading level="4">Algebra</heading>
      <paragraph>See Example 9.</paragraph>
    </note>
  </example>

title: Example 1
snippet: Example 1: Example 1 Given the equation y^{2} = x , find \frac{dy}{dx} . Solution Differentiating both sides of the equation with respect to x , we obtain \frac{d}{dx}(y^{2}) = \frac{d}{dx}(x) To carry out the differentiation of the term...
body_xml:
<example number="1">
    <heading level="4">Example 1</heading>
    <paragraph>Given the equation $$y^{2} = x$$ , find $$\frac{dy}{dx}$$ .</paragraph>
    <heading level="4">Solution</heading>
    <paragraph>Differentiating both sides of the equation with respect to $$x$$ , we obtain</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{d}{dx}(y^{2}) = \frac{d}{dx}(x)$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>To carry out the differentiation of the term $$\frac{d}{dx}(y^{2})$$ , we note that $$y$$ (with suitable restrictions) is a function of $$x$$ . Writing $$y = f(x)$$ to remind us of this fact, we find that</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {\frac{d}{dx}(y^{2}) = \frac{d}{dx}\left\lbrack f(x) \right\rbrack^{2} { \text{Write} y = f(x).}} \\ {\phantom{\frac{d}{dx}(y^{2})} = 2f(x)f^{\prime}(x) \text{Use the Chain Rule.} } \\ {\phantom{\frac{d}{dx}(y^{2})} = 2y\frac{dy}{dx} { \text{Replace} f(x) \text{with} y.}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Therefore, the equation</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{d}{dx}(y^{2}) = \frac{d}{dx}(x)$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>is equivalent to</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$2y\frac{dy}{dx} = 1$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solving for $$\frac{dy}{dx}$$ yields</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{1}{2y}$$</paragraph>
  </example>

snippet: Example 2: Example 2 Find \frac{dy}{dx} given the equation y^{3} - y + 2x^{3} - x = 8 Solution Differentiating both sides of the given equation with respect to x , we obtain \begin{array}{rcl} {\frac{d}{dx}(y^{3} - y + 2x^{3} - x)} & = &...
body_xml:
<example number="2">
    <heading level="4">Example 2</heading>
    <paragraph>Find $$\frac{dy}{dx}$$ given the equation</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$y^{3} - y + 2x^{3} - x = 8$$</paragraph>
    <heading level="4">Solution</heading>
    <paragraph>Differentiating both sides of the given equation with respect to $$x$$ , we obtain</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} {\frac{d}{dx}(y^{3} - y + 2x^{3} - x)} & = & {\frac{d}{dx}(8)} \\ {\frac{d}{dx}(y^{3}) - \frac{d}{dx}(y) + \frac{d}{dx}(2x^{3}) - \frac{d}{dx}(x)} & = & 0 \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Now, recalling that $$y$$ is a function of $$x$$ , we apply the Chain Rule to the first two terms on the left. Thus,</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} {3y^{2}\frac{dy}{dx} - \frac{dy}{dx} + 6x^{2} - 1} & = & 0 \\ {(3y^{2} - 1)\frac{dy}{dx}} & = & {1 - 6x^{2}} \\ \frac{dy}{dx} & = & \frac{1 - 6x^{2}}{3y^{2} - 1} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <note type="theorem" source_type="">
      <heading level="4">Explore and Discuss</heading>
      <paragraph>Refer to Example 2. Suppose we think of the equation $$y^{3} - y + 2x^{3} - x = 8$$ as defining $$x$$ implicitly as a function of $$y$$ . Find $$dx \slash dy$$ , and justify your method of solution.</paragraph>
    </note>
  </example>

title: Example 3
snippet: Example 3: Example 3 Consider the equation x^{2} + y^{2} = 4 . Find dy \slash dx by implicit differentiation. Find the slope of the tangent line to the graph of the function y = f(x) at the point (1,\sqrt{3}) . Find an equation of the...
body_xml: Example 3 Consider the equation $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 4$$ . Find $$dy \slash dx$$ by implicit differentiation. Find the slope of the tangent line to the graph of the function $$y = f(x)$$ at the point $$(1,\sqrt{3})$$ . Find an equation of the tangent line of part (b). Solution Differentiating both sides of the equation with respect to $$x$$ , we obtain $$\begin{array}{rcl} {\frac{d}{dx}(x^{2} + y^{2})} & = & {\frac{d}{dx}(4)} \\ {\frac{d}{dx}(x^{2}) + \frac{d}{dx}(y^{2})} & = & 0 \\ {2x + 2y\frac{dy}{dx}} & = & 0 \\ {2y\frac{dy}{dx}} & = & {- 2x} \\ \frac{dy}{dx} & = & {- \frac{x}{y} (y \neq 0)} \end{array}$$ The slope of the tangent line to the graph of the function at the point $$(1,\sqrt{3})$$ is given by $$\left. \frac{dy}{dx} \middle| {}_{(1,\sqrt{3})} = - \frac{x}{y} \middle| {}_{(1,\sqrt{3})} = - \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \right.$$ (Note: This notation is read “ $$dy \slash dx$$ evaluated at the point $$(1,\sqrt{3})$$ .”) An equation of the tangent line in question is found by using the point-slope form of the equation of a line with the slope $$m = - 1 \slash \sqrt{3}$$ and the point $$(1,\sqrt{3})$$ . Thus, $$\begin{array}{rcl} {y - \sqrt{3}} & = & {- \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\left( {x - 1} \right)} \\ {\sqrt{3}y - 3} & = & {- x + 1} \\ {x + \sqrt{3}y - 4} & = & 0 \end{array}$$ Algebra See Example 6. A sketch of this tangent line and the graph of $$y = f(x)$$ are shown in Figure 18. We can also solve the equation $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 4$$ explicitly for $$y$$ in terms of $$x$$ . If we do this, we obtain $$y = \pm \sqrt{4 - x^{2}}$$ From this, we see that the equation $$x^{2} + y^{2} = 4$$ defines the two functions $$\begin{array}{l} {y = f(x) = \sqrt{4 - x^{2}}} \\ {y = g(x) = - \sqrt{4 - x^{2}}} \end{array}$$ Since the point $$(1,\sqrt{3})$$ does not lie on the graph of $$y = g(x)$$ , we conclude that $$y = f(x) = \sqrt{4 - x^{2}}$$ is the required function. The graph of $$f$$ is the semicircle shown in Figure 18.

title: Example 4
snippet: Example 4: Example 4 Find \frac{dy}{dx} given that x and y are related by the equation x^{2}y^{3} + 6x^{2} = y + 12 and that y = 2 when x = 1 . Solution Differentiating both sides of the given equation with respect to x , we obtain...
body_xml:
<example number="4">
    <heading level="4">Example 4</heading>
    <paragraph>Find $$\frac{dy}{dx}$$ given that $$x$$ and $$y$$ are related by the equation</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$x^{2}y^{3} + 6x^{2} = y + 12$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>and that $$y = 2$$ when $$x = 1$$ .</paragraph>
    <heading level="4">Solution</heading>
    <paragraph>Differentiating both sides of the given equation with respect to $$x$$ , we obtain</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} {\frac{d}{dx}(x^{2}y^{3}) + \frac{d}{dx}(6x^{2})} & = & {\frac{d}{dx}(y) + \frac{d}{dx}(12)} \\ {x^{2} \cdot \frac{d}{dx}(y^{3}) + y^{3} \cdot \frac{d}{dx}(x^{2}) + 12x} & = & {\frac{dy}{dx} { \text{Use the Product Rule on} \frac{d}{dx}(x^{2}y^{3}).}} \\ {3x^{2}y^{2}\frac{dy}{dx} + 2xy^{3} + 12x} & = & \frac{dy}{dx} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Substituting $$x = 1$$ and $$y = 2$$ into this equation gives</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} {3(1)^{2}(2)^{2}\frac{dy}{dx} + 2(1)(2)^{3} + 12(1)} & = & \frac{dy}{dx} \\ {12\frac{dy}{dx} + 16 + 12} & = & \frac{dy}{dx} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solving for $$\frac{dy}{dx}$$ , we have</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{dy}{dx} = - \frac{28}{11}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Note that it is not necessary to find an explicit expression for $$dy \slash dx$$ .</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Example 5
snippet: Example 5: Example 5 Find \frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}} if xy - y^{3} = 4 . Solution Differentiating both sides of the given equation with respect to x , we obtain \begin{array}{rcl} {\frac{d}{dx}(xy) - \frac{d}{dx}(y^{3})} & = & {\frac{d}{dx}(4)}...
body_xml:
<example number="5">
    <heading level="4">Example 5</heading>
    <paragraph>Find $$\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}$$ if $$xy - y^{3} = 4$$ .</paragraph>
    <heading level="4">Solution</heading>
    <paragraph>Differentiating both sides of the given equation with respect to $$x$$ , we obtain</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} {\frac{d}{dx}(xy) - \frac{d}{dx}(y^{3})} & = & {\frac{d}{dx}(4)} \\ {x\frac{dy}{dx} + y - 3y^{2}\frac{dy}{dx}} & = & 0 \\ {y - (3y^{2} - x)\frac{dy}{dx}} & = & 0 \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>or</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{y}{3y^{2} - x}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Next, we differentiate both sides of the last equation with respect to $$x$$ again, obtaining</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} {\frac{d}{dx}\left( \frac{dy}{dx} \right)} & = & {\frac{d}{dx}\left( \frac{y}{3y^{2} - x} \right)} \\ \frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}} & = & \frac{(3y^{2} - x)\frac{d}{dx}(y) - y\frac{d}{dx}(3y^{2} - x)}{{(3y^{2} - x)}^{2}} \\ & = & {\frac{(3y^{2} - x)\frac{dy}{dx} - y\left( 6y\frac{dy}{dx} - 1 \right)}{{(3y^{2} - x)}^{2}} = \frac{y - (3y^{2} + x)\frac{dy}{dx}}{{(3y^{2} - x)}^{2}}} \\ & = & {\frac{y - (3y^{2} + x)\left( \frac{y}{3y^{2} - x} \right)}{{(3y^{2} - x)}^{2}} = \frac{3y^{3} - xy - 3y^{3} - xy}{{(3y^{2} - x)}^{3}}} \\ & = & {- \frac{2xy}{{(3y^{2} - x)}^{3}}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
  </example>

    <heading level="4">Solution</heading>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>Let $$f(x) = x^{3}$$ . Then, $$dy = f^{\prime}(x)dx = 3x^{2}dx$$</item>
      <item>Here, $$x = 2$$ and $$dx = 2.01 - 2 = 0.01$$ . Therefore, $$dy = 3x^{2}dx = 3(2)^{2}(0.01) = 0.12$$</item>
      <item>Here, $$x = 2$$ and $$dx = 1.98 - 2 = - 0.02$$ . Therefore, $$dy = 3x^{2}dx = 3(2)^{2}( - 0.02) = - 0.24$$</item>
      <item>As you can see, both approximations $$0.12$$ and $$- 0.24$$ are quite close to the actual changes $$\Delta y$$ obtained in Example 2: $$0.120601$$ and $$- 0.237608$$ .</item>
    </list>

title: Example 4

<example number="4">
    <heading level="4">Example 4</heading>
    <paragraph>Approximate the value of $$\sqrt{26.5}$$ using differentials. Verify your result using the $$\boxed{\sqrt{}}$$ key on your calculator.</paragraph>
    <heading level="4">Solution</heading>
    <paragraph>Since we want to compute the square root of a number, let’s consider the function $$y = f(x) = \sqrt{x}$$ . Since $$25$$ is the number nearest $$26.5$$ whose square root is readily recognized, let’s take $$x = 25$$ . We want to know the change in $$y$$ , $$\Delta y$$ , as $$x$$ changes from $$x = 25$$ to $$x = 26.5$$ , an increase of $$\Delta x = 1.5$$ units. Using Equation (12), we find</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {\Delta y \approx dy = f^{\prime}(x)\Delta x} \\ {\phantom{\Delta y \approx dy} = \left( \left. \frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}} \right|_{x = 25} \right) \cdot (1.5) = \left( \frac{1}{10} \right)(1.5) = 0.15} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Therefore,</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} {\sqrt{26.5} - \sqrt{25}} & = & {\Delta y \approx 0.15} \\ \sqrt{26.5} & \approx & {\sqrt{25} + 0.15 = 5.15} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The exact value of $$\sqrt{26.5}$$ , rounded off to five decimal places, is $$5.14782$$ . Thus, the error incurred in the approximation is $$0.00218$$ .</paragraph>
  </example>

<example number="3">
    <heading level="4">Example 3</heading>
    <paragraph>Find the interval where the function $$f(x) = x^{2 \slash 3}$$ is increasing and the interval where it is decreasing.</paragraph>
    <heading level="4">Solution</heading>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>The derivative of $$f$$ is $$f^{\prime}(x) = \frac{2}{3}x^{- 1 \slash 3} = \frac{2}{3x^{1 \slash 3}}$$ The function $$f^{\prime}$$ is not defined at $$x = 0$$ , so $$f^{\prime}$$ is discontinuous there. It is continuous everywhere else. Furthermore, $$f^{\prime}$$ is not equal to zero anywhere. The number $$0$$ divides the real line (the domain of $$f$$ ) into the intervals $$\left( {- \infty,0} \right)$$ and $$\left( {0,\infty} \right)$$ .</item>
      <item>Pick a test point (say, $$x = - 1$$ ) in the interval $$\left( {- \infty,0} \right)$$ and compute $$f^{\prime}\left( {- 1} \right) = - \frac{2}{3}$$ Since $$f^{\prime}( - 1) < 0$$ , we know that $$f^{\prime}(x) < 0$$ on $$\left( {- \infty,0} \right)$$ . Next, we pick a test point (say, $$x = 1$$ ) in the interval $$\left( {0,\infty} \right)$$ and compute $$f^{\prime}(1) = \frac{2}{3}$$ Since $$f^{\prime}(1) > 0$$ , we know that $$f^{\prime}(x) > 0$$ on $$\left( {0,\infty} \right)$$ . Figure 7 shows these results in the form of a sign diagram. Figure 7 Details A sign diagram shows a number line labeled x with marks negative 1, 0, and 1. Above the line, negative signs appear from just before 0 and extending to the left extreme; positive signs appear from just after 0, and extending to the right. The text f prime is not defined at x = 0 appears above the number line from which an arrow points toward the number 0. Sign diagram for $$f^{\prime}$$ We conclude that $$f$$ is decreasing on the interval $$\left( {- \infty,0} \right)$$ and increasing on the interval $$\left( {0,\infty} \right)$$ . The graph of $$f$$ , shown in Figure 8, confirms these results. Figure 8 Details The curve labeled y = x^(2/3) enters the second quadrant from the left around (negative 4, 2.5), slopes almost linearly downward to the right, gently bulges upward and reaches the origin. The curve then enters the first quadrant, slopes almost linearly upward to the right, gently bulges up and exits the viewing window at around (4, 2.5). $$f$$ decreases on $$\left( {- \infty,0} \right)$$ and increases on $$\left( {0,\infty} \right)$$ .</item>
