body_xml: Example 2 In Section 6.3, we conjectured that the area of the region $$R$$ under the graph of $$f(x) = x^{2}$$ on the interval $$\left\lbrack {0,1} \right\rbrack$$ was $$\frac{1}{3}$$ . Use the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus to verify this conjecture. Solution The region $$R$$ is reproduced in Figure 17. Observe that $$f$$ is nonnegative on $$\left\lbrack {0,1} \right\rbrack$$ , so the area of $$R$$ is given by $$A = {\int_{0}^{1}{x^{2}dx}}$$ . Since an antiderivative of $$f(x) = x^{2}$$ is $$F(x) = \frac{1}{3}x^{3}$$ , we see, using the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, that $$\begin{array}{l} {A{= {\int_{0}^{1}{x^{2}dx}} = \left. \frac{1}{3}x^{3} \right|_{0}^{1}}} \\ {\phantom{A}{= \frac{1}{3}(1) - \frac{1}{3}(0) = \frac{1}{3}}} \end{array}$$ as we wished to show.

body_xml: Example 3 Find the area of the region $$R$$ under the graph of $$y = x^{2} + 1$$ from $$x = - 1$$ to $$x = 2$$ . Solution The region $$R$$ is shown in Figure 18. Using the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus, we find that the required area is $$\begin{array}{l} {{\int_{- 1}^{2}({x^{2} + 1})}dx{= {\left( {\frac{1}{3}x^{3} + x} \right)|}_{- 1}^{2}}} \\ {\phantom{{\int_{- 1}^{2}({x^{2} + 1})}dx}{= \left\lbrack {\frac{1}{3}(2)^{3} + 2} \right\rbrack - \left\lbrack {\frac{1}{3}\left( {- 1} \right)^{3} + \left( {- 1} \right)} \right\rbrack = 6}} \end{array}$$

    </list>
  </note>

snippet: Example 1: Example 1 Evaluate \int_{0}^{4}{x\sqrt{9 + x^{2}}dx} . Solution Method 1 We first find the corresponding indefinite integral: I = {\int{x\sqrt{9 + x^{2}}dx}} Make the substitution u = 9 + x^{2} , so that \begin{aligned} {du} &...
body_xml:
<example number="1">
    <heading level="4">Example 1</heading>
    <paragraph>Evaluate $$\int_{0}^{4}{x\sqrt{9 + x^{2}}dx}$$ .</paragraph>
    <heading level="4">Solution</heading>
    <paragraph>Method 1 We first find the corresponding indefinite integral:</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$I = {\int{x\sqrt{9 + x^{2}}dx}}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Make the substitution $$u = 9 + x^{2}$$ , so that</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{aligned} {du} & {= \frac{d}{dx}{({9 + x^{2}})}dx} \\ & {= 2xdx} \\ {xdx} & {= \frac{1}{2}du { \text{Divide both sides by} 2.}} \end{aligned}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Then</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {I = {\int{\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{u}}}du = \frac{1}{2}{\int u^{1 \slash 2}}du} \\ {{\phantom{I} = \frac{1}{3}u^{3 \slash 2} + C = \frac{1}{3}{({9 + x^{2}})}^{3 \slash 2} + C} { \text{Substitute} 9 + x^{2} \text{for} u.}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Using this result, we now evaluate the given definite integral:</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {{\int_{0}^{4}{x\sqrt{9 + x^{2}}dx}} = \left. \frac{1}{3}{({9 + x^{2}})}^{3 \slash 2} \right|_{0}^{4}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{0}^{4}{x\sqrt{9 + x^{2}}dx}} = \frac{1}{3}\left\lbrack {\left( {9 + 16} \right)^{3 \slash 2} - 9^{3 \slash 2}} \right\rbrack} \\ {\phantom{\int_{0}^{4}{x\sqrt{9 + x^{2}}dx}} = \frac{1}{3}\left( {125 - 27} \right) = \frac{98}{3} = 32\frac{2}{3}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Method 2 Changing the Limits of Integration. As before, we make the substitution</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$u = 9 + x^{2}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>so that</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} {du} & = & {2xdx} \\ {xdx} & = & {\frac{1}{2}du} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Next, observe that the given definite integral is evaluated with respect to $$x$$ with the range of integration given by the interval $$\left\lbrack {0,4} \right\rbrack$$ . If we perform the integration with respect to $$u$$ via the substitution (11), then we must adjust the range of integration to reflect the fact that the integration is being performed with respect to the new variable $$u$$ . To determine the proper range of integration, note that when $$x = 0$$ , Equation (11) implies that</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$u = 9 + 0^{2} = 9$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>which gives the required lower limit of integration with respect to $$u$$ . Similarly, when $$x = 4$$ ,</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$u = 9 + 16 = 25$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>is the required upper limit of integration with respect to $$u$$ . Thus, the range of integration when the integration is performed with respect to $$u$$ is given by the interval $$\left\lbrack {9,25} \right\rbrack$$ . Therefore, we have</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {{\int_{0}^{4}{x\sqrt{9 + x^{2}}dx}} = {\int_{9}^{25}{\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{u}du = \frac{1}{2}{\int_{9}^{25}u^{1 \slash 2}}du}}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{0}^{4}{x\sqrt{9 + x^{2}}dx}} = {\left. \frac{1}{3}u^{3 \slash 2} \right|_{9}^{25} = \frac{1}{3}{({25^{3 \slash 2} - 9^{3 \slash 2}})}}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{0}^{4}{x\sqrt{9 + x^{2}}dx}} = {\frac{1}{3}\left( {125 - 27} \right) = \frac{98}{3} = 32\frac{2}{3}}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>which agrees with the result obtained by using Method 1.</paragraph>
  </example>

  </example>

<example number="3">
    <heading level="4">Example 3</heading>
    <paragraph>Evaluate $$\int_{0}^{1}{\frac{x^{2}}{x^{3} + 1}dx}$$ .</paragraph>
    <heading level="4">Solution</heading>
    <paragraph>Let $$u = x^{3} + 1$$ , so that $$du = 3x^{2}dx$$ , or $$x^{2}dx = \frac{1}{3}du$$ . When $$x = 0$$ , $$u = 1$$ ; and when $$x = 1$$ , $$u = 2$$ . These give the lower and upper limits of integration with respect to $$u$$ . Making the indicated substitutions, we find</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {{\int_{0}^{1}{\frac{x^{2}}{x^{3} + 1}dx}} = \frac{1}{3}{\int_{1}^{2}{\frac{du}{u} = \left. \frac{1}{3}\ln|u| \right|_{1}^{2}}}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{0}^{1}{\frac{x^{2}}{x^{3} + 1}dx}} = \frac{1}{3}\left( {\ln 2 - \ln 1} \right) = \frac{1}{3}\ln 2} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
  </example>

body_xml: Example 4 Find the area of the region $$R$$ under the graph of $$f(x) = e^{({1 \slash 2})x}$$ from $$x = - 1$$ to $$x = 1$$ . Solution The region $$R$$ is shown in Figure 25. Its area is given by $$A = {\int_{- 1}^{1}e^{({1 \slash 2})x}}dx$$ To evaluate this integral, we make the substitution $$u = \frac{1}{2}x$$ so that $$\begin{array}{rcl} {du} & = & {\frac{1}{2}dx} \\ {dx} & = & {2du} \end{array}$$ When $$x = - 1$$ , $$u = - \frac{1}{2}$$ , and when $$x = 1$$ , $$u = \frac{1}{2}$$ . Making the indicated substitutions, we obtain $$\begin{array}{l} {A = {\int_{- 1}^{1}e^{({1 \slash 2})x}}dx = 2{\int_{- 1 \slash 2}^{1 \slash 2}e^{u}}du} \\ {\phantom{A} = \left. 2e^{u} \right|_{- 1 \slash 2}^{1 \slash 2} = 2{({e^{1 \slash 2} - e^{- 1 \slash 2}})}} \end{array}$$ or approximately $$2.08$$ .

body_xml: Example 1 Find the area of the region bounded by the $$x$$ -axis, the graph of $$y = - x^{2} + 4x - 8$$ , and the lines $$x = - 1$$ and $$x = 4$$ . Solution The region $$R$$ under consideration is shown in Figure 31. We can view $$R$$ as the region bounded above by the graph of $$f(x) = 0$$ (the $$x$$ -axis) and below by the graph of $$g{(x)} = - x^{2} + 4x - 8$$ on $$\lbrack - 1,4\rbrack$$ . Therefore, the area of $$R$$ is given by $$\begin{array}{l} {{\int_{a}^{b}{\lbrack f(x) - g(x)\rbrack\mathit{dx}}} = {\int_{- 1}^{4}{\lbrack{0 - {({- x^{2} + 4x - 8})}\rbrack}\mathit{dx}}}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{a}^{b}{\left\lbrack f(x) - g(x) \right\rbrack\mathit{dx}}} = {\int_{- 1}^{4}{({x^{2} - 4x + 8})}\mathit{dx}}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{a}^{b}{\left\lbrack f(x) - g(x) \right\rbrack\mathit{dx}}} = \left. \frac{1}{3}x^{3} - 2x^{2} + 8x \right|_{- 1}^{4}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{a}^{b}{\left\lbrack f(x) - g(x) \right\rbrack\mathit{dx}}} = \left\lbrack {\frac{1}{3}{(64)} - 2{(16)} + 8{(4)}} \right\rbrack - \left\lbrack {\frac{1}{3}{({- 1})} - 2{(1)} + 8{({- 1})}} \right\rbrack} \\ {\phantom{\int_{a}^{b}{\left\lbrack f(x) - g(x) \right\rbrack\mathit{dx}}} = {31\frac{2}{3}}} \end{array}$$

body_xml: Example 2 Find the area of the region $$R$$ bounded by the graphs of $$f(x) = 2x - 1$$ and $$g{(x)} = x^{2} - 4$$ and the vertical lines $$x = 1$$ and $$x = 2$$ . Solution We first sketch the graphs of the functions $$f(x) = 2x - 1$$ and $$g{(x)} = x^{2} - 4$$ and the vertical lines $$x = 1$$ and $$x = 2$$ , and then we identify the region $$R$$ whose area is to be calculated (Figure 32). $$\begin{array}{l} {{\int_{1}^{2}{\left\lbrack f(x) - g(x) \right\rbrack\mathit{dx}}} = {\int_{1}^{2}{\lbrack{({2x - 1})} - {({x^{2} - 4})}\rbrack}\mathit{dx}}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{1}^{2}{\left\lbrack f(x) - g(x) \right\rbrack\mathit{dx}}} = {\int_{1}^{2}{({- x^{2} + 2x + 3})\mathit{dx}}}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{1}^{2}{\left\lbrack f(x) - g(x) \right\rbrack\mathit{dx}}} = \left. - \frac{1}{3}x^{3} + x^{2} + 3x \right|_{1}^{2}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{1}^{2}{\left\lbrack f(x) - g(x) \right\rbrack\mathit{dx}}} = \left( {- \frac{8}{3} + 4 + 6} \right) - \left( {- \frac{1}{3} + 1 + 3} \right) = \frac{11}{3}} \end{array}$$

body_xml: Example 3 Find the area of the region $$R$$ that is completely enclosed by the graphs of the functions $$f(x) = 2x - 1$$ and $$g{(x)} = x^{2} - 4$$ Solution The region $$R$$ is shown in Figure 33. First, we find the points of intersection of the two curves. To do this, we solve the system that consists of the two equations $$y = 2x - 1$$ and $$y = x^{2} - 4$$ . Equating the two values of $$y$$ gives $$\begin{array}{rcl} {x^{2} - 4} & = & {2x - 1} \\ {x^{2} - 2x - 3} & = & 0 \\ {\left( {x + 1} \right)\left( {x - 3} \right)} & = & 0 \end{array}$$ so $$x = - 1$$ or $$x = 3$$ . That is, the two curves intersect when $$x = - 1$$ and $$x = 3$$ . Observe that we could also view the region $$R$$ as the region bounded above by the graph of the function $$f(x) = 2x - 1$$ , below by the graph of the function $$g{(x)} = x^{2} - 4$$ , and to the left and right by the vertical lines $$x = - 1$$ and $$x = 3$$ , respectively. Next, since the graph of the function $$f$$ always lies above that of the function $$g$$ on $$\lbrack - 1,3\rbrack$$ , we can use integral (13) to compute the desired area: $$\begin{array}{l} {{\int_{a}^{b}{\left\lbrack f(x) - g(x) \right\rbrack\mathit{dx}}} = {\int_{- 1}^{3}{\lbrack{({2x - 1})} - {({x^{2} - 4})}\rbrack}\mathit{dx}}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{a}^{b}{\left\lbrack f(x) - g(x) \right\rbrack\mathit{dx}}} = {\int_{- 1}^{3}{({- x^{2} + 2x + 3})}\mathit{dx}}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{a}^{b}{\left\lbrack f(x) - g(x) \right\rbrack\mathit{dx}}} = \left. - \frac{1}{3}x^{3} + x^{2} + 3x \right|_{- 1}^{3}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{a}^{b}{\left\lbrack f(x) - g(x) \right\rbrack\mathit{dx}}} = {({- 9 + 9 + 9})} - \left( {\frac{1}{3} + 1 - 3} \right) = \frac{32}{3}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{a}^{b}{\left\lbrack f(x) - g(x) \right\rbrack\mathit{dx}}} = {10\frac{2}{3}}} \end{array}$$

title: Example 4
snippet: Example 4: Example 4 Find the area of the region R bounded by the graphs of the functions f{(x)} = x^{2} - 2x - 1 and g{(x)} = - e^{x} - 1 and the vertical lines x = - 1 and x = 1 . Solution The region R is shown in Figure 34. Since the...
body_xml: Example 4 Find the area of the region $$R$$ bounded by the graphs of the functions $$f{(x)} = x^{2} - 2x - 1$$ and $$g{(x)} = - e^{x} - 1$$ and the vertical lines $$x = - 1$$ and $$x = 1$$ . Solution The region $$R$$ is shown in Figure 34. Since the graph of the function $$f$$ always lies above that of the function $$g$$ , the area of the region $$R$$ is given by $$\begin{array}{l} {{\int_{a}^{b}\left\lbrack f(x) - g(x) \right\rbrack}\mathit{dx} = {\int_{- 1}^{1}{\lbrack{({x^{2} - 2x - 1})} - {({- e^{x} - 1})}\rbrack}\mathit{dx}}} \\ {\phantom{{\int_{a}^{b}\left\lbrack f(x) - g(x) \right\rbrack}\mathit{dx}} = {\int_{- 1}^{1}{({x^{2} - 2x + e^{x}})}\mathit{dx}}} \\ {\phantom{{\int_{a}^{b}\left\lbrack f(x) - g(x) \right\rbrack}\mathit{dx}} = \left. \frac{1}{3}x^{3} - x^{2} + e^{x} \right|_{- 1}^{1}} \\ {\phantom{{\int_{a}^{b}\left\lbrack f(x) - g(x) \right\rbrack}\mathit{dx}} = \left( {\frac{1}{3} - 1 + e} \right) - \left( {- \frac{1}{3} - 1 + e^{- 1}} \right)} \\ {\phantom{{\int_{a}^{b}\left\lbrack f(x) - g(x) \right\rbrack}\mathit{dx}} = {\frac{2}{3} + e - \frac{1}{e} \approx 3.02}} \end{array}$$

title: Example 5
snippet: Example 5: Example 5 Find the area of the region bounded by the graph of the function f{(x)} = x^{3} , the x -axis, and the lines x = - 1 and x = 1 . Solution The region R under consideration can be thought of as being composed of the two...
body_xml: Example 5 Find the area of the region bounded by the graph of the function $$f{(x)} = x^{3}$$ , the $$x$$ -axis, and the lines $$x = - 1$$ and $$x = 1$$ . Solution The region $$R$$ under consideration can be thought of as being composed of the two subregions $$R_{1}$$ and $$R_{2}$$ , as shown in Figure 35. Recall that the $$x$$ -axis is represented by the function $$g(x) = 0$$ . Since $$g(x) \geq f(x)$$ on $$\lbrack - 1,0\rbrack$$ , we see that the area of $$R_{1}$$ is given by $$\begin{array}{l} {{\int_{a}^{b}\left\lbrack {g(x) - f(x)} \right\rbrack dx} = {\int_{- 1}^{0}{({0 - x^{3}})}\mathit{dx} = - {\int_{- 1}^{0}{x^{3}\mathit{dx}}}}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{a}^{b}\left\lbrack {g(x) - f(x)} \right\rbrack dx} = {\left. - \frac{1}{4}x^{4} \right|_{- 1}^{0} = 0 - \left( {- \frac{1}{4}} \right) = \frac{1}{4}}} \end{array}$$ To find the area of $$R_{2}$$ , we observe that $$f(x) \geq g(x)$$ on $$\lbrack 0,1\rbrack$$ , so it is given by $$\begin{array}{l} {{\int_{a}^{b}\left\lbrack f(x) - g(x) \right\rbrack}\mathit{dx} = {\int_{0}^{1}{({x^{3} - 0})}\mathit{dx} = {\int_{0}^{1}{x^{3}\mathit{dx}}}}} \\ {\phantom{{\int_{a}^{b}\left\lbrack f(x) - g(x) \right\rbrack}\mathit{dx}} = {\left. \frac{1}{4}x^{4} \right|_{0}^{1} = \left( \frac{1}{4} \right) - 0 = \frac{1}{4}}} \end{array}$$ Therefore, the area of $$R$$ is $$\frac{1}{4} + \frac{1}{4}$$ , or $$\frac{1}{2}$$ . By making use of symmetry, we could have obtained the same result by computing $$- 2{\int_{- 1}^{0}{x^{3}\mathit{dx}}}$$ or $$2{\int_{0}^{1}{x^{3}\mathit{dx}}}$$ as you may verify.

title: Example 6
snippet: Example 6: Example 6 Find the area of the region completely enclosed by the graphs of the functions f{(x)} = x^{3} - 3x + 3 and g(x) = x + 3 Solution First, we sketch the graphs of y = x^{3} - 3x + 3 and y = x + 3 , and we then identify...
body_xml: Example 6 Find the area of the region completely enclosed by the graphs of the functions $$f{(x)} = x^{3} - 3x + 3$$ and $$g(x) = x + 3$$ Solution First, we sketch the graphs of $$y = x^{3} - 3x + 3$$ and $$y = x + 3$$ , and we then identify the required region $$R$$ . We can view the region $$R$$ as being composed of the two subregions $$R_{1}$$ and $$R_{2}$$ , as shown in Figure 36. By solving the equations $$y = x + 3$$ and $$y = x^{3} - 3x + 3$$ simultaneously, we find the points of intersection of the two curves. Equating the two values of $$y$$ , we have $$\begin{array}{rcl} {x^{3} - 3x + 3} & = & {x + 3} \\ {x^{3} - 4x} & = & 0 \\ {x{({x^{2} - 4})}} & = & 0 \\ {x\left( {x + 2} \right)\left( {x - 2} \right)} & = & 0 \\ x & = & {0, - 2,2} \end{array}$$ Hence the points of intersection of the two curves are $$\left( {- 2,1} \right)$$ , $$\left( {0,3} \right)$$ , and $$\left( {2,5} \right)$$ . For $$- 2 \leq x \leq 0$$ , we see that the graph of the function $$f$$ lies above that of the function $$g$$ , so the area of the region $$R_{1}$$ is, by Equation (13), $$\begin{array}{l} {{\int_{- 2}^{0}{\lbrack{({x^{3} - 3x + 3})} - {({x + 3})}\rbrack}\mathit{dx}} = \int_{- 2}^{0}{({x^{3} - 4x})\mathit{dx}}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{- 2}^{0}{\lbrack{({x^{3} - 3x + 3})} - {({x + 3})}\rbrack}\mathit{dx}} = \left. \frac{1}{4}x^{4} - 2x^{2} \right|_{- 2}^{0}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{- 2}^{0}{\lbrack{({x^{3} - 3x + 3})} - {({x + 3})}\rbrack}\mathit{dx}} = {- \left( {4 - 8} \right)}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{- 2}^{0}{\lbrack{({x^{3} - 3x + 3})} - {({x + 3})}\rbrack}\mathit{dx}} = 4} \end{array}$$ For $$0 \leq x \leq 2$$ , the graph of the function $$g$$ lies above that of the function $$f$$ , and the area of $$R_{2}$$ is given by $$\begin{array}{l} {{\int_{0}^{2}{\lbrack{({x + 3})} - {({x^{3} - 3x + 3})}\rbrack}\mathit{dx}} = {\int_{0}^{2}{({- x^{3} + 4x})}\mathit{dx}}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{0}^{2}{\lbrack{({x + 3})} - {({x^{3} - 3x + 3})}\rbrack}\mathit{dx}} = \left. - \frac{1}{4}x^{4} + 2x^{2} \right|_{0}^{2}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{0}^{2}{\lbrack{({x + 3})} - {({x^{3} - 3x + 3})}\rbrack}\mathit{dx}} = {- 4 + 8}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{0}^{2}{\lbrack{({x + 3})} - {({x^{3} - 3x + 3})}\rbrack}\mathit{dx}} = 4} \end{array}$$ Therefore, the required area is the sum of the areas of the two regions $$R_{1}$$ and $$R_{2}$$ —that is, $$4 + 4$$ , or $$8$$ .

body_xml: Example 1 Use a graphing utility to find the area of the smaller region $$R$$ that is completely enclosed by the graphs of the functions $$f(x) = 2x^{3} - 8x^{2} + 4x - 3$$ and $$g(x) = 3x^{2} + 10x - 11$$ Solution The graphs of $$f$$ and $$g$$ in the viewing window $$\left\lbrack {- 3,4} \right\rbrack \times \left\lbrack {- 20,5} \right\rbrack$$ are shown in Figure T1. Using the intersection operation of a graphing utility, we find the $$x$$ -coordinates of the points of intersection of the two graphs to be approximately $$- 1.04$$ and $$0.65$$ , respectively. Since the graph of $$f$$ lies above that of $$g$$ on the interval $$\left\lbrack {- 1.04,0.65} \right\rbrack$$ , we see that the area of $$R$$ is given by $$\begin{array}{l} {A \approx {\int_{- 1.04}^{0.65}{\lbrack{({2x^{3} - 8x^{2} + 4x - 3}) - {({3x^{2} + 10x - 11})}}\rbrack}}\mathit{dx}} \\ {\phantom{A} = {\int_{- 1.04}^{0.65}{({2x^{3} - 11x^{2} - 6x + 8})}}\mathit{dx}} \end{array}$$ Using the numerical integration function of a graphing utility, we find $$A \approx 9.87$$ , so the area of $$R$$ is approximately $$9.87$$ .

title: Example 1
snippet: Example 1: Example 1 The demand function for a certain make of ten-speed bicycle is given by p = D(x) = - 0.001x^{2} + 250 where p is the unit price in dollars and x is the quantity demanded in thousands of units. The supply function for...
body_xml: Example 1 The demand function for a certain make of ten-speed bicycle is given by $$p = D(x) = - 0.001x^{2} + 250$$ where $$p$$ is the unit price in dollars and $$x$$ is the quantity demanded in thousands of units. The supply function for these bicycles is given by $$p = S(x) = 0.0006x^{2} + 0.02x + 100$$ where $$p$$ stands for the unit price in dollars and $$x$$ stands for the number of bicycles that the supplier will put on the market, in units of a thousand. Determine the consumers’ surplus and the producers’ surplus if the market price of a bicycle is set at the equilibrium price. Solution Recall that the equilibrium price is the unit price of the commodity when market equilibrium occurs. We determine the equilibrium price by solving for the point of intersection of the demand curve and the supply curve (Figure 43). To solve the system of equations $$\begin{array}{ll} p & {= - 0.001x^{2} + 250} \\ p & {= 0.0006x^{2} + 0.02x + 100} \end{array}$$ we simply substitute the second equation into the first, obtaining $$\begin{array}{ll} {0.0006x^{2} + 0.02x + 100} & {= - 0.001x^{2} + 250} \\ {0.0016x^{2} + 0.02x - 150} & {= 0} \\ {16x^{2} + 200x - 1,500,000} & {= 0} \\ {2x^{2} + 25x - 187,500} & {= 0} \end{array}$$ Factoring this last equation, we obtain $$\left( {2x + 625} \right)\left( {x - 300} \right) = 0$$ Thus, $$x = - 625 \slash 2$$ or $$x = 300$$ . The first number lies outside the interval of interest, so we are left with the solution $$x = 300$$ , with a corresponding value of $$p = - 0.001(300)^{2} + 250 = 160$$ Thus, the equilibrium point is $$\left( {300,160} \right)$$ ; that is, the equilibrium quantity is $$300,000$$ , and the equilibrium price is $$\$ 160$$ . Setting the market price at $$\$ 160$$ per unit and using Formula (16) with $$\overline{p} = 160$$ and $$\overline{x} = 300$$ , we find that the consumers’ surplus is given by $$\begin{array}{l} {\mathit{CS}{= \int_{0}^{300}{({- 0.001x^{2} + 250})}dx - (160)(300)}} \\ {\phantom{\mathit{CS}}{= {\left( {- \frac{1}{3000}x^{3} + 250x} \right)|}_{0}^{300} - 48,000}} \\ {\phantom{\mathit{CS}}{= - \frac{300^{3}}{3000} + (250)(300) - 48,000}} \\ {\phantom{\mathit{CS}}{= 18,000}} \end{array}$$ or $$\$ 18,000,000$$ . (Recall that $$x$$ is measured in units of a thousand.) Next, using Equation (17), we find that the producers’ surplus is given by $$\begin{array}{l} {\mathit{PS} = {(160)}{(300)} - \int_{0}^{300}{({0.0006x^{2} + 0.02x + 100})}dx} \\ {\phantom{\mathit{PS}}{= 48,000 - \left. ({0.0002x^{3} + 0.01x^{2} + 100x}) \right|_{0}^{300}}} \\ {\phantom{\mathit{PS}}{= 48,000 - {\lbrack(0.0002)(300)^{3} + (0.01)(300)^{2} + 100(300)}\rbrack}} \\ {\phantom{\mathit{PS}}{= 11,700}} \end{array}$$ or $$\$ 11,700,000$$ .

body_xml:
<example number="1">
    <heading level="4">Example 1</heading>
    <paragraph>Evaluate $$\int{xe^{x}dx}$$</paragraph>
    <heading level="4">Solution</heading>
    <paragraph>No method of integration developed thus far enables us to evaluate the given indefinite integral in its present form. Therefore, we attempt to write it in terms of an indefinite integral that will be easier to evaluate. Let’s use the integration by parts Formula (3) by letting</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$u = x$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>and</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$dv = e^{x}dx$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>so that</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$du = dx$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>and</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$v = e^{x}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Therefore,</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {{\int{xe^{x}}\mathit{dx}} = {\int{udv}}} \\ {\phantom{\int{xe^{x}}\mathit{dx}} = {uv - {\int{vdu}}}} \\ {\phantom{\int{xe^{x}}\mathit{dx}} = {xe^{x} - {\int{e^{x}dx}}}} \\ {\phantom{\int{xe^{x}}\mathit{dx}} = {xe^{x} - e^{x} + C}} \\ {\phantom{\int{xe^{x}}\mathit{dx}} = \left( {x - 1} \right)e^{x} + C} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
  </example>

<example number="2">
    <heading level="4">Example 2</heading>
    <paragraph>Evaluate $$\int{x\ln xdx}$$ .</paragraph>
    <heading level="4">Solution</heading>
    <paragraph>Letting</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$u = \ln x$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>and</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$dv = xdx$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>we have</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$du = \frac{1}{x}dx$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>and</paragraph>

    <paragraph>Therefore,</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {{\int{x\ln xdx}} = {\int{udv = uv - {\int{vdu}}}}} \\ {\phantom{\int{x\ln xdx}} = {\frac{1}{2}x^{2}\ln x - {\int{\frac{1}{2}x^{2} \cdot \left( \frac{1}{x} \right)dx}}}} \\ {\phantom{\int{x\ln xdx}} = {\frac{1}{2}x^{2}\ln x - \frac{1}{2}{\int{xdx}}}} \\ {\phantom{\int{x\ln xdx}} = {\frac{1}{2}x^{2}\ln x - \frac{1}{4}x^{2} + C}} \\ {\phantom{\int{x\ln xdx}} = {\frac{1}{4}x^{2}\left( {2\ln x - 1} \right) + C}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>

body_xml:
<example number="3">
    <heading level="4">Example 3</heading>
    <paragraph>Evaluate $$\int{\frac{xe^{x}}{\left( {x + 1} \right)^{2}}dx}$$ .</paragraph>
    <heading level="4">Solution</heading>
    <paragraph>Let</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$u = xe^{x}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>and</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$dv = \frac{1}{\left( {x + 1} \right)^{2}}dx$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Then</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$du = \left( {xe^{x} + e^{x}} \right)dx = e^{x}\left( {x + 1} \right)dx$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>and</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$v = - \frac{1}{x + 1}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Therefore,</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {{\int{\frac{xe^{x}}{\left( {x + 1} \right)^{2}}dx}} = {\int{udv = uv - {\int{vdu}}}}} \\ {\phantom{\int{\frac{xe^{x}}{\left( {x + 1} \right)^{2}}dx}} = {xe^{x}\left( {- \frac{1}{x + 1}} \right) - {\int{\left( {- \frac{1}{x + 1}} \right)e^{x}\left( {x + 1} \right)dx}}}} \\ {\phantom{\int{\frac{xe^{x}}{\left( {x + 1} \right)^{2}}dx}} = {- \frac{xe^{x}}{x + 1} + {\int e^{x}}dx}} \\ {\phantom{\int{\frac{xe^{x}}{\left( {x + 1} \right)^{2}}dx}} = {- \frac{xe^{x}}{x + 1} + e^{x} + C}} \\ {\phantom{\int{\frac{xe^{x}}{\left( {x + 1} \right)^{2}}dx}} = {\frac{e^{x}}{x + 1} + C} {Combine first two terms.}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>

<example number="5">
    <heading level="4">Example 5</heading>
    <paragraph>Use the table of integrals to find $$\int{x^{2}e^{( - 1 \slash 2)x}dx}$$ .</paragraph>
    <heading level="4">Solution</heading>
    <paragraph>Scanning the table of integrals for a formula involving $$e^{\mathit{ax}}$$ in the integrand, we are led to Formula (24),</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\int{u^{n}e^{\mathit{au}}du = \frac{1}{a}u^{n}e^{\mathit{au}} - \frac{n}{a}{\int{u^{n - 1}e^{\mathit{au}}du}}}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>With $$n = 2$$ , $$a = - \frac{1}{2}$$ , and $$u = x$$ , we have</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{matrix} {{\int{x^{2}e^{( - 1 \slash 2)x}dx}} = \left( \frac{1}{- \frac{1}{2}} \right)x^{2}e^{({- 1 \slash 2})x} - \frac{2}{\left( {- \frac{1}{2}} \right)}{\int{xe^{({- 1 \slash 2})x}dx}}} \\ {\phantom{\int{x^{2}e^{( - 1 \slash 2)x}dx}} = {- 2x^{2}e^{({- 1 \slash 2})x} + 4{\int{xe^{({- 1 \slash 2})x}dx}}}} \end{matrix}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>If we use Formula (24) once again, with $$n = 1$$ , $$a = - \frac{1}{2}$$ , and $$u = x$$ , to evaluate the integral on the right, we obtain</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{matrix} {{\int{x^{2}e^{({- 1 \slash 2})x}dx}} = {- 2x^{2}e^{({- 1 \slash 2})x} + 4\left\lbrack {\left( \frac{1}{- \frac{1}{2}} \right)xe^{({- 1 \slash 2})x} - \frac{1}{\left( {- \frac{1}{2}} \right)}{\int{e^{({- 1 \slash 2})x}dx}}} \right\rbrack}} \\ {\phantom{\int{x^{2}e^{({- 1 \slash 2})x}dx}} = {- 2x^{2}e^{({- 1 \slash 2})x} + 4\left\lbrack {- 2xe^{({- 1 \slash 2})x} + 2 \cdot \frac{1}{\left( {- \frac{1}{2}} \right)}e^{({- 1 \slash 2})x}} \right\rbrack + C}} \\ {\phantom{\int{x^{2}e^{({- 1 \slash 2})x}dx}} = {- 2e^{({- 1 \slash 2})x}{({x^{2} + 4x + 8})} + C}} \end{matrix}$$</paragraph>
  </example>

<example number="1">
    <heading level="4">Example 1</heading>
    <paragraph>Approximate the value of</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\int_{1}^{2}{\frac{1}{x}dx}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>using the Trapezoidal Rule with $$n = 10$$ . Compare this result with the exact value of the integral.</paragraph>
    <heading level="4">Solution</heading>
    <paragraph>Here, $$a = 1$$ , $$b = 2$$ , and $$n = 10$$ , so</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\Delta x = \frac{b - a}{n} = \frac{1}{10} = 0.1$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>and</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$${x_{0} = 1} {x_{1} = 1.1} {x_{2} = 1.2} {x_{3} = 1.3} \cdots {x_{9} = 1.9} {x_{10} = 2}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The Trapezoidal Rule yields</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {{\int_{1}^{2}{\frac{1}{x}dx}} \approx {\frac{0.1}{2}\left\lbrack {1 + 2\left( \frac{1}{1.1} \right) + 2\left( \frac{1}{1.2} \right) + 2\left( \frac{1}{1.3} \right) + \cdots + 2\left( \frac{1}{1.9} \right) + \frac{1}{2}} \right\rbrack}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{1}^{2}{\frac{1}{x}dx}} \approx 0.693771} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>In this case, we can easily compute the actual value of the definite integral under consideration. In fact,</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {\left. \int_{1}^{2}{\frac{1}{x}dx} = \ln x \right|_{1}^{2} = \ln 2 - \ln 1 = \ln 2} \\ {\phantom{\int_{1}^{2}{\frac{1}{x}dx}} \approx 0.693147} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Thus, the Trapezoidal Rule with $$n = 10$$ yields a result with an error of $$0.000624$$ to six decimal places.</paragraph>
  </example>

<example number="3">
    <heading level="4">Example 3</heading>
    <paragraph>Find an approximation of</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\int_{1}^{2}{\frac{1}{x}dx}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>using Simpson’s Rule with $$n = 10$$ . Compare this result with that of Example 1 and also with the exact value of the integral.</paragraph>
    <heading level="4">Solution</heading>
    <paragraph>We have $$a = 1$$ , $$b = 2$$ , $$f(x) = \frac{1}{x}$$ and $$n = 10$$ , so</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\Delta x = \frac{b - a}{n} = \frac{1}{10} = 0.1$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>and</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$${x_{0} = 1} {x_{1} = 1.1} {x_{2} = 1.2} {x_{3} = 1.3} \ldots {x_{9} = 1.9} {x_{10} = 2}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Simpson’s Rule yields</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {\int_{1}^{2}{\frac{1}{x}dx \approx \frac{0.1}{3}\left\lbrack {f(1) + 4f(1.1) + 2f(1.2) + \cdots + 4f(1.9) + f(2)} \right\rbrack}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{1}^{2}{\frac{1}{x}dx}} = \frac{0.1}{3}\left\lbrack {1 + 4\left( \frac{1}{1.1} \right) + 2\left( \frac{1}{1.2} \right) + 4\left( \frac{1}{1.3} \right) + 2\left( \frac{1}{1.4} \right) + 4\left( \frac{1}{1.5} \right) + 2\left( \frac{1}{1.6} \right) + 4\left( \frac{1}{1.7} \right) + 2\left( \frac{1}{1.8} \right) + 4\left( \frac{1}{1.9} \right) + \frac{1}{2}} \right\rbrack} \\ {\phantom{\int_{1}^{2}{\frac{1}{x}dx}} \approx 0.693150} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The Trapezoidal Rule with $$n = 10$$ yielded an approximation of $$0.693771$$ , which is $$0.000624$$ off the value of $$\ln 2 \approx 0.693147$$ to six decimal places. Simpson’s Rule yields an approximation with an error of $$0.000003$$ , a definite improvement over the Trapezoidal Rule.</paragraph>
  </example>

<note type="theorem" source_type="Errors in the Trapezoidal and Simpson Approximations" title="Errors in the Trapezoidal and Simpson Approximations">
    <heading level="4">Errors in the Trapezoidal and Simpson Approximations</heading>
    <paragraph>Suppose the definite integral</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\int_{a}^{b}{f(x)dx}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>is approximated with $$n$$ subintervals.</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>The maximum error incurred in using the Trapezoidal Rule is (8) $$\frac{M\left( {b - a} \right)^{3}}{12n^{2}}$$ where $$M$$ is a number such that $$\left| {f^{''}{(x)|}} \right. \leq M$$ for all $$x$$ in $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ .</item>
      <item>The maximum error incurred in using Simpson’s Rule is (9) $$\frac{M\left( {b - a} \right)^{5}}{180n^{4}}$$ where $$M$$ is a number such that $$\left| {f^{(4)}\left. (x) \right|} \right. \leq M$$ for all $$x$$ in $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ .</item>
    </list>
  </note>

snippet: Example 6: Example 6 Find bounds on the errors incurred when \int_{1}^{2}{\frac{1}{x}dx} is approximated by using (a) the Trapezoidal Rule and (b) Simpson’s Rule with n = 10 . Compare these with the actual errors found in Examples 1 and 3....
body_xml:
<example number="6">
    <heading level="4">Example 6</heading>
    <paragraph>Find bounds on the errors incurred when</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\int_{1}^{2}{\frac{1}{x}dx}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>is approximated by using (a) the Trapezoidal Rule and (b) Simpson’s Rule with $$n = 10$$ . Compare these with the actual errors found in Examples 1 and 3.</paragraph>
    <heading level="4">Solution</heading>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>Here, $$a = 1$$ , $$b = 2$$ , and $$f(x) = 1 \slash x$$ Next, to find a value for $$M$$ , we compute $$f^{\prime}(x) = - \frac{1}{x^{2}}$$ and $$f^{''}(x) = \frac{2}{x^{3}}$$ Since $$f^{''}(x)$$ is positive and decreasing on $$(1,2)$$ (Why?), it attains its maximum value of $$2$$ at $$x = 1$$ , the left endpoint of the interval. Therefore, if we take $$M = 2$$ , then $$\left| {f^{''}{(x)|}} \right. \leq 2$$ . Using (8), we see that the maximum error incurred is $$\frac{2\left( {2 - 1} \right)^{3}}{12(10)^{2}} = \frac{2}{1200} = 0.0016667$$ The actual error found in Example 1, $$0.000624$$ , is much less than the upper bound just found.</item>
      <item>We compute $$f^{'''}(x) = \frac{- 6}{x^{4}}$$ and $$f^{(4)}{(x)} = \frac{24}{x^{5}}$$ Since $$f^{(4)}(x)$$ is positive and decreasing on $$(1,2)$$ (just look at $$f^{(5)}$$ to verify this fact), it attains its maximum at the left endpoint of $$\lbrack 1,2\rbrack$$ . Now, $$f^{(4)}(1) = 24$$ so we may take $$M = 24$$ . Using (9), we obtain the maximum error of $$\frac{24\left( {2 - 1} \right)^{5}}{180(10)^{4}} = 0.0000133$$ The actual error is $$0.000003$$ (see Example 3).</item>
    </list>
  </example>

<example number="1">
    <heading level="4">Example 1</heading>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>Evaluate the definite integral $$I(b)$$ in Equation (11).</item>
      <item>Compute $$I(b)$$ for $$b = 10,100,1000,10,000$$ .</item>
      <item>Evaluate the limit in Equation (11).</item>
      <item>Interpret the results of parts (b) and (c).</item>
    </list>
    <heading level="4">Solution</heading>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>$${I(b) = \int}_{1}^{b}\frac{1}{x^{2}}dx = \left. {- \frac{1}{x}} \right|_{1}^{b} = - \frac{1}{b} + 1$$</item>
      <item>From the result of part (a), $$I(b) = 1 - \frac{1}{b}$$ Therefore, $$\begin{array}{rcl} {I(10)} & = & {1 - \frac{1}{10} = 0.9} \\ {I(100)} & = & {1 - \frac{1}{100} = 0.99} \\ {I(1000)} & = & {1 - \frac{1}{1000} = 0.999} \\ {I(10,000)} & = & {1 - \frac{1}{10,000} = 0.9999} \end{array}$$</item>
      <item>Once again, using the result of part (a), we find $$\begin{array}{l} {{\lim\limits_{b\rightarrow\infty}I(b)}{= \lim\limits_{b\rightarrow\infty}{\int_{1}^{b}{\frac{1}{x^{2}}dx}}}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{b\rightarrow\infty}I(b)}{= \lim\limits_{b\rightarrow\infty}\left( {1 - \frac{1}{b}} \right)}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{b\rightarrow\infty}I(b)}{= 1}} \end{array}$$</item>
      <item>The result of part (c) tells us that the area of the region $$R$$ is $$1$$ . The results of the computations performed in part (b) reinforce our expectation that $$I(b)$$ should approach $$1$$ , the area of the region $$R$$ , as $$b$$ approaches infinity.</item>
    </list>
  </example>

snippet: Example 2: Example 2 Evaluate \int_{2}^{\infty}{\frac{1}{x}dx} if it converges. Solution \begin{array}{l} {\int_{2}^{\infty}{\frac{1}{x}dx} = \lim\limits_{b\rightarrow\infty}\int_{2}^{b}{\frac{1}{x}dx}} \\...
body_xml:
<example number="2">
    <heading level="4">Example 2</heading>
    <paragraph>Evaluate $$\int_{2}^{\infty}{\frac{1}{x}dx}$$ if it converges.</paragraph>
    <heading level="4">Solution</heading>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {\int_{2}^{\infty}{\frac{1}{x}dx} = \lim\limits_{b\rightarrow\infty}\int_{2}^{b}{\frac{1}{x}dx}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{2}^{\infty}{\frac{1}{x}dx}}{= \left. \lim\limits_{b\rightarrow\infty}\ln x \right|_{2}^{b}}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{2}^{\infty}{\frac{1}{x}dx}}{= \lim\limits_{b\rightarrow\infty}\left( {\ln b - \ln 2} \right)}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Since $$\left. \ln b\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ as $$\left. b\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ , the limit does not exist, and we conclude that the given improper integral is divergent.</paragraph>
  </example>

body_xml: Example 3 Find the area of the region $$R$$ under the curve $$y = e^{- {x \slash 2}}$$ for $$x \geq 0$$ . Solution The region $$R$$ is shown in Figure 13. Taking $$b > 0$$ , we compute the area of the region under the curve $$y = e^{- {x \slash 2}}$$ from $$x = 0$$ to $$x = b$$ , namely, $$I(b) = \left. \int_{0}^{b}e^{- {x \slash 2}}dx = - 2e^{- {x \slash 2}} \right|_{0}^{b} = - 2e^{- {b \slash 2}} + 2$$ Then the area of the region $$R$$ is given by $$\begin{array}{l} {\lim\limits_{b\rightarrow\infty}I(b) = \lim\limits_{b\rightarrow\infty}{({2 - 2e^{- {b \slash 2}}})} = 2 - 2\lim\limits_{b\rightarrow\infty}\frac{1}{e^{b \slash 2}}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{b\rightarrow\infty}I(b)} = 2} \end{array}$$

body_xml: Example 4 Find the area of the region $$R$$ bounded above by the $$x$$ -axis, below by the curve $$y = - e^{2x}$$ , and on the right by the vertical line $$x = 1$$ . Solution The region $$R$$ is shown in Figure 14. Taking $$a < 1$$ , compute the area of the region bounded above by the $$x$$ -axis $$\left( {y = 0} \right)$$ , and below by the curve $$y = - e^{2x}$$ from $$x = a$$ to $$x = 1$$ , namely, $$\begin{array}{l} {{I(a)} = {\int_{a}^{1}{\lbrack{0 - {({- e^{2x}})}\rbrack dx = {\int_{a}^{1}{e^{2x}dx}}}}}} \\ {\phantom{I(a)} = {\left. \frac{1}{2}e^{2x} \right|_{a}^{1} = \frac{1}{2}e^{2} - \frac{1}{2}e^{2a}}} \end{array}$$ Then the area of the required region is given by $$\begin{array}{l} {{\lim\limits_{a\rightarrow - \infty}I(a)} = {\lim\limits_{a\rightarrow - \infty}\left( {\frac{1}{2}e^{2} - \frac{1}{2}e^{2a}} \right)}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{a\rightarrow - \infty}I(a)} = {\frac{1}{2}e^{2} - \frac{1}{2}\lim\limits_{a\rightarrow - \infty}e^{2a}}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{a\rightarrow - \infty}I(a)} = {\frac{1}{2}e^{2}}} \end{array}$$

title: Improper Integral of f Over ( - ∞ , ∞ )
snippet: Improper Integral of f Over ( - ∞ , ∞ ): Improper Integral of f Over ( - ∞ , ∞ ) Let f be a continuous function over the unbounded interval \left( {- \infty,\infty} \right) . Let c be any real number, and suppose that both the improper...
body_xml:
<note type="theorem" source_type="Improper Integral of f Over ( - ∞ , ∞ )" title="Improper Integral of f Over ( - ∞ , ∞ )">
    <heading level="4">Improper Integral of f Over ( - ∞ , ∞ )</heading>
    <paragraph>Let $$f$$ be a continuous function over the unbounded interval $$\left( {- \infty,\infty} \right)$$ . Let $$c$$ be any real number, and suppose that both the improper integrals</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\int_{- \infty}^{c}{f(x)dx}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>and</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\int_{c}^{\infty}{f(x)dx}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>are convergent. Then the improper integral of $$f$$ over $$\left( {- \infty,\infty} \right)$$ is defined by</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$${\int_{- \infty}^{\infty}{f(x)dx =}}{\int_{- \infty}^{c}{f(x)dx + {\int_{c}^{\infty}{f(x)dx}}}}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>In this case, we say that the improper integral on the left in Equation (15) is convergent. If either one of the two improper integrals on the right in (15) is divergent, then the improper integral on the left is not defined.</paragraph>
    <note type="sidebar" source_type="Note" title="Note">
      <heading level="4">Note</heading>
      <paragraph>Usually, we choose $$c = 0$$ .</paragraph>
    </note>
  </note>

title: Example 5
snippet: Example 5: Example 5 Evaluate the improper integral \int_{- \infty}^{\infty}{xe^{- x^{2}}dx} and give a geometric interpretation of the results. Solution Take the number c in Equation (15) to be 0 . Let’s first evaluate \begin{array}{l}...
body_xml: Example 5 Evaluate the improper integral $$\int_{- \infty}^{\infty}{xe^{- x^{2}}dx}$$ and give a geometric interpretation of the results. Solution Take the number $$c$$ in Equation (15) to be $$0$$ . Let’s first evaluate $$\begin{array}{l} {{\int_{- \infty}^{0}{xe^{- x^{2}}dx}} = \lim\limits_{a\rightarrow - \infty}{\int_{a}^{0}{xe^{- x^{2}}dx}}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{- \infty}^{\infty}{xe^{- x^{2}}dx}} = \left. \lim\limits_{a\rightarrow - \infty} - \frac{1}{2}e^{- x^{2}} \right|_{a}^{0}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{- \infty}^{\infty}{xe^{- x^{2}}dx}} = {\lim\limits_{a\rightarrow - \infty}\left\lbrack {- \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2}e^{- a^{2}}} \right\rbrack = - \frac{1}{2}}} \end{array}$$ Next, we evaluate $$\begin{array}{l} {{\int_{0}^{\infty}{xe^{- x^{2}}dx}} = \lim\limits_{b\rightarrow\infty}\int_{0}^{b}{xe^{- x^{2}}dx}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{0}^{\infty}{xe^{- x^{2}}dx}} = \left. \lim\limits_{b\rightarrow\infty} - \frac{1}{2}e^{- x^{2}} \right|_{0}^{b}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{0}^{\infty}{xe^{- x^{2}}dx}} = {\lim\limits_{b\rightarrow\infty}\left( {- \frac{1}{2}e^{- b^{2}} + \frac{1}{2}} \right) = \frac{1}{2}}} \end{array}$$ Therefore, $$\begin{array}{l} {{\int_{- \infty}^{\infty}{xe^{- x^{2}}dx}} = {\int_{- \infty}^{0}{xe^{- x^{2}}}}dx + {\int_{0}^{\infty}{xe^{- x^{2}}dx}}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{- \infty}^{\infty}{xe^{- x^{2}}dx}}{= - \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2}}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{- \infty}^{\infty}{xe^{- x^{2}}dx}}{= 0}} \end{array}$$ The graph of $$y = xe^{- x^{2}}$$ is sketched in Figure 15. A glance at the figure tells us that the improper integral $${\int_{- \infty}^{0}{xe^{- x^{2}}}}dx$$ gives the negative of the area of the region $$R_{1}$$ , bounded above by the $$x$$ -axis, below by the curve $$y = xe^{- x^{2}}$$ , and on the right by the $$y$$ -axis $$\left( {x = 0} \right)$$ , provided that the integral is convergent. Also, the improper integral $$\int_{0}^{\infty}{xe^{- x^{2}}dx}$$ gives the area of the region $$R_{2}$$ under the curve $$y = xe^{- x^{2}}$$ for $$x \geq 0$$ . Since the graph of $$f$$ is symmetric with respect to the origin, the area of $$R_{1}$$ is equal to the area of $$R_{2}$$ . In other words, $$\int_{- \infty}^{0}{xe^{- x^{2}}dx = - {\int_{0}^{\infty}{xe^{- x^{2}}dx}}}$$ Therefore, $$\begin{array}{l} {{\int_{- \infty}^{\infty}{xe^{- x^{2}}dx}} = {\int_{- \infty}^{0}{xe^{- x^{2}}dx + {\int_{0}^{\infty}{xe^{- x^{2}}dx}}}}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{- \infty}^{\infty}{xe^{- x^{2}}dx}}{= - {\int_{0}^{\infty}{xe^{- x^{2}}dx + {\int_{0}^{\infty}{xe^{- x^{2}}dx}}}}}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{- \infty}^{\infty}{xe^{- x^{2}}dx}}{= 0}} \end{array}$$ as was shown earlier.

title: Example 1
snippet: Example 1: Example 1 Find the volume of the solid of revolution obtained by revolving the region under the curve y = f(x) = \sqrt{x} from x = 0 to x = 2 about the x -axis. Solution The region under the curve and the resulting solid of...
body_xml: Example 1 Find the volume of the solid of revolution obtained by revolving the region under the curve $$y = f(x) = \sqrt{x}$$ from $$x = 0$$ to $$x = 2$$ about the $$x$$ -axis. Solution The region under the curve and the resulting solid of revolution are shown in Figure 20. Using Formula (18), we find that the required volume is given by $$\begin{array}{l} {{\pi{\int_{0}^{2}{\left( \sqrt{x} \right)^{2}dx}}}{= \pi{\int_{0}^{2}{xdx}}}} \\ {\phantom{\pi{\int_{0}^{2}{\left( \sqrt{x} \right)^{2}dx}}}{= \left. \frac{\pi}{2}x^{2} \right|_{0}^{2} = \frac{\pi}{2}\left( {4 - 0} \right) = 2\pi}} \end{array}$$

title: Example 2
concept_tags: volume of a right circular cone
snippet: Example 2: Example 2 Derive a formula for the volume of a right circular cone of radius r and height h . Solution The cone is shown in Figure 21a. It is the solid of revolution obtained by revolving the region R of Figure 21b about the x...
body_xml: Example 2 Derive a formula for the volume of a right circular cone of radius $$r$$ and height $$h$$ . Solution The cone is shown in Figure 21a. It is the solid of revolution obtained by revolving the region $$R$$ of Figure 21b about the $$x$$ -axis. The region $$R$$ is the region under the straight line $$y = f(x) = \left( {r \slash h} \right)x$$ between $$x = 0$$ and $$x = h$$ . Using Formula (18), we see that the required volume is given by $$\begin{array}{l} {V{= \pi{\int_{0}^{h}{\left\lbrack {\left( \frac{r}{h} \right)x} \right\rbrack^{2}dx = \frac{\pi r^{2}}{h^{2}}{\int_{0}^{h}{x^{2}dx}}}}}} \\ {\phantom{V}{\left. = \left( \frac{\pi r^{2}}{3h^{2}} \right)x^{3} \right|_{0}^{h} = \frac{1}{3}\pi r^{2}h}} \end{array}$$

title: Example 3
snippet: Example 3: Example 3 Find the volume of the solid of revolution obtained by revolving the region bounded by the curves y = e^{x} and y = x^{2} + \frac{1}{2} from x = 0 to x = 1 about the x -axis (Figure 23). Solution Using Formula (19)...
body_xml: Example 3 Find the volume of the solid of revolution obtained by revolving the region bounded by the curves $$y = e^{x}$$ and $$y = x^{2} + \frac{1}{2}$$ from $$x = 0$$ to $$x = 1$$ about the $$x$$ -axis (Figure 23). Solution Using Formula (19) with $$f(x) = e^{x}$$ and $$g(x) = x^{2} + \frac{1}{2}$$ , we see that the required volume is given by $$\begin{array}{l} {V{= \pi{\int_{0}^{1}{\left\lbrack {\left( e^{x} \right)^{2} - \left( {x^{2} + \frac{1}{2}} \right)^{2}} \right\rbrack dx}}}} \\ {\phantom{V}{= \pi{\int_{0}^{1}{\left( {e^{2x} - x^{4} - x^{2} - \frac{1}{4}} \right)dx}}}} \\ {\phantom{V}{= \left. \pi\left( {\frac{1}{2}e^{2x} - \frac{1}{5}x^{5} - \frac{1}{3}x^{3} - \frac{1}{4}x} \right) \right|_{0}^{1}}} \\ {\phantom{V}{= \pi\left\lbrack {\left( {\frac{1}{2}e^{2} - \frac{1}{5} - \frac{1}{3} - \frac{1}{4}} \right) - \frac{1}{2}} \right\rbrack}} \\ {\phantom{V}{= \frac{\pi}{60}\left( {30e^{2} - 77} \right)}} \end{array}$$ or approximately $$7.57$$ .

title: Example 4
snippet: Example 4: Example 4 Find the volume of the solid obtained by revolving the region bounded by the curves y = f(x) = x^{2} and y = g(x) = x^{3} about the x -axis. Solution We first find the point(s) of intersection of the two curves by...
body_xml: Example 4 Find the volume of the solid obtained by revolving the region bounded by the curves $$y = f(x) = x^{2}$$ and $$y = g(x) = x^{3}$$ about the $$x$$ -axis. Solution We first find the point(s) of intersection of the two curves by solving the system of equations $$\left\{ \begin{array}{l} {y = x^{2}} \\ {y = x^{3}} \end{array} \right.$$ We have $$\begin{array}{rcl} x^{3} & = & x^{2} \\ {x^{3} - x^{2}} & = & 0 \\ {x^{2}\left( {x - 1} \right)} & = & 0 \end{array}$$ so $$x = 0$$ or $$x = 1$$ , and the points of intersection are $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ and $$\left( {1,1} \right)$$ (Figure 24). Next, observe that $$g(x) \leq f(x)$$ for all values of $$x$$ between $$x = 0$$ and $$x = 1$$ , so using Formula (19), we find the required volume to be $$\begin{array}{l} {V{= \pi{\int_{0}^{1}{\lbrack{{(x^{2})}^{2} - {(x^{3})}^{2}}\rbrack}}dx}} \\ {\phantom{V}{= \pi{\int_{0}^{1}{({x^{4} - x^{6}})dx}}}} \\ {\phantom{V}{= \pi{\left( {\frac{1}{5}x^{5} - \frac{1}{7}x^{7}} \right)\left. \right|}_{0}^{1}}} \\ {\phantom{V}{= \pi\left( {\frac{1}{5} - \frac{1}{7}} \right)}} \\ {\phantom{V}{= \frac{2\pi}{35}}} \end{array}$$

body_xml: Example 2 Find the domain of each function. $$f(x,y) = x^{2} + y^{2}$$ $$g(x,y) = \frac{2}{x - y}$$ $$h{({x,y})} = \sqrt{1 - x^{2} - y^{2}}$$ Solution $$f{({x,y})}$$ is defined for all real values of $$x$$ and $$y$$ , so the domain of the function $$f$$ is the set of all points $$({x,y})$$ in the $$xy$$ -plane. $$g(x,y)$$ is defined for all $$x \neq y$$ , so the domain of the function $$g$$ is the set of all points in the $$xy$$ -plane except those lying on the line $$y = x$$ (Figure 1a). We require that $$1 - x^{2} - y^{2} \geq 0$$ or $$x^{2} + y^{2} \leq 1$$ , which is just the set of all points $$({x,y})$$ lying on and inside the circle of radius $$1$$ with center at the origin (Figure 1b).

    <paragraph math="block">$$f(x,y) = x^{2} - xy^{2} + y^{3}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>What is the rate of change of the function $$f$$ in the $$x$$ -direction at the point $$\left( {1,2} \right)$$ ?</paragraph>
    <paragraph>What is the rate of change of the function $$f$$ in the $$y$$ -direction at the point $$\left( {1,2} \right)$$ ?</paragraph>
    <heading level="4">Solution</heading>
    <paragraph>To compute $$\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}$$ , think of the variable $$y$$ as a constant and differentiate the resulting function of $$x$$ with respect to $$x$$ . Let’s write</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$f(x,y) = x^{2} - xy^{2} + y^{3}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>where the variable $$y$$ to be treated as a constant is shown in color. Then,</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{\partial f}{\partial x} = 2x - y^{2}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>To compute $$\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}$$ , think of the variable $$x$$ as being fixed—that is, as a constant—and differentiate the resulting function of $$y$$ with respect to $$y$$ . In this case,</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$f(x,y) = x^{2} - xy^{2} + y^{3}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>so</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{\partial f}{\partial y} = - 2xy + 3y^{2}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The rate of change of the function $$f$$ in the $$x$$ -direction at the point $$\left( {1,2} \right)$$ is given by</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$f_{x}{({1,2})} = \left. \frac{\partial f}{\partial x} \right|_{({1,2})} = 2(1) - 2^{2} = - 2$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>That is, $$f$$ decreases $$2$$ units for each unit increase in the $$x$$ -direction, $$y$$ being kept constant $$\left( {y = 2} \right)$$ . The rate of change of the function $$f$$ in the $$y$$ -direction at the point $$\left( {1,2} \right)$$ is given by</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$f_{y}{({1,2})} = \left. \frac{\partial f}{\partial y} \right|_{({1,2})} = - 2(1)(2) + 3(2)^{2} = 8$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>That is, $$f$$ increases $$8$$ units for each unit increase in the $$y$$ -direction, $$x$$ being kept constant $$\left( {x = 1} \right)$$ .</paragraph>
  </example>

snippet: Example 2: Example 2 Compute the first partial derivatives of each function. f\left( {x,y} \right) = \frac{\mathit{xy}}{x^{2} + y^{2}} g(s,t) = {(s^{2} - st + t^{2})}^{5} h(u,v) = e^{u^{2} - v^{2}} f(x,y) = \ln(x^{2} + 2y^{2}) Solution To...
body_xml:
<example number="2">
    <heading level="4">Example 2</heading>
    <paragraph>Compute the first partial derivatives of each function.</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>$$f\left( {x,y} \right) = \frac{\mathit{xy}}{x^{2} + y^{2}}$$</item>
      <item>$$g(s,t) = {(s^{2} - st + t^{2})}^{5}$$</item>
      <item>$$h(u,v) = e^{u^{2} - v^{2}}$$</item>
      <item>$$f(x,y) = \ln(x^{2} + 2y^{2})$$</item>
    </list>
    <heading level="4">Solution</heading>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>To compute $$\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}$$ , think of the variable $$y$$ as a constant. Thus, $$f\left( {x,y} \right) = \frac{xy}{x^{2} + y^{2}}$$ Then using the Quotient Rule, we have $$\begin{array}{l} {\frac{\partial f}{\partial x} = {\frac{{({x^{2} + y^{2}})}y - xy{({2x})}}{{({x^{2} + y^{2}})}^{2}} = \frac{x^{2}y + y^{3} - 2x^{2}y}{{({x^{2} + y^{2}})}^{2}}}} \\ {\phantom{\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}} = \frac{y{({y^{2} - x^{2}})}}{{({x^{2} + y^{2}})}^{2}}} \end{array}$$ upon simplification and factorization. To compute $$\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}$$ , think of the variable $$x$$ as a constant. Thus, $$f\left( {x,y} \right) = \frac{xy}{x^{2} + y^{2}}$$ Then using the Quotient Rule once again, we obtain $$\begin{array}{l} {\frac{\partial f}{\partial y} = {\frac{{({x^{2} + y^{2}})}x - xy{({2y})}}{{({x^{2} + y^{2}})}^{2}} = \frac{x^{3} + xy^{2} - 2xy^{2}}{{({x^{2} + y^{2}})}^{2}}}} \\ {\phantom{\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}} = \frac{x{({x^{2} - y^{2}})}}{{({x^{2} + y^{2}})}^{2}}} \end{array}$$</item>
      <item>To compute $$\frac{\partial g}{\partial s}$$ , we treat the variable $$t$$ as if it were a constant. Thus, $$g(s,t) = {(s^{2} - st + t^{2})}^{5}$$ Using the General Power Rule, we find $$\begin{array}{l} {\frac{\partial g}{\partial s} = {5{({s^{2} - st + t^{2}})}^{4} \cdot {({2s - t})}}} \\ {\phantom{\frac{\partial g}{\partial s}} = {5{({2s - t})}{({s^{2} - st + t^{2}})}^{4}}} \end{array}$$ To compute $$\frac{\partial g}{\partial t}$$ , we treat the variable $$s$$ as if it were a constant. Thus, $$\begin{array}{rcl} {g(s,t)} & = & {(s^{2} - st + t^{2})}^{5} \\ \frac{\partial g}{\partial t} & = & {5{(s^{2} - st + t^{2})}^{4}( - s + 2t)} \\ & = & {5(2t - s){(s^{2} - st + t^{2})}^{4}} \end{array}$$</item>
      <item>To compute $$\frac{\partial h}{\partial u}$$ , think of the variable $$v$$ as a constant. Thus, $$h(u,v) = e^{u^{2} - v^{2}}$$ Using the Chain Rule for Exponential Functions, we have $$\frac{\partial h}{\partial u} = e^{u^{2} - v^{2}} \cdot 2u = 2ue^{u^{2} - v^{2}}$$ Next, we treat the variable $$u$$ as if it were a constant, $$h(u,v) = e^{u^{2} - v^{2}}$$ and we obtain $$\frac{\partial h}{\partial v} = e^{u^{2} - v^{2}} \cdot \left( {- 2v} \right) = - 2ve^{u^{2} - v^{2}}$$</item>
      <item>To compute $$\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}$$ , think of the variable $$y$$ as a constant. Thus, $$f(x,y) = \ln(x^{2} + 2y^{2})$$ so the Chain Rule for Logarithmic Functions gives $$\frac{\partial f}{\partial x} = \frac{2x}{x^{2} + 2y^{2}}$$ Next, treating the variable $$x$$ as if it were a constant, we find $$\begin{array}{rcl} {f{({x,y})}} & = & {\ln{({x^{2} + 2y^{2}})}} \\ \frac{\partial f}{\partial y} & = & \frac{4y}{x^{2} + 2y^{2}} \end{array}$$</item>
    </list>
  </example>

    <paragraph>Compute the first partial derivatives of the function</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$w = f(x,y,z) = xyz - xe^{yz} + x\ln y$$</paragraph>
    <heading level="4">Solution</heading>
    <paragraph>Here we have a function of three variables, $$x$$ , $$y$$ , and $$z$$ , and we are required to compute</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}, \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}, \frac{\partial f}{\partial z}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>To compute $$f_{x}$$ , we think of the other two variables, $$y$$ and $$z$$ , as fixed, and we differentiate the resulting function of $$x$$ with respect to $$x$$ , thereby obtaining</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$f_{x} = yz - e^{yz} + \ln y$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>To compute $$f_{y}$$ , we think of the other two variables, $$x$$ and $$z$$ , as constants, and we differentiate the resulting function of $$y$$ with respect to $$y$$ . We then obtain</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$f_{y} = xz - xze^{yz} + \frac{x}{y}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Finally, to compute $$f_{z}$$ , we treat the variables $$x$$ and $$y$$ as constants and differentiate the function $$f$$ with respect to $$z$$ , obtaining</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$f_{z} = xy - xye^{yz}$$</paragraph>

title: Portfolio Karthik Ramachandran
snippet: Portfolio Karthik Ramachandran: Portfolio Karthik Ramachandran Title Principal Software Engineer Institution Iron Mountain Iron Mountain is the world’s largest provider of document management solutions. Although the company has its roots...
body_xml: Portfolio Karthik Ramachandran Title Principal Software Engineer Institution Iron Mountain Iron Mountain is the world’s largest provider of document management solutions. Although the company has its roots in paper document storage, it has become the leader in digital document solutions as well. In addition to providing online backup and digital archiving services, Iron Mountain offers various digital document management tools. As a principal software engineer at Iron Mountain, I help to develop eDiscovery products and services designed specifically for lawyers. When lawyers search for information relating to a corporate lawsuit, for example, it can be very difficult for them to find the information they need if they are searching through terabytes of unorganized data. To address this challenge, Iron Mountain has developed a variety of techniques to organize data automatically based on the statistical analysis of words and phrases contained within documents and email messages. Although we use statistical analysis to initiate the organization of data, we apply calculus to refine our products and services. When word sets are very large, it is important to focus on particular words and phrases that convey vital information. At Iron Mountain, we use optimization techniques involving partial derivatives to detect the most informative words and phrases within documents and allot them an apportioned weight in the organization process. The methods outlined above allow us to organize data into folders—or clusters—of related documents. Ultimately, this enables us to improve upon traditional search capabilities by grouping search results into concept folders, minimizing cost and reducing the time needed for lawyers to find relevant documents. With the aid of mathematical analysis, we provide robust eDiscovery products and services that radically improve legal workflow. As the amount of electronically stored information grows, our application of statistics and calculus allows us to remain at the forefront of our field.

    <heading level="4">Substitute and Complementary Commodities</heading>
    <paragraph>Two commodities $$A$$ and $$B$$ are substitute commodities if</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{\partial f}{\partial q} > 0$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>and</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{\partial g}{\partial p} > 0$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Two commodities $$A$$ and $$B$$ are complementary commodities if</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{\partial f}{\partial q} < 0$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>and</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{\partial g}{\partial p} < 0$$</paragraph>
  </note>

body_xml:
<example number="6">
    <heading level="4">Example 6</heading>
    <paragraph>Find the second-order partial derivatives of the function</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$f(x,y) = x^{3} - 3x^{2}y + 3xy^{2} + y^{2}$$</paragraph>
    <heading level="4">Solution</heading>
    <paragraph>The first partial derivatives of $$f$$ are</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} f_{x} & = & {\frac{\partial}{\partial x}{({x^{3} - 3x^{2}y + 3xy^{2} + y^{2}})}} \\ & = & {3x^{2} - 6xy + 3y^{2}} \\ f_{y} & = & {\frac{\partial}{\partial y}{({x^{3} - 3x^{2}y + 3xy^{2} + y^{2}})}} \\ & = & {- 3x^{2} + 6xy + 2y} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Therefore,</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} f_{\mathit{xx}} & = & {\frac{\partial}{\partial x}{(f_{x})} = \frac{\partial}{\partial x}{({3x^{2} - 6xy + 3y^{2}})}} \\ & = & {6x - 6y = 6{({x - y})}} \\ f_{\mathit{xy}} & = & {\frac{\partial}{\partial y}{(f_{x})} = \frac{\partial}{\partial y}{({3x^{2} - 6xy + 3y^{2}})}} \\ & = & {- 6x + 6y = 6{({y - x})}} \\ f_{\mathit{yx}} & = & {\frac{\partial}{\partial x}{(f_{y})} = \frac{\partial}{\partial x}{({- 3x^{2} + 6xy + 2y})}} \\ & = & {- 6x + 6y = 6{({y - x})}} \\ f_{\mathit{yy}} & = & {\frac{\partial}{\partial y}{(f_{y})} = \frac{\partial}{\partial y}{({- 3x^{2} + 6xy + 2y})}} \\ & = & {6x + 2} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Note that $$f_{\mathit{xy}} = f_{\mathit{yx}}$$ everywhere.</paragraph>
  </example>

body_xml:
<example number="7">
    <heading level="4">Example 7</heading>
    <paragraph>Find the second-order partial derivatives of the function</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$f(x,y) = e^{xy^{2}}$$</paragraph>
    <heading level="4">Solution</heading>
    <paragraph>We have</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} f_{x} & = & {\frac{\partial}{\partial x}{(e^{xy^{2}})}} \\ & = & {y^{2}e^{xy^{2}}} \\ f_{y} & = & {\frac{\partial}{\partial y}{(e^{xy^{2}})}} \\ & = & {2xye^{xy^{2}}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>so the required second-order partial derivatives of $$f$$ are</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} f_{\mathit{xx}} & = & {\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(f_{x}) = \frac{\partial}{\partial x}(y^{2}e^{xy^{2}})} \\ & = & {y^{4}e^{xy^{2}}} \\ f_{\mathit{xy}} & = & {\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(f_{x}) = \frac{\partial}{\partial y}(y^{2}e^{xy^{2}})} \\ & = & {2ye^{xy^{2}} + 2xy^{3}e^{xy^{2}}} \\ & = & {2ye^{xy^{2}}(1 + xy^{2})} \\ f_{\mathit{yx}} & = & {\frac{\partial}{\partial x}(f_{y}) = \frac{\partial}{\partial x}(2xye^{xy^{2}})} \\ & = & {2ye^{xy^{2}} + 2xy^{3}e^{xy^{2}}} \\ & = & {2ye^{xy^{2}}(1 + xy^{2})} \\ f_{\mathit{yy}} & = & {\frac{\partial}{\partial y}(f_{y}) = \frac{\partial}{\partial y}(2xye^{xy^{2}})} \\ & = & {2xe^{xy^{2}} + (2xy)(2xy)e^{xy^{2}}} \\ & = & {2xe^{xy^{2}}(1 + 2xy^{2})} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <note type="theorem" source_type="">
      <heading level="4">Algebra</heading>
      <paragraph>See Example 8.</paragraph>
    </note>
    <paragraph>Note that $$f_{\mathit{xy}} = f_{\mathit{yx}}$$ everywhere.</paragraph>

<note type="theorem" source_type="Relative Extrema of a Function of Two Variables" title="Relative Extrema of a Function of Two Variables">
    <heading level="4">Relative Extrema of a Function of Two Variables</heading>
    <paragraph>Let $$f$$ be a function defined on a region $$R$$ containing the point $$({a,b})$$ . Then $$f$$ has a relative maximum at $$({a,b})$$ if $$f{({x,y})} \leq f(a,b)$$ for all points $$({x,y})$$ that are sufficiently close to $$({a,b})$$ . The number $$f(a,b)$$ is called a relative maximum value . Similarly, $$f$$ has a relative minimum at $$({a,b})$$ , with relative minimum value $$f(a,b)$$ , if $$f{({x,y})} \geq f(a,b)$$ for all points $$({x,y})$$ that are sufficiently close to $$({a,b})$$ .</paragraph>
  </note>

<note type="theorem" source_type="Determining Relative Extrema" title="Determining Relative Extrema">
    <heading level="4">Determining Relative Extrema</heading>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>Find the critical points of $$f(x,y)$$ by solving the system of simultaneous equations $$\begin{array}{l} {f_{x}{({x,y})} = 0} \\ {f_{y}{({x,y})} = 0} \end{array}$$</item>
      <item>The second derivative test: Let $$D\left( {x,y} \right) = f_{xx}\left( {x,y} \right)f_{yy}\left( {x,y} \right) - f_{xy}^{2}\left( {x,y} \right)$$ Then $$D{({a,b})} > 0$$ and $$f_{\mathit{xx}}{({a,b})} < 0$$ implies that $$f(x,y)$$ has a relative maximum at the point $$({a,b})$$ . $$D{({a,b})} > 0$$ and $$f_{\mathit{xx}}{({a,b})} > 0$$ implies that $$f(x,y)$$ has a relative minimum at the point $$({a,b})$$ . $$D{({a,b})} < 0$$ implies that $$f(x,y)$$ has neither a relative maximum nor a relative minimum at the point $$({a,b})$$ . The point $$({a,b,f(a,b)})$$ is called a saddle point. $$D{({a,b})} = 0$$ implies that the test is inconclusive, so some other technique must be used to solve the problem.</item>
    </list>
  </note>

snippet: Example 1: Example 1 Find the relative extrema of the function f{({x,y})} = x^{2} + y^{2} Solution We have \begin{array}{l} {f_{x}{({x,y})} = 2x} \\ {f_{y}{({x,y})} = 2y} \end{array} To find the critical point(s) of f , we set...
body_xml: Example 1 Find the relative extrema of the function $$f{({x,y})} = x^{2} + y^{2}$$ Solution We have $$\begin{array}{l} {f_{x}{({x,y})} = 2x} \\ {f_{y}{({x,y})} = 2y} \end{array}$$ To find the critical point(s) of $$f$$ , we set $$f_{x}{({x,y})} = 0$$ and $$f_{y}{({x,y})} = 0$$ and solve the resulting system of simultaneous equations $$2x = 0$$ and $$2y = 0$$ . We obtain $$x = 0$$ , $$y = 0$$ , or $$({0,0})$$ , as the sole critical point of $$f$$ . Next, we apply the second derivative test to determine the nature of the critical point $$({0,0})$$ . We compute $${f_{\mathit{xx}}{({x,y})} = 2}{f_{\mathit{xy}}{({x,y})} = 0}{f_{\mathit{yy}}{({x,y})} = 2}$$ and $$D{({x,y})} = f_{\mathit{xx}}{({x,y})}f_{\mathit{yy}}{({x,y})} - f_{xy}^{2}{({x,y})} = {(2)}{(2)} - 0 = 4$$ In particular, $$D{({0,0})} = 4$$ . Since $$D{({0,0})} > 0$$ and $$f_{\mathit{xx}}{({0,0})} = 2 > 0$$ , we conclude that $$f(x,y)$$ has a relative minimum at the point $$({0,0})$$ . The relative minimum value, $$0$$ , also happens to be the absolute minimum of $$f$$ . The graph of the function $$f$$ , shown in Figure 20, confirms these results.

body_xml:
<example number="2">
    <heading level="4">Example 2</heading>
    <paragraph>Find the relative extrema of the function</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$f{({x,y})} = 3x^{2} - 4xy + 4y^{2} - 4x + 8y + 4$$</paragraph>
    <heading level="4">Solution</heading>
    <paragraph>We have</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{lcl} {f_{x}{({x,y})}} & = & {6x - 4y - 4} \\ {f_{y}{({x,y})}} & = & {- 4x + 8y + 8} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>To find the critical points of $$f$$ , we set $$f_{x}{({x,y})} = 0$$ and $$f_{y}{({x,y})} = 0$$ and solve the resulting system of simultaneous equations</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcr} {6x - 4y} & = & 4 \\ {- 4x + 8y} & = & {- 8} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Multiplying the first equation by $$2$$ and the second equation by $$3$$ , we obtain the equivalent system</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{ccr} {12x - 8y} & = & 8 \\ {- 12x + 24y} & = & {- 24} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Adding the two equations gives $$16y = - 16$$ , or $$y = - 1$$ . We substitute this value for $$y$$ into either equation in the system to get $$x = 0$$ . Thus, the only critical point of $$f$$ is the point $$({0, - 1})$$ . Next, we apply the second derivative test to determine whether the point $$({0, - 1})$$ gives rise to a relative extremum of $$f$$ . We compute</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$${f_{\mathit{xx}}{({x,y})} = 6}{f_{\mathit{xy}}{({x,y})} = - 4}{f_{\mathit{yy}}{({x,y})} = 8}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>and</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$D{({x,y})} = f_{\mathit{xx}}{({x,y})}f_{\mathit{yy}}{({x,y})} - f_{xy}^{2}{({x,y})} = {(6)}{(8)} - {({- 4})}^{2} = 32$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Since $$D\left( {0, - 1} \right) = 32 > 0$$ and $$f_{\mathit{xx}}{({0, - 1})} = 6 > 0$$ , we conclude that $$f(x,y)$$ has a relative minimum at the point $$({0, - 1})$$ . The value of $$f(x,y)$$ at the point $$({0, - 1})$$ is given by</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$f{({0, - 1})} = 3{(0)}^{2} - 4{(0)}{({- 1})} + 4{({- 1})}^{2} - 4{(0)} + 8{({- 1})} + 4 = 0$$</paragraph>
  </example>

    <paragraph math="block">$$f{({x,y})} = 4y^{3} + x^{2} - 12y^{2} - 36y + 2$$</paragraph>
    <heading level="4">Solution</heading>
    <paragraph>To find the critical points of $$f$$ , we set $$f_{x} = 0$$ and $$f_{y} = 0$$ simultaneously, obtaining</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{lcl} {f_{x}{({x,y})}} & = & {2x = 0} \\ {f_{y}{({x,y})}} & = & {12y^{2} - 24y - 36 = 0} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The first equation implies that $$x = 0$$ . The second equation implies that</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} {y^{2} - 2y - 3} & = & 0 \\ {{({y + 1})}{({y - 3})}} & = & 0 \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>that is, $$y = - 1$$ or $$3$$ . Therefore, there are two critical points of the function $$f$$ : $$({0, - 1})$$ and $$({0,3})$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Next, we apply the second derivative test to determine the nature of each of the two critical points. We compute</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$${f_{\mathit{xx}}{({x,y})} = 2}{f_{\mathit{xy}}{({x,y})} = 0}{f_{\mathit{yy}}{({x,y})} = 24y - 24 = 24{({y - 1})}}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Therefore,</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$D{({x,y})} = f_{\mathit{xx}}{({x,y})}f_{\mathit{yy}}{({x,y})} - f_{xy}^{2}{({x,y})} = 48{({y - 1})}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>For the point $$({0, - 1})$$ ,</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$D{({0, - 1})} = 48{({- 1 - 1})} = - 96 < 0$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Since $$D\left( {0, - 1} \right) < 0$$ , we conclude that the point $$({0, - 1})$$ gives a saddle point of $$f$$ . For the point $$({0,3})$$ ,</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$D{({0,3})} = 48{({3 - 1})} = 96 > 0$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Since $$D{({0,3})} > 0$$ and $$f_{\mathit{xx}}{({0,3})} > 0$$ , we conclude that the function $$f$$ has a relative minimum at the point $$({0,3})$$ . Furthermore, since</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {{f{({0,3})}} = {4{(3)}^{3} + {(0)}^{2} - 12{(3)}^{2} - 36{(3)} + 2}} \\ {\phantom{f{({0,3})}} = {- 106}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>we see that the relative minimum value of $$f$$ is $$- 106$$ .</paragraph>
  </example>

<note type="procedure" source_type="The Method of Least Squares" title="The Method of Least Squares">
    <heading level="4">The Method of Least Squares</heading>
    <paragraph>Suppose we are given $$n$$ data points:</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$${P_{1}\left( {x_{1},y_{1}} \right), P_{2}\left( {x_{2},y_{2}} \right), P_{3}\left( {x_{3},y_{3}} \right),}\ldots,P_{n}\left( {x_{n},y_{n}} \right)$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Then the least-squares (regression) line for the data is given by the linear equation</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$y = f(x) = mx + b$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>where the constants $$m$$ and $$b$$ satisfy the equations</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{matrix} {{({x_{1}^{2} + x_{2}^{2} + x_{3}^{2} + \cdots + x_{n}^{2}})}m + {({x_{1} + x_{2} + x_{3} + \cdots + x_{n}})}b} \\ {= x_{1}y_{1} + x_{2}y_{2} + x_{3}y_{3} + \cdots + x_{n}y_{n}} \end{matrix}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>and</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{matrix} {\left( {x_{1} + x_{2} + x_{3} + \cdots + x_{n}} \right)m + nb} \\ {= y_{1} + y_{2} + y_{3} + \cdots + y_{n}} \end{matrix}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>simultaneously. Equations (8) and (9) are called normal equations .</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Example 1
snippet: Example 1: Example 1 Find the relative minimum of the function f\left( {x,y} \right) = 2x^{2} + y^{2} subject to the constraint g\left( {x,y} \right) = x + y - 1 = 0 . Solution Solving the constraint equation for y explicitly in terms of x...
body_xml: Example 1 Find the relative minimum of the function $$f\left( {x,y} \right) = 2x^{2} + y^{2}$$ subject to the constraint $$g\left( {x,y} \right) = x + y - 1 = 0$$ . Solution Solving the constraint equation for $$y$$ explicitly in terms of $$x$$ , we obtain $$y = - x + 1$$ . Substituting this value of $$y$$ into the function $$f\left( {x,y} \right) = 2x^{2} + y^{2}$$ results in a function of $$x$$ , $$h(x) = 2x^{2} + \left( {- x + 1} \right)^{2} = 3x^{2} - 2x + 1$$ The function $$h$$ describes the curve $$C$$ lying on the graph of $$f$$ on which the constrained relative minimum of $$f$$ occurs. To find this point, use the technique developed in Chapter 4 to determine the relative extrema of a function of one variable: $$h^{\prime}(x) = 6x - 2 = 2\left( {3x - 1} \right)$$ Setting $$h^{\prime}(x) = 0$$ gives $$x = \frac{1}{3}$$ as the sole critical number of the function $$h$$ . Next, we find $$h^{''}(x) = 6$$ and, in particular, $$h^{''}\left( \frac{1}{3} \right) = 6 > 0$$ Therefore, by the second derivative test, the point $$x = \frac{1}{3}$$ gives rise to a relative minimum of $$h$$ . Substitute this value of $$x$$ into the constraint equation $$x + y - 1 = 0$$ to get $$y = \frac{2}{3}$$ . Thus, the point $$\left( {\frac{1}{3},\frac{2}{3}} \right)$$ gives rise to the required constrained relative minimum of $$f$$ . Since $$f\left( {\frac{1}{3},\frac{2}{3}} \right) = 2\left( \frac{1}{3} \right)^{2} + \left( \frac{2}{3} \right)^{2} = \frac{2}{3}$$ the required constrained relative minimum value of $$f$$ is $$\frac{2}{3}$$ at the point $$\left( {\frac{1}{3},\frac{2}{3}} \right)$$ . It may be shown that $$\frac{2}{3}$$ is in fact a constrained absolute minimum value of $$f$$ (Figure 27).

title: The Method of Lagrange Multipliers
snippet: The Method of Lagrange Multipliers: The Method of Lagrange Multipliers To find the relative extrema of the function f\left( {x,y} \right) subject to the constraint g\left( {x,y} \right) = 0 (assuming that these extreme values exist), Form...
body_xml:
<note type="procedure" source_type="The Method of Lagrange Multipliers" title="The Method of Lagrange Multipliers">
    <heading level="4">The Method of Lagrange Multipliers</heading>
    <paragraph>To find the relative extrema of the function $$f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ subject to the constraint $$g\left( {x,y} \right) = 0$$ (assuming that these extreme values exist),</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>Form an auxiliary function $$F\left( {x,y,\lambda} \right) = f\left( {x,y} \right) + \lambda g\left( {x,y} \right)$$ called the Lagrangian function (the variable $$\lambda$$ is called the Lagrange multiplier).</item>
      <item>Solve the system that consists of the equations $$F_{x} = 0 F_{y} = 0 F_{\lambda} = 0$$ for all values of $$x$$ , $$y$$ , and $$\lambda$$ . The solutions of the system are candidates for the extrema of $$f$$ .</item>
      <item>Evaluate $$f$$ at each point found in Step 2. The largest value yields the constrained maximum of $$f$$ , and the smallest value yields the constrained minimum of $$f$$ .</item>
    </list>
  </note>

title: Example 2
snippet: Example 2: Example 2 Using the method of Lagrange multipliers, find the relative minimum of the function f\left( {x,y} \right) = 2x^{2} + y^{2} subject to the constraint x + y = 1 . Solution Write the constraint equation x + y = 1 in the...
body_xml:
<example number="2">
    <heading level="4">Example 2</heading>
    <paragraph>Using the method of Lagrange multipliers, find the relative minimum of the function</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$f\left( {x,y} \right) = 2x^{2} + y^{2}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>subject to the constraint $$x + y = 1$$ .</paragraph>
    <heading level="4">Solution</heading>
    <paragraph>Write the constraint equation $$x + y = 1$$ in the form $$g\left( {x,y} \right) = x + y - 1 = 0$$ . Then, form the Lagrangian function</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {{F\left( {x,y,\lambda} \right)} = {f\left( {x,y} \right) + \lambda g\left( {x,y} \right)}} \\ {\phantom{F\left( {x,y,\lambda} \right)} = {2x^{2} + y^{2} + \lambda\left( {x + y - 1} \right)}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>To find the critical point(s) of the function $$F$$ , solve the system composed of the equations</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rclcc} F_{x} & = & {4x + \lambda} & = & 0 \\ F_{y} & = & {2y + \lambda} & = & 0 \\ F_{\lambda} & = & {x + y - 1} & = & 0 \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solving the first and second equations in this system for $$x$$ and $$y$$ in terms of $$\lambda$$ , we obtain</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$x = - \frac{1}{4}\lambda$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>and</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$y = - \frac{1}{2}\lambda$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>which, upon substitution into the third equation, yields</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$- \frac{1}{4}\lambda - \frac{1}{2}\lambda - 1 = 0$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>or</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\lambda = - \frac{4}{3}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Therefore, $$x = \frac{1}{3}$$ and $$y = \frac{2}{3}$$ , and $$\left( {\frac{1}{3},\frac{2}{3}} \right)$$ affords a constrained minimum of the function $$f$$ , in agreement with the result obtained earlier.</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Example 3
snippet: Example 3: Example 3 Use the method of Lagrange multipliers to find the minimum of the function f\left( {x,y,z} \right) = 2xy + 6yz + 8xz subject to the constraint xyz = 12,000 (Note: The existence of the minimum is suggested by the...
body_xml:
<example number="3">
    <heading level="4">Example 3</heading>
    <paragraph>Use the method of Lagrange multipliers to find the minimum of the function</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$f\left( {x,y,z} \right) = 2xy + 6yz + 8xz$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>subject to the constraint</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$xyz = 12,000$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>(Note: The existence of the minimum is suggested by the geometry of the problem.)</paragraph>
    <heading level="4">Solution</heading>
    <paragraph>Write the constraint equation $$xyz = 12,000$$ in the form $$g\left( {x,y,z} \right) = xyz - 12,000 = 0$$ . Then the Lagrangian function is</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {{F\left( {x,y,z,\lambda} \right)} = {f\left( {x,y,z} \right) + \lambda g\left( {x,y,z} \right)}} \\ {\phantom{F\left( {x,y,z,\lambda} \right)} = {2xy + 6yz + 8xz + \lambda\left( {xyz - 12,000} \right)}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>To find the critical point(s) of the function $$F$$ we solve the system composed of the equations</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{lcl} F_{x} & = & {{2y + 8z + \lambda yz} = 0} \\ F_{y} & = & {{2x + 6z + \lambda xz} = 0} \\ F_{z} & = & {{6y + 8x + \lambda xy} = 0} \\ F_{\lambda} & = & {{xyz - 12,000} = 0} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Solving the first three equations of the system for $$\lambda$$ in terms of $$x$$ , $$y$$ , and $$z$$ , we have</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{lcl} \lambda & = & {- \frac{2y + 8z}{\mathit{yz}}} \\ \lambda & = & {- \frac{2x + 6z}{\mathit{xz}}} \\ \lambda & = & {- \frac{6y + 8x}{\mathit{xy}}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Equating the first two expressions for $$\lambda$$ leads to</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} \frac{2y + 8z}{\mathit{yz}} & = & \frac{2x + 6z}{\mathit{xz}} \\ {2xy + 8xz} & = & {2xy + 6yz} \\ x & = & {\frac{3}{4}y} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Next, equating the second and third expressions for $$\lambda$$ above yields</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{ccl} \frac{2x + 6z}{\mathit{xz}} & = & \frac{6y + 8x}{\mathit{xy}} \\ {2xy + 6yz} & = & {6yz + 8xz} \\ z & = & {\frac{1}{4}y} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Finally, substituting these values of $$x$$ and $$z$$ into the equation $$xyz - 12,000 = 0$$ , the fourth equation of the first system of equations, we have</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{ccl} {\left( {\frac{3}{4}y} \right)(y)\left( {\frac{1}{4}y} \right) - 12,000} & = & 0 \\ y^{3} & = & {\frac{(12,000)(4)(4)}{3} = 64,000} \\ y & = & 40 \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The corresponding values of $$x$$ and $$z$$ are given by $$x = \frac{3}{4}(40) = 30$$ and $$z = \frac{1}{4}(40) = 10$$ . Therefore, we see that the point $$\left( {30,40,10} \right)$$ gives the constrained minimum of $$f$$ . The minimum value is</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$f\left( {30,40,10} \right) = 2(30)(40) + 6(40)(10) + 8(30)(10) = 7200$$</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Example 1
snippet: Example 1: Example 1 Let z = f\left( {x,y} \right) = 2x^{2} - xy . Find \Delta z . Then use your result to find the change in z if \left( {x,y} \right) changes from \left( {1,1} \right) to \left( {0.98,1.03} \right) . Solution Using (16),...
body_xml:
<example number="1">
    <heading level="4">Example 1</heading>
    <paragraph>Let $$z = f\left( {x,y} \right) = 2x^{2} - xy$$ . Find $$\Delta z$$ . Then use your result to find the change in $$z$$ if $$\left( {x,y} \right)$$ changes from $$\left( {1,1} \right)$$ to $$\left( {0.98,1.03} \right)$$ .</paragraph>
    <heading level="4">Solution</heading>
    <paragraph>Using (16), we obtain</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {{\Delta z}{= f(x + \Delta x,y + \Delta y) - f(x,y)}} \\ {\phantom{\Delta z}{= \lbrack 2{(x + \Delta x)}^{2} - (x + \Delta x)(y + \Delta y)\rbrack - (2x^{2} - xy)}} \\ {\phantom{\Delta z}{= 2x^{2} + 4x\Delta x + 2{(\Delta x)}^{2} - xy - x\Delta y - y\Delta x - \Delta x\Delta y - 2x^{2} + xy}} \\ {\phantom{\Delta z}{= (4x - y)\Delta x - x\Delta y + 2{(\Delta x)}^{2} - \Delta x\Delta y}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Next, to find the increment in $$z$$ if $$\left( {x,y} \right)$$ changes from $$\left( {1,1} \right)$$ to $$\left( {0.98,1.03} \right)$$ , we note that $$\Delta x = 0.98 - 1 = - 0.02$$ and $$\Delta y = 1.03 - 1 = 0.03$$ . Therefore, using the result obtained earlier with $$x = 1$$ , $$y = 1$$ , $$\Delta x = - 0.02$$ , and $$\Delta y = 0.03$$ , we obtain</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {\Delta z = \left\lbrack {4(1) - 1} \right\rbrack\left( {- 0.02} \right) - (1)(0.03) + 2\left( {- 0.02} \right)^{2} - \left( {- 0.02} \right)(0.03)} \\ {\phantom{\Delta z}{= - 0.0886}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>You can verify the correctness of this result by calculating the quantity $$f\left( {0.98,1.03} \right) - f\left( {1,1} \right)$$ .</paragraph>
  </example>
