title: Example 2
snippet: Example 2: Example 2 Let z = 2x^{2}y + y^{3} . Find the differential dz of z . Find the approximate change in z when x changes from x = 1 to x = 1.01 and y changes from y = 2 to y = 1.98 . Find the actual change in z when x changes from x...
body_xml:
<example number="2">
    <heading level="4">Example 2</heading>
    <paragraph>Let $$z = 2x^{2}y + y^{3}$$ .</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>Find the differential $$dz$$ of $$z$$ .</item>
      <item>Find the approximate change in $$z$$ when $$x$$ changes from $$x = 1$$ to $$x = 1.01$$ and $$y$$ changes from $$y = 2$$ to $$y = 1.98$$ .</item>
      <item>Find the actual change in $$z$$ when $$x$$ changes from $$x = 1$$ to $$x = 1.01$$ and $$y$$ changes from $$y = 2$$ to $$y = 1.98$$ . Compare the result with that obtained in part (b).</item>
    </list>
    <heading level="4">Solution</heading>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>Let $$f\left( {x,y} \right) = 2x^{2}y + y^{3}$$ . Then the required differential is $$dz = \frac{\partial f}{\partial x}dx + \frac{\partial f}{\partial y}dy = 4xydx + {({2x^{2} + 3y^{2}})}dy$$</item>
      <item>Here $$x = 1$$ , $$y = 2$$ , and $$dx = 1.01 - 1 = 0.01$$ and $$dy = 1.98 - 2 = - 0.02$$ . Therefore, $$\Delta z \approx dz = 4(1)(2)(0.01) + \left\lbrack {2(1) + 3(4)} \right\rbrack\left( {- 0.02} \right) = - 0.20$$</item>
      <item>The actual change in $$z$$ is given by $$\begin{array}{ll} {\Delta z} & {= f\left( {1.01,1.98} \right) - f\left( {1,2} \right)} \\ \phantom{\Delta z} & {= \left\lbrack {2(1.01)^{2}(1.98) + (1.98)^{3}} \right\rbrack - \left\lbrack {2(1)^{2}(2) + (2)^{3}} \right\rbrack} \\ \phantom{\Delta z} & {= 11.801988 - 12} \\ \phantom{\Delta z} & {\approx - 0.1980} \end{array}$$</item>
    </list>
    <paragraph>We see that $$\Delta z \approx dz$$ , as expected.</paragraph>
  </example>

snippet: Example 1: Example 1 Evaluate \int_{R}{\int{f\left( {x,y} \right)dA}} , where f\left( {x,y} \right) = x + 2y and R is the rectangle defined by 1 \leq x \leq 4 and 1 \leq y \leq 2 . Solution Using Equation (19), we find...
body_xml:
<example number="1">
    <heading level="4">Example 1</heading>
    <paragraph>Evaluate $$\int_{R}{\int{f\left( {x,y} \right)dA}}$$ , where $$f\left( {x,y} \right) = x + 2y$$ and $$R$$ is the rectangle defined by $$1 \leq x \leq 4$$ and $$1 \leq y \leq 2$$ .</paragraph>
    <heading level="4">Solution</heading>
    <paragraph>Using Equation (19), we find</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\int_{R}{\int{f\left( {x,y} \right)dA = {\int_{1}^{2}{\left\lbrack {\int_{1}^{4}{\left( {x + 2y} \right)dx}} \right\rbrack dy}}}}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>To compute</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\int_{1}^{4}{\left( {x + 2y} \right)dx}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>we treat $$y$$ as if it were a constant (remember that $$\mathit{dx}$$ reminds us that we are integrating with respect to $$x$$ ). We obtain</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {{\int_{1}^{4}{\left( {x + 2y} \right)dx}}{= \left. {\frac{1}{2}x^{2} + 2xy} \right|_{x = 1}^{x = 4}}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{1}^{4}{\left( {x + 2y} \right)dx}}{= \left\lbrack {\frac{1}{2}(16) + 2(4)y} \right\rbrack - \left\lbrack {\frac{1}{2}(1) + 2(1)y} \right\rbrack}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{1}^{4}{\left( {x + 2y} \right)dx}}{= \frac{15}{2} + 6y}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Thus,</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {{\int_{R}{\int{f\left( {x,y} \right)dA}}}{= {\int_{1}^{2}{\left( {\frac{15}{2} + 6y} \right)dy = \left. \left( {\frac{15}{2}y + 3y^{2}} \right) \right|_{1}^{2}}}}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{R}{\int{f\left( {x,y} \right)dA}}}{= \left( {15 + 12} \right) - \left( {\frac{15}{2} + 3} \right) = 16\frac{1}{2}}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Theorem 1
snippet: Theorem 1: Theorem 1 Suppose g_{1}(x) and g_{2}(x) are continuous functions on \left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack and the region R is defined by R = \left\{ {\left. \left( {x,y} \right) \right|g_{1}(x) \leq y \leq g_{2}(x);a \leq x \leq b}...
body_xml:
<note type="theorem" source_type="Theorem 1" title="Theorem 1">
    <heading level="4">Theorem 1</heading>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>Suppose $$g_{1}(x)$$ and $$g_{2}(x)$$ are continuous functions on $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ and the region $$R$$ is defined by $$R = \left\{ {\left. \left( {x,y} \right) \right|g_{1}(x) \leq y \leq g_{2}(x);a \leq x \leq b} \right\}$$ . Then (20) $$\int_{R}{\int{f\left( {x,y} \right)dA = {\int_{a}^{b}{\left\lbrack {\int_{g_{1}{(x)}}^{g_{2}{(x)}}{f\left( {x,y} \right)dy}} \right\rbrack dx}}}}$$ (Figure 36a). Figure 36 Details Two images a and b. In image a, the two curves are graphed on the x y coordinate plane. The horizontal x has a tick mark labeled a close to the origin and another tick mark labeled b, which is away from the origin. Two vertical lines are raised upward from the tick marks a and b till they reach the top curve. The first curve labeled y = g_1(x) enters the second quadrant close to the y axis, slopes downward to the right, concave up, cuts the y axis and enters into the first quadrant, reaches a low point, rises up, then cuts the vertical line raised from the tick mark a in the x axis, inflects, then slopes upward, but now concave down, reaches the high point, then slopes downward to the right, cuts the vertical line raised from the tick mark b in the x axis. The second curve labeled y = g_2(x) enters the second quadrant close to the y axis, slopes upward to the right, concave down, cuts the y axis and enters into the first quadrant, touches the vertical line raised from the tick mark a in the x axis, reaches the high point, slopes down, inflects, then slopes downward to the right, but now concave up, reaches the low point, then slopes upward to the right, and touches the vertical line raised from the tick mark b in the x axis. The region bounded by the two curves and two vertical lines is shaded and labeled R. In image b, the two curves are graphed on the x y coordinate plane. The y axis has a tick mark labeled c close to the origin and another tick mark labeled d, which is away from the origin. Two horizontal lines run rightward from the tick marks c and d respectively. The first curve labeled x = h_1(y) enters the first quadrant near the y axis, slopes downward to the right, concave down, cuts the horizontal line at d, bulges away from the y axis, and slowly turns to the left, bulges downward towards the y axis, cuts the horizontal line at c, then slopes downward to the right above the x axis. The second curve labeled x = h_2(y) enters the first quadrant to the right of the first curve, slopes downward to the left, bulges towards the y axis, touches the horizontal line at d and slowly turns to the right, bulges away from the y axis, touches the horizontal line at c, then slopes slightly downward to the left before it reaches above the x axis. The region bounded by the two curves, and the two vertical lines is shaded and labeled R.</item>
      <item>Suppose $$h_{1}(y)$$ and $$h_{2}(y)$$ are continuous functions on $$\left\lbrack {c,d} \right\rbrack$$ and the region $$R$$ is defined by $$R = \left\{ {\left. \left( {x,y} \right) \right|h_{1}(y) \leq x \leq h_{2}(y);c \leq y \leq d} \right\}$$ . Then (21) $$\int_{R}{\int{f\left( {x,y} \right)dA = {\int_{c}^{d}{\left\lbrack {\int_{h_{1}{(y)}}^{h_{2}{(y)}}{f\left( {x,y} \right)dx}} \right\rbrack dy}}}}$$ (Figure 36b).</item>
    </list>
  </note>

body_xml: Example 2 Evaluate $$\int_{R}{\int{f\left( {x,y} \right)dA}}$$ given that $$f\left( {x,y} \right) = x^{2} + y^{2}$$ and $$R$$ is the region bounded by the graphs of $$g_{1}(x) = x$$ and $$g_{2}(x) = 2x$$ for $$0 \leq x \leq 2$$ . Solution The region under consideration is shown in Figure 37. Using Equation (20), we find $$\begin{array}{l} {{\int_{R}{\int{f{({x,y})}dA}}}{= {\int_{0}^{2}{\left\lbrack {\int_{x}^{2x}{{({x^{2} + y^{2}})}dy}} \right\rbrack dx}}}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{R}{\int{f\left( {x,y} \right)dA}}}{= {\int_{0}^{2}{\left\lbrack \left. \left( {x^{2}y + \frac{1}{3}y^{3}} \right) \right|_{x}^{2x} \right\rbrack dx}}}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{R}{\int{f\left( {x,y} \right)dA}}}{= {\int_{0}^{2}{\left\lbrack {\left( {2x^{3} + \frac{8}{3}x^{3}} \right) - \left( {x^{3} + \frac{1}{3}x^{3}} \right)} \right\rbrack dx}}}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{R}{\int{f\left( {x,y} \right)dA}}}{= {\int_{0}^{2}{\frac{10}{3}x^{3}dx = \left. {\frac{5}{6}x^{4}} \right|_{0}^{2} = 13\frac{1}{3}}}}} \end{array}$$

title: Example 3
snippet: Example 3: Example 3 Evaluate \int_{R}{\int{f\left( {x,y} \right)dA}} , where f\left( {x,y} \right) = xe^{y} and R is the plane region bounded by the graphs of y = x^{2} and y = x . Solution The region in question is shown in Figure 38....
body_xml: Example 3 Evaluate $$\int_{R}{\int{f\left( {x,y} \right)dA}}$$ , where $$f\left( {x,y} \right) = xe^{y}$$ and $$R$$ is the plane region bounded by the graphs of $$y = x^{2}$$ and $$y = x$$ . Solution The region in question is shown in Figure 38. The points of intersection of the two curves are found by solving the equation $$x^{2} = x$$ , giving $$x = 0$$ and $$x = 1$$ . Using Equation (20), we find $$\begin{array}{l} {{\int_{R}{\int{f\left( {x,y} \right)dA}}}{= {\int_{0}^{1}{\left( {\int_{x^{2}}^{x}{xe^{y}dy}} \right)dx = {\int_{0}^{1}{\left( \left. {xe^{y}} \right|_{x^{2}}^{x} \right)dx}}}}}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{R}{\int{f\left( {x,y} \right)dA}}}{= {\int_{0}^{1}{{({xe^{x} - xe^{x^{2}}})}dx = {\int_{0}^{1}{xe^{x}dx - {\int_{0}^{1}{xe^{x^{2}}dx}}}}}}}} \end{array}$$ Next, integrating the first integral on the right-hand side by parts, we have $$\begin{array}{l} {{\int_{R}{\int{f\left( {x,y} \right)dA}}}{= \left. \left\lbrack {\left( {x - 1} \right)e^{x} - \frac{1}{2}e^{x^{2}}} \right\rbrack \right|_{0}^{1}}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{R}{\int{f\left( {x,y} \right)dA}}}{= - \frac{1}{2}e - \left( {- 1 - \frac{1}{2}} \right) = \frac{1}{2}\left( {3 - e} \right)}} \end{array}$$

title: Example 4
snippet: Example 4: Example 4 Evaluate \int\int\limits_{R}xe^{y^{2}}dA where R is the plane region bounded by the y -axis, x = 0 , the horizontal line y = 4 , and the graph of y = x^{2} . Solution The region R is shown in Figure 39. The point of...
body_xml: Example 4 Evaluate $$\int\int\limits_{R}xe^{y^{2}}dA$$ where $$R$$ is the plane region bounded by the $$y$$ -axis, $$x = 0$$ , the horizontal line $$y = 4$$ , and the graph of $$y = x^{2}$$ . Solution The region $$R$$ is shown in Figure 39. The point of intersection of the line $$y = 4$$ and the graph of $$y = x^{2}$$ is found by solving the equation $$x^{2} = 4$$ , giving $$x = 2$$ and the required point $$\left( {2,4} \right)$$ . Using Equation (20) with $$y = g_{1}(x) = x^{2}$$ and $$y = g_{2}(x) = 4$$ we obtain $$\int\int\limits_{R}{xe^{y^{2}}dA = {\int_{0}^{2}{\left\lbrack {\int_{x^{2}}^{4}{xe^{y^{2}}dy}} \right\rbrack dx}}}$$ Evaluation of the integral $$\int_{x^{2}}^{4}{xe^{y^{2}}dy = x{\int_{x^{2}}^{4}{e^{y^{2}}dy}}}$$ calls for finding the antiderivative of the integrand $$e^{y^{2}}$$ in terms of elementary functions, a task that, as was pointed out in Section 7.3, cannot be done. Let’s begin afresh and attempt to make use of Equation (21). Since the equation $$y = x^{2}$$ is equivalent to the equation $$x = \sqrt{y}$$ , which expresses $$x$$ as a function of $$y$$ , we may write, with $$x = h_{1}(y) = 0$$ and $$h_{2}(y) = \sqrt{y}$$ , $$\begin{array}{l} {{\int{\int\limits_{R}{xe^{y^{2}}dA}}}{= {\int_{0}^{4}{\left\lbrack {\int_{0}^{\sqrt{y}}{xe^{y^{2}}dx}} \right\rbrack dy = {\int_{0}^{4}\left\lbrack \left. {\frac{1}{2}x^{2}e^{y^{2}}} \right|_{0}^{\sqrt{y}} \right\rbrack}dy}}}} \\ {\phantom{\int{\int\limits_{R}{xe^{y^{2}}dA}}}{= {\int_{0}^{4}{\frac{1}{2}ye^{y^{2}}dy = \left. {\frac{1}{4}e^{y^{2}}} \right|_{0}^{4} = \frac{1}{4}{({e^{16} - 1})}}}}} \end{array}$$

<note type="theorem" source_type="The Volume of a Solid Under a Surface" title="The Volume of a Solid Under a Surface">
    <heading level="4">The Volume of a Solid Under a Surface</heading>
    <paragraph>Let $$R$$ be a region in the $$\mathit{xy}$$ -plane and let $$f$$ be continuous and nonnegative on $$R$$ . Then, the volume of a solid under a surface bounded above by $$z = f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ and below by $$R$$ is given by</paragraph>

snippet: Example 1: Example 1 Find the volume of the solid bounded above by the plane z = f\left( {x,y} \right) = y and below by the plane region R defined by y = \sqrt{1 - x^{2}}\left( {0 \leq x \leq 1} \right) . Solution The region R is sketched...
body_xml: Example 1 Find the volume of the solid bounded above by the plane $$z = f\left( {x,y} \right) = y$$ and below by the plane region $$R$$ defined by $$y = \sqrt{1 - x^{2}}\left( {0 \leq x \leq 1} \right)$$ . Solution The region $$R$$ is sketched in Figure 40. Observe that $$f\left( {x,y} \right) = y \geq 0$$ for $$\left( {x,y} \right) \in R$$ . Therefore, the required volume is given by $$\begin{array}{l} {{\int_{R}{\int{ydA}}}{= {\int_{0}^{1}{\left( {\int_{0}^{\sqrt{1 - x^{2}}}{ydy}} \right)dx = {\int_{0}^{1}{\left( \left. {\frac{1}{2}y^{2}} \right|_{0}^{\sqrt{1 - x^{2}}} \right)dx}}}}}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{R}{\int{ydA}}}{= {\int_{0}^{1}{\frac{1}{2}\left( {1 - x^{2}} \right)dx = \left. {\frac{1}{2}\left( {x - \frac{1}{3}x^{3}} \right)} \right|_{0}^{1} = \frac{1}{3}}}}} \end{array}$$ The solid is shown in Figure 41. Note that it is not necessary to make a sketch of the solid in order to compute its volume.

<note type="theorem" source_type="Average Value of f ( x , y ) over the Region R" title="Average Value of f ( x , y ) over the Region R">

title: Example 3
snippet: Example 3: Example 3 Find the average value of the function f\left( {x,y} \right) = xy over the plane region R bounded by the graph of y = e^{x} and the lines x = 0 and x = 1 . Solution The region R is shown in Figure 44. The area of the...
body_xml: Example 3 Find the average value of the function $$f\left( {x,y} \right) = xy$$ over the plane region $$R$$ bounded by the graph of $$y = e^{x}$$ and the lines $$x = 0$$ and $$x = 1$$ . Solution The region $$R$$ is shown in Figure 44. The area of the region $$R$$ is given by $$\begin{array}{l} {{{\int^{}}_{0}^{1}\left( {{\int^{}}_{0}^{e^{x}}dy} \right)dx} = {{\int^{}}_{0}^{1}\left( {y|_{0}^{e^{x}}} \right)dx}} \\ {\phantom{{\int^{}}_{0}^{1}\left( {{\int^{}}_{0}^{e^{x}}dy} \right)dx} = {{\int^{}}_{0}^{1}e^{x}dx}} \\ {\phantom{{\int^{}}_{0}^{1}\left( {{\int^{}}_{0}^{e^{x}}dy} \right)dx} = {e^{x}|_{0}^{1}}} \\ {\phantom{{\int^{}}_{0}^{1}\left( {{\int^{}}_{0}^{e^{x}}dy} \right)dx} = {e - 1}} \end{array}$$ We would obtain the same result had we viewed the area of this region as the area of the region under the curve $$y = e^{x}$$ from $$x = 0$$ to $$x = 1$$ . Next, we compute $$\begin{array}{l} {{\int_{R}{\int{f(x,y)dA}}} = {\int_{0}^{1}{\left( {\int_{0}^{e^{x}}{xydy}} \right)dx}}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{R}{\int{f(x,y)dA}}} = {{\int_{0}^{1}\left( \left. \frac{1}{2}xy^{2} \right|_{0}^{e^{x}} \right)}dx}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{R}{\int{f(x,y)dA}}} = {\int_{0}^{1}{\frac{1}{2}xe^{2x}dx}}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{R}{\int{f(x,y)dA}}}{= \left. \frac{1}{4}xe^{2x} - \frac{1}{8}e^{2x} \right|}_{0}^{1} \text{Integrate by parts.} } \\ {\phantom{\int_{R}{\int{f(x,y)dA}}} = {\left( {\frac{1}{4}e^{2} - \frac{1}{8}e^{2}} \right) + \frac{1}{8}}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{R}{\int{f(x,y)dA}}} = {\frac{1}{8}(e^{2} + 1)}} \end{array}$$ Therefore, the required average value is given by $$\frac{{\int_{R}{\int{f\left( {x,y} \right)}}}dA}{\int_{R}{\int{dA}}} = \frac{\frac{1}{8}\left( {e^{2} + 1} \right)}{e - 1} = \frac{e^{2} + 1}{8\left( {e - 1} \right)}$$

body_xml:
<example number="1">
    <heading level="4">Example 1</heading>
    <paragraph>Show that the function $$f(x) = e^{- x} + x - 1$$ is a solution of the differential equation</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$y^{\prime} + y = x$$</paragraph>
    <heading level="4">Solution</heading>
    <paragraph>Let</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$y = f(x) = e^{- x} + x - 1$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Then</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$y^{\prime} = f^{\prime}(x) = - e^{- x} + 1$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Substituting these equations into the left side of the given differential equation yields</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\overset{y^{\prime}}{\overset{︷}{\left( {- e^{- x} + 1} \right)}} + \overset{y}{\overset{︷}{\left( {e^{- x} + x - 1} \right)}} = - e^{- x} + 1 + e^{- x} + x - 1 = x$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>which is equal to the right side of the given equation for all values of $$x$$ . Therefore, $$f(x) = e^{- x} + x - 1$$ is a solution of the given differential equation.</paragraph>
  </example>

snippet: Example 2: Example 2 Show that any function of the form f(x) = \mathit{ce}^{- x} + x - 1 , where c is a constant, is a solution of the differential equation y^{\prime} + y = x Solution Let y = f(x) = \mathit{ce}^{- x} + x - 1 Then...
body_xml:
<example number="2">
    <heading level="4">Example 2</heading>
    <paragraph>Show that any function of the form $$f(x) = \mathit{ce}^{- x} + x - 1$$ , where $$c$$ is a constant, is a solution of the differential equation</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$y^{\prime} + y = x$$</paragraph>
    <heading level="4">Solution</heading>
    <paragraph>Let</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$y = f(x) = \mathit{ce}^{- x} + x - 1$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Then</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$y^{\prime} = f^{\prime}(x) = - \mathit{ce}^{- x} + 1$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Substituting these equations into the left side of the given differential equation yields</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\overset{y^{\prime}}{\overset{︷}{- \mathit{ce}^{- x} + 1}} + \overset{y}{\overset{︷}{\mathit{ce}^{- x} + x - 1}} = x$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>and we have verified the assertion.</paragraph>
  </example>

<example number="3">
    <heading level="4">Example 3</heading>
    <paragraph>Use the results of Example 2 to find the particular solution of the equation $$y^{\prime} + y = x$$ that satisfies the condition $$y(0) = 0$$ ; that is, $$f(0) = 0$$ , where $$f$$ denotes the solution.</paragraph>
    <heading level="4">Solution</heading>
    <paragraph>From the results of Example 2, we see that</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$y = f(x) = \mathit{ce}^{- x} + x - 1$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>is a solution of the given differential equation for all constants $$c$$ . Using the given condition, we see that</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$f(0) = \mathit{ce}^{0} + 0 - 1 = c - 1 = 0$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>or</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$c = 1$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Therefore, the required particular solution is $$y = e^{- x} + x - 1$$ .</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Example 1
snippet: Example 1: Example 1 Find the general solution of the differential equation \frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}} = \frac{y}{x} . Solution Step 1 Since the differential equation has the form \frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}} = \frac{1}{x} \cdot y...
body_xml:
<example number="1">
    <heading level="4">Example 1</heading>
    <paragraph>Find the general solution of the differential equation $$\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}} = \frac{y}{x}$$ .</paragraph>
    <heading level="4">Solution</heading>
    <heading level="4">Step 1</heading>
    <paragraph>Since the differential equation has the form</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}} = \frac{1}{x} \cdot y = f(x)g(y)$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>where $$f(x) = 1 \slash x$$ and $$g(y) = y$$ , it is separable. Separating the variables, we obtain</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{\mathit{dy}}{y} = \frac{\mathit{dx}}{x}$$</paragraph>
    <heading level="4">Step 2</heading>
    <paragraph>Integrating each side of the last equation with respect to the appropriate variable, we have</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$${\int\frac{\mathit{dy}}{y}} = {\int\frac{\mathit{dx}}{x}}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>or</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\ln|y| + C_{1} = \ln|x| + C_{2}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>where $$C_{1}$$ and $$C_{2}$$ are arbitrary constants. If we choose $$C$$ such that $$C_{2} - C_{1} = \ln|C|$$ , then</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {{\ln|y|} = {\ln|x| + \ln|C|}} \\ {\phantom{\ln|y|} = {\ln\left( {|C||x|} \right) = \ln\left| \mathit{Cx} \right| {\ln A + \ln B = \ln AB}}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>so the general solution is $$y = Cx$$ .</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Example 2
snippet: Example 2: Example 2 Find the general solution of the differential equation y^{\prime} = \frac{\mathit{xy}}{x^{2} + 1} Solution Step 1 Observe that the differential equation has the form \frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}} = \left(...
body_xml:
<example number="2">
    <heading level="4">Example 2</heading>
    <paragraph>Find the general solution of the differential equation</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$y^{\prime} = \frac{\mathit{xy}}{x^{2} + 1}$$</paragraph>
    <heading level="4">Solution</heading>
    <heading level="4">Step 1</heading>
    <paragraph>Observe that the differential equation has the form</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}} = \left( \frac{x}{x^{2} + 1} \right)y = f(x)g(y)$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>where $$f(x) = x \slash {({x^{2} + 1})}$$ and $$g(y) = y$$ and is therefore separable. Separating the variables, we obtain</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{\mathit{dy}}{y} = \left( \frac{x}{x^{2} + 1} \right)\mathit{dx}$$</paragraph>
    <heading level="4">Step 2</heading>
    <paragraph>Integrating each side of the last equation with respect to the appropriate variable, we have</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\int\frac{\mathit{dy}}{y} = \int\frac{x}{x^{2} + 1}\mathit{dx}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>or</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} {\ln|y| + C_{1}} & = & {\frac{1}{2}\ln{({x^{2} + 1})} + C_{2}} \\ {\ln|y|} & = & {\frac{1}{2}\ln{({x^{2} + 1})} + C_{2} - C_{1}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>where $$C_{1}$$ and $$C_{2}$$ are arbitrary constants of integration. If we choose $$C$$ such that $$\left. {C_{2} - C_{1}} \right| = \ln|C|$$ , then we have</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {{\ln|y|} = {\frac{1}{2}\ln{({x^{2} + 1})} + \ln|C|}} \\ {\phantom{\ln|y|} = {\ln\sqrt{x^{2} + 1} + \ln|C|}} \\ {\phantom{\ln|y|} = {\ln\left| {C\sqrt{x^{2} + 1}} \right| {\ln A + \ln B = \ln AB}}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>so the general solution is</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$y = C\sqrt{x^{2} + 1}$$</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Example 3
snippet: Example 3: Example 3 Find the particular solution of the differential equation \mathit{ye}^{x} + {({y^{2} - 1})}y^{\prime} = 0 that satisfies the condition y(0) = 1 . Solution Step 1 Writing the given differential equation in the form...
body_xml:
<example number="3">
    <heading level="4">Example 3</heading>
    <paragraph>Find the particular solution of the differential equation</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\mathit{ye}^{x} + {({y^{2} - 1})}y^{\prime} = 0$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>that satisfies the condition $$y(0) = 1$$ .</paragraph>
    <heading level="4">Solution</heading>
    <heading level="4">Step 1</heading>
    <paragraph>Writing the given differential equation in the form</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\mathit{ye}^{x} + {({y^{2} - 1})}\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}} = 0$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>or</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$${({y^{2} - 1})}\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}} = - \mathit{ye}^{x}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>and separating the variables, we obtain</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{y^{2} - 1}{y}\mathit{dy} = - e^{x}\mathit{dx}$$</paragraph>
    <heading level="4">Step 2</heading>
    <paragraph>Integrating each side of this equation with respect to the appropriate variable, we have</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} {\int{\frac{y^{2} - 1}{y}\mathit{dy}}} & = & {- {\int{e^{x}\mathit{dx}}}} \\ {\int{\left( {y - \frac{1}{y}} \right)\mathit{dy}}} & = & {- {\int{e^{x}\mathit{dx}}}} \\ {\frac{1}{2}y^{2} - \ln|y|} & = & {- e^{x} + C_{1}} \\ {y^{2} - \ln y^{2}} & = & {- 2e^{x} + C {C = 2C_{1}}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Using the condition $$y(0) = 1$$ , we have</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$1 - \ln 1 = - 2 + C$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>or</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$C = 3$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Therefore, the required solution is</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$y^{2} - \ln y^{2} = - 2e^{x} + 3$$</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Example 4
snippet: Example 4: Example 4 Find an equation satisfying the following conditions: (1) the slope of the tangent line to the graph of the equation at any point P\left( {x,y} \right) is given by - x \slash \left( {2y} \right) and (2) the graph of...
body_xml: Example 4 Find an equation satisfying the following conditions: (1) the slope of the tangent line to the graph of the equation at any point $$P\left( {x,y} \right)$$ is given by $$- x \slash \left( {2y} \right)$$ and (2) the graph of the equation passes through the point $$P\left( {1,2} \right)$$ . Solution The slope of the tangent line at any point $$P\left( {x,y} \right)$$ on the graph of the equation is given by $$y^{\prime} = \frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}} = - \frac{x}{2y}$$ which is a separable differential equation. Separating the variables, we obtain $$2y\mathit{dy} = - x\mathit{dx}$$ which, upon integration, yields $$y^{2} = - \frac{1}{2}x^{2} + C_{1}$$ or $$x^{2} + 2y^{2} = C {C = 2C_{1}}$$ where $$C$$ is an arbitrary constant. To evaluate $$C$$ , we use the second condition, which implies that when $$x = 1$$ , $$y = 2$$ . This gives $$1^{2} + 2{(2^{2})} = C$$ or $$C = 9$$ Hence the required equation is $$x^{2} + 2y^{2} = 9$$ The graph of this equation appears in Figure 6.

title: Euler’s Method
snippet: Euler’s Method: Euler’s Method Suppose we are given the differential equation \frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}} = F\left( {x,y} \right) subject to the initial condition y\left( x_{0} \right) = y_{0} and we wish to find an approximation of...
body_xml:
<note type="procedure" source_type="Euler’s Method" title="Euler’s Method">
    <heading level="4">Euler’s Method</heading>
    <paragraph>Suppose we are given the differential equation</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}} = F\left( {x,y} \right)$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>subject to the initial condition $$y\left( x_{0} \right) = y_{0}$$ and we wish to find an approximation of $$y(b)$$ , where $$b$$ is a number greater than $$x_{0}$$ and $$n$$ is a positive integer. Compute</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$h = \frac{b - x_{0}}{n}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$x_{1} = x_{0} + h x_{2} = x_{0} + 2h x_{3} = x_{0} + 3h \ldots x_{n} = x_{0} + nh = b$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>and</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rcl} y_{0} & = & {y\left( x_{0} \right)} \\ y_{1} & = & {y_{0} + hF\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right)} \\ y_{2} & = & {y_{1} + hF\left( {x_{1},y_{1}} \right)} \\ & \vdots & \\ y_{n} & = & {y_{n - 1} + hF\left( {x_{n - 1},y_{n - 1}} \right)} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Then $$y_{n}$$ gives an approximation of the true value $$y(b)$$ of the solution to the initial-value problem at $$x = b$$ .</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Example 1
snippet: Example 1: Example 1 Use Euler’s method with n = 8 to obtain an approximation of the solution of the initial-value problem y^{\prime} = x - y y(0) = 1 when x = 2 . Solution Here, x_{0} = 0 and b = 2 , so taking n = 8 , we find h = \frac{2...
body_xml:
<example number="1">
    <heading level="4">Example 1</heading>
    <paragraph>Use Euler’s method with $$n = 8$$ to obtain an approximation of the solution of the initial-value problem</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$y^{\prime} = x - y y(0) = 1$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>when $$x = 2$$ .</paragraph>
    <heading level="4">Solution</heading>
    <paragraph>Here, $$x_{0} = 0$$ and $$b = 2$$ , so taking $$n = 8$$ , we find</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$h = \frac{2 - 0}{8} = \frac{1}{4}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>and</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$x_{0} = 0 x_{1} = \frac{1}{4} x_{2} = \frac{1}{2} x_{3} = \frac{3}{4} x_{4} = 1$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$x_{5} = \frac{5}{4} x_{6} = \frac{3}{2} x_{7} = \frac{7}{4} x_{8} = b = 2$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Also,</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$F{\left( {x,y} \right) = x - y}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>and</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$y_{0} = y(0) = 1$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Therefore, the approximations of the actual solution at the points $$x_{0},x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n} = b$$ are</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{rll} y_{0} & = & {y(0) = 1} \\ y_{1} & = & {y_{0} + hF\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right) = 1 + \frac{1}{4}\left( {0 - 1} \right) = \frac{3}{4}} \\ y_{2} & = & {y_{1} + hF\left( {x_{1},y_{1}} \right) = \frac{3}{4} + \frac{1}{4}\left( {\frac{1}{4} - \frac{3}{4}} \right) = \frac{5}{8}} \\ y_{3} & = & {y_{2} + hF\left( {x_{2},y_{2}} \right) = \frac{5}{8} + \frac{1}{4}\left( {\frac{1}{2} - \frac{5}{8}} \right) = \frac{19}{32}} \\ y_{4} & = & {y_{3} + hF\left( {x_{3},y_{3}} \right) = \frac{19}{32} + \frac{1}{4}\left( {\frac{3}{4} - \frac{19}{32}} \right) = \frac{81}{128}} \\ y_{5} & = & {y_{4} + hF\left( {x_{4},y_{4}} \right) = \frac{81}{128} + \frac{1}{4}\left( {1 - \frac{81}{128}} \right) = \frac{371}{512}} \\ y_{6} & = & {y_{5} + hF\left( {x_{5},y_{5}} \right) = \frac{371}{512} + \frac{1}{4}\left( {\frac{5}{4} - \frac{371}{512}} \right) = \frac{1753}{2048}} \\ y_{7} & = & {y_{6} + hF\left( {x_{6},y_{6}} \right) = \frac{1753}{2048} + \frac{1}{4}\left( {\frac{3}{2} - \frac{1753}{2048}} \right) = \frac{8331}{8192}} \\ y_{8} & = & {y_{7} + hF\left( {x_{7},y_{7}} \right) = \frac{8331}{8192} + \frac{1}{4}\left( {\frac{7}{4} - \frac{8331}{8192}} \right) = \frac{39,329}{32,768}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Thus, the approximate value of $$y(2)$$ is</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\frac{39,329}{32,768} \approx 1.2002$$</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Example 2
snippet: Example 2: Example 2 Use Euler’s method with (a) n = 5 and (b) n = 10 to approximate the solution of the initial-value problem y^{\prime} = - 2\mathit{xy}^{2} y(0) = 1 on the interval \lbrack 0,0.5\rbrack . Find the actual solution of the...
body_xml: Example 2 Use Euler’s method with (a) $$n = 5$$ and (b) $$n = 10$$ to approximate the solution of the initial-value problem $$y^{\prime} = - 2\mathit{xy}^{2} y(0) = 1$$ on the interval $$\lbrack 0,0.5\rbrack$$ . Find the actual solution of the initial-value problem. Finally, sketch the graphs of the approximate solutions and the actual solution for $$0 \leq x \leq 0.5$$ on the same set of axes. Solution Here, $$x_{0} = 0$$ and $$b = 0.5$$ . Taking $$n = 5$$ , we find $$h = \frac{0.5 - 0}{5} = 0.1$$ and $$x_{0} = 0$$ , $$x_{1} = 0.1$$ , $$x_{2} = 0.2$$ , $$x_{3} = 0.3$$ , $$x_{4} = 0.4$$ , and $$x_{5} = b = 0.5$$ . Also, $$F\left( {x,y} \right) = - 2\mathit{xy}^{2}$$ and $$y_{0} = y(0) = 1$$ Therefore, $$\begin{array}{rll} y_{0} & = & {y(0) = 1} \\ y_{1} & = & {y_{0} + hF\left( {x_{0},y_{0}} \right) = 1 + 0.1\left( {- 2} \right)(0)(1)^{2} = 1} \\ y_{2} & = & {y_{1} + hF\left( {x_{1},y_{1}} \right) = 1 + 0.1\left( {- 2} \right)(0.1)(1)^{2} = 0.98} \\ y_{3} & = & {y_{2} + hF\left( {x_{2},y_{2}} \right) = 0.98 + 0.1\left( {- 2} \right)(0.2)(0.98)^{2} \approx 0.9416} \\ y_{4} & = & {y_{3} + hF\left( {x_{3},y_{3}} \right) = 0.9416 + 0.1\left( {- 2} \right)(0.3)(0.9416)^{2} \approx 0.8884} \\ y_{5} & = & {y_{4} + hF\left( {x_{4},y_{4}} \right) = 0.8884 + 0.1\left( {- 2} \right)(0.4)(0.8884)^{2} \approx 0.8253} \end{array}$$ Here, $$x_{0} = 0$$ and $$b = 0.5$$ . Taking $$n = 10$$ , we find $$h = \frac{0.5 - 0}{10}$$ and $$x_{0} = 0,x_{1} = 0.05,x_{2} = 0.10,\ldots,x_{9} = 0.45,$$ and $$x_{10} = 0.5 = b$$ . Proceeding as in part (a), we obtain the approximate solutions listed in the following table: $$\mathbf{x}$$ 0.00 0.05 0.10 0.15 0.20 0.25 $$\mathbf{y}_{\mathbf{n}}$$ 1.0000 1.0000 0.9950 0.9851 0.9705 0.9517 $$\mathbf{x}$$ 0.30 0.35 0.40 0.45 0.50 $$\mathbf{y}_{\mathbf{n}}$$ 0.9291 0.9032 0.8746 0.8440 0.8119 To obtain the actual solution of the differential equation, we separate variables, obtaining $$\frac{\mathit{dy}}{y^{2}} = - 2x\mathit{dx}$$ Integrating each side of the last equation with respect to the appropriate variable, we have $${\int\frac{\mathit{dy}}{y^{2}}} = - {\int{2x\mathit{dx}}}$$ or $$\begin{array}{rll} {- \frac{1}{y} + C_{1}} & = & {- x^{2} + C_{2}} \\ \frac{1}{y} & = & {{x^{2} + C} {C = C_{1} - C_{2}}} \\ y & = & \frac{1}{x^{2} + C} \end{array}$$ Using the condition $$y(0) = 1$$ , we have $$1 = \frac{1}{0 + C}$$ or $$C = 1$$ Therefore, the required solution is given by $$y = \frac{1}{x^{2} + 1}$$ The graphs of the approximate solutions and the actual solution are sketched in Figure 16.

body_xml:
<note type="theorem" source_type="Probability Density Function" title="Probability Density Function">
    <heading level="4">Probability Density Function</heading>
    <paragraph>A probability density function of a random variable $$X$$ in an interval $$I$$ , where $$I$$ may be bounded or unbounded, is a nonnegative function $$f$$ having the following properties.</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>The total area of the region under the graph of $$f$$ is equal to $$1$$ (Figure 2a).</item>
      <item>The probability that an observed value of the random variable $$X$$ lies in the interval $$\lbrack a,b\rbrack$$ is given by $$P(a \leq X \leq b) = {\int_{a}^{b}f(x)\mathit{dx}}$$ (Figure 2b). Figure 2 Details There are two images a and b each graphed a bell shaped curve in the first quadrant of the x y coordinate plane. In image a, the x and y axes are unmarked and unlabeled. The curve starts just above the x axis, a short distance away from the origin, slopes upward to the right, concave up, after it reaches the inflection point, it goes up, now concave down, and reaches the high point. From its high point, the curve goes down to the right, still concave down, after it reaches its inflection point, it goes down to the right, but concave up and ends very close to the x axis. The region below the curve is shaded and is labeled R. In image b, the x axis has marks labeled a and b, appear at unequal intervals. The curve starts just above the x axis, a short distance away from the origin, slopes upward to the right, concave up, after it reaches the inflection point, it goes up, now concave down, and reaches the high point. From its high point, the curve goes down to the right, still concave down, after it reaches its inflection point, it goes down to the right, but concave up and ends very close to the x axis. Two vertical lines rises from the marks a and b on the x axis, till it reaches the curve. The region bounded by the curve, x axis and the two vertical lines is shaded and the region is labeled P (a <= X <= b).</item>
    </list>
  </note>

title: Example 1
snippet: Example 1: Example 1 Show that each of the following functions satisfies the nonnegativity condition and Property 1 of probability density functions. f(x) = \frac{2}{27}x(x - 1) (1 \leq x \leq 4) f(x) = \frac{1}{3}e^{( - 1 \slash 3)x} (0...
body_xml:
<example number="1">
    <heading level="4">Example 1</heading>
    <paragraph>Show that each of the following functions satisfies the nonnegativity condition and Property 1 of probability density functions.</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>$$f(x) = \frac{2}{27}x(x - 1) (1 \leq x \leq 4)$$</item>
      <item>$$f(x) = \frac{1}{3}e^{( - 1 \slash 3)x} (0 \leq x < \infty)$$</item>
    </list>
    <heading level="4">Solution</heading>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>Since the factors $$x$$ and $$(x - 1)$$ are both nonnegative on $$\left\lbrack {1,4} \right\rbrack$$ , we see that $$f(x) \geq 0$$ on $$\left\lbrack {1,4} \right\rbrack$$ . Next, we compute $$\begin{array}{l} {{\int_{1}^{4}{\frac{2}{27}x\left( {x - 1} \right)dx}} = {\frac{2}{27}{\int_{1}^{4}{({x^{2} - x})}dx}}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{1}^{4}{\frac{2}{27}x\left( {x - 1} \right)dx}} = \left. \frac{2}{27}\left( {\frac{1}{3}x^{3} - \frac{1}{2}x^{2}} \right) \right|_{1}^{4}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{1}^{4}{\frac{2}{27}x\left( {x - 1} \right)dx}} = \left. \frac{2}{27}\left\lbrack \left( {\frac{64}{3} - 8} \right) - \left( {\frac{1}{3} - \frac{1}{2}} \right) \right. \right\rbrack} \\ {\phantom{\int_{1}^{4}{\frac{2}{27}x\left( {x - 1} \right)dx}} = {\frac{2}{27}\left( \frac{27}{2} \right)}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{1}^{4}{\frac{2}{27}x\left( {x - 1} \right)dx}} = 1} \end{array}$$ showing that Property 1 of probability density functions holds as well.</item>
      <item>First, $$f(x) = \frac{1}{3}e^{( - 1 \slash 3)x} \geq 0$$ for all values of $$x$$ in $$\lbrack 0,\infty)$$ . Next, $$\begin{array}{l} {{\int_{0}^{\infty}{\frac{1}{3}e^{{({- 1 \slash 3})}x}dx}} = {\lim\limits_{b\rightarrow\infty}{\int_{0}^{b}{\frac{1}{3}e^{{({- 1 \slash 3})}x}dx}}}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{0}^{\infty}{\frac{1}{3}e^{{({- 1 \slash 3})}x}dx}} = \left. \lim\limits_{b\rightarrow\infty} - e^{{({- 1 \slash 3})}x} \right|_{0}^{b}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{0}^{\infty}{\frac{1}{3}e^{{({- 1 \slash 3})}x}dx}} = {\lim\limits_{b\rightarrow\infty}{({- e^{{({- 1 \slash 3})}b} + 1})}}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{0}^{\infty}{\frac{1}{3}e^{{({- 1 \slash 3})}x}dx}} = 1} \end{array}$$ so the area under the graph of $$f(x) = \frac{1}{3}e^{( - 1 \slash 3)x}$$ on $$\lbrack 0,\infty)$$ is equal to $$1$$ , as we set out to show.</item>
    </list>
  </example>

title: Example 2
snippet: Example 2: Example 2 Determine the value of the constant k such that the function f(x) = kx^{2} is a probability density function on the interval \left\lbrack {0,5} \right\rbrack . If X is a continuous random variable with the probability...
body_xml:
<example number="2">
    <heading level="4">Example 2</heading>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>Determine the value of the constant $$k$$ such that the function $$f(x) = kx^{2}$$ is a probability density function on the interval $$\left\lbrack {0,5} \right\rbrack$$ .</item>
      <item>If $$X$$ is a continuous random variable with the probability density function given in part (a), compute the probability that $$X$$ will assume a value between $$1$$ and $$2$$ .</item>
      <item>Find the probability that $$X$$ will assume a value at $$3$$ .</item>
    </list>
    <heading level="4">Solution</heading>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>We compute $$\begin{array}{l} {{\int_{0}^{5}{kx^{2}dx}} = {k{\int_{0}^{5}{x^{2}dx}}}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{0}^{5}{kx^{2}dx}} = \left. \frac{k}{3}x^{3} \right|_{0}^{5}} \\ {\phantom{\int_{0}^{5}{kx^{2}dx}} = {\frac{125}{3}k}} \end{array}$$ Since this value must be equal to $$1$$ , we find that $$k = \frac{3}{125}$$ .</item>
      <item>The required probability is given by $$\begin{array}{l} {{P\left( {1 \leq X \leq 2} \right)} = {\int_{1}^{2}{f(x)dx = {\int_{1}^{2}{\frac{3}{125}x^{2}dx}}}}} \\ {\phantom{P\left( {1 \leq X \leq 2} \right)} = \left. \frac{1}{125}x^{3} \right|_{1}^{2} = \frac{1}{125}\left( {8 - 1} \right)} \\ {\phantom{P\left( {1 \leq X \leq 2} \right)} = \frac{7}{125}} \end{array}$$ The graph of the probability density function $$f$$ and the area corresponding to the probability $$P(1 \leq X \leq 2)$$ are shown in Figure 3. Figure 3 Details Alt-text: A curve is graphed in the first quadrant of the x y coordinate plane. The x axis ranges from 0 to beyond 5 and the y axis ranges from 0 to over 0.6. The curve starts from the origin, slopes upward to the right, concave up, passes through (2, 0.1), and ends at (5, 0.6). From the point (5, 0.6), perpendiculars are dropped to each of the axes. From the mark 2 on the x axis, a vertical line rises till it reaches the curve. The region below the curve from the line x = 1 to x = 2 is shaded. $$P(1 \leq X \leq 2)$$ for the probability density function $$y = \frac{3}{125}x^{2}$$</item>
      <item>The required probability is given by $$\begin{array}{l} {{P\left( {X = 3} \right)} = {\int_{3}^{3}{f(x)dx}}} \\ {\phantom{P\left( {X = 3} \right)} = {\int_{3}^{3}{\frac{3}{125}x^{2}dx = 0}}} \end{array}$$</item>
    </list>
  </example>

title: Example 3
snippet: Example 3: Example 3 Let f be a constant function defined on an interval \left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack . What properties must f satisfy in order for f to be a probability density function on \left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack ? Find an...
body_xml:
<example number="3">
    <heading level="4">Example 3</heading>
    <paragraph>Let $$f$$ be a constant function defined on an interval $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ . What properties must $$f$$ satisfy in order for $$f$$ to be a probability density function on $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ ? Find an expression for $$f$$ .</paragraph>
    <heading level="4">Solution</heading>
    <paragraph>Let $$f(x) = k$$ for $$x$$ in the interval $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ , where $$k$$ is a constant. Clearly, $$k$$ must be positive on $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ . Next, we compute</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\int_{a}^{b}f(x)dx = \left. \int_{a}^{b}kdx = {kx} \right|_{a}^{b} = k\left( {b - a} \right)$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Since the area of $$f$$ under $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ must be equal to $$1$$ , we have</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$k\left( {b - a} \right) = 1$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>or</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$k = \frac{1}{b - a}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>So the required function is defined by</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$f(x) = \frac{1}{b - a} \left( {a \leq x \leq b} \right)$$</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Joint Probability Density Function
snippet: Joint Probability Density Function: Joint Probability Density Function A joint probability density function of the random variables X and Y on a region D is a nonnegative function f\left( {x,y} \right) having the property...
body_xml:
<note type="theorem" source_type="Joint Probability Density Function" title="Joint Probability Density Function">
    <heading level="4">Joint Probability Density Function</heading>
    <paragraph>A joint probability density function of the random variables $$X$$ and $$Y$$ on a region $$D$$ is a nonnegative function $$f\left( {x,y} \right)$$ having the property</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\iint\limits_{D}{f(x,y)dA = 1}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Thus, the volume of the solid under the graph of $$f$$ is equal to $$1$$ .</paragraph>
    <paragraph>The probability that the observed values of the random variables $$X$$ and $$Y$$ lie in a region $$R \subset D$$ is given by</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$P\left\lbrack {\left( {X,Y} \right){in}R} \right\rbrack = {\iint\limits_{R}{f(x,y)dA}}$$</paragraph>
  </note>

title: Example 6
snippet: Example 6: Example 6 Show that the function f\left( {x,y} \right) = xy is a joint probability density function on D = \left\{ \left( {x,y} \right) \middle| 0 \leq x \leq 1;0 \leq y \leq 2 \right\} . Solution First, observe that f\left(...
body_xml:
<example number="6">
    <heading level="4">Example 6</heading>
    <paragraph>Show that the function $$f\left( {x,y} \right) = xy$$ is a joint probability density function on $$D = \left\{ \left( {x,y} \right) \middle| 0 \leq x \leq 1;0 \leq y \leq 2 \right\}$$ .</paragraph>
    <heading level="4">Solution</heading>
    <paragraph>First, observe that $$f\left( {x,y} \right) = xy$$ is nonnegative on $$D$$ . Next, we compute</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {{\iint\limits_{D}{f(x,y)dA}} = {\int_{0}^{2}{\int_{0}^{1}{xydxdy}}}} \\ {\phantom{\iint\limits_{D}{f(x,y)dA}} = {{\int_{0}^{2}\left( \left. \frac{1}{2}x^{2}y \right|_{0}^{1} \right)}dy}} \\ {\phantom{\iint\limits_{D}{f(x,y)dA}} = {\int_{0}^{2}{\frac{1}{2}ydy = \left. {\frac{1}{4}y^{2}} \right|_{0}^{2} = 1}}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Therefore, $$f$$ is a joint probability density function on $$D$$ .</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Example 7
snippet: Example 7: Example 7 Let f\left( {x,y} \right) = xy be the joint probability density function for the random variables X and Y on D = \left\{ \left. \left( {x,y} \right) \middle| 0 \leq x \leq 1;0 \leq y \leq 2 \right\} \right. . Find (a)...
body_xml:
<example number="7">
    <heading level="4">Example 7</heading>
    <paragraph>Let $$f\left( {x,y} \right) = xy$$ be the joint probability density function for the random variables $$X$$ and $$Y$$ on $$D = \left\{ \left. \left( {x,y} \right) \middle| 0 \leq x \leq 1;0 \leq y \leq 2 \right\} \right.$$ . Find</paragraph>
    <list type="unordered">
      <item>(a) $$P{({0 \leq X \leq \frac{1}{2};1 \leq Y \leq 2})}$$ and</item>
      <item>(b) $$P\left( {X + Y \leq 1} \right)$$ .</item>
    </list>
    <heading level="4">Solution</heading>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>The required probability is given by $$\begin{array}{l} {{P\left( {0 \leq X \leq \frac{1}{2};1 \leq Y \leq 2} \right)} = {\int_{1}^{2}{\int_{0}^{1 \slash 2}{xydxdy}}}} \\ {\phantom{P\left( {0 \leq X \leq \frac{1}{2};1 \leq Y \leq 2} \right)} = {\int_{1}^{2}{\left( \left. {\frac{1}{2}x^{2}y} \right|_{0}^{1 \slash 2} \right)dy}}} \\ {\phantom{P\left( {0 \leq X \leq \frac{1}{2};1 \leq Y \leq 2} \right)} = {\int_{1}^{2}{\frac{1}{8}ydy = \left. {\frac{1}{16}y^{2}} \right|_{1}^{2} = \frac{3}{16}}}} \end{array}$$</item>
      <item>The region $$R = \left\{ \left( {x,y} \right) \middle| x + y \leq 1 \right\}$$ is shown in Figure 5. The required probability is $$\begin{array}{l} {{P\left( {X + Y \leq 1} \right)} = {\int_{0}^{1}{\int_{0}^{1 - x}{xydydx}}}} \\ {\phantom{P\left( {X + Y \leq 1} \right)} = {\int_{0}^{1}{\left( \left. {\frac{1}{2}xy^{2}} \right|_{0}^{1 - x} \right)dx}}} \\ {\phantom{P\left( {X + Y \leq 1} \right)} = {\int_{0}^{1}{\frac{1}{2}x\left( {1 - x} \right)^{2}dx}}} \\ {\phantom{P\left( {X + Y \leq 1} \right)} = {\frac{1}{2}{\int_{0}^{1}{{({x - 2x^{2} + x^{3}})}dx}}}} \\ {\phantom{P\left( {X + Y \leq 1} \right)} = {\frac{1}{2}\left. \left( {\frac{1}{2}x^{2} - \frac{2}{3}x^{3} + \frac{1}{4}x^{4}} \right) \right|_{0}^{1}}} \\ {\phantom{P\left( {X + Y \leq 1} \right)} = {\frac{1}{2}\left( {\frac{1}{2} - \frac{2}{3} + \frac{1}{4}} \right) = \frac{1}{24}}} \end{array}$$ Figure 5 Details A line x + y = 1 is graphed on the x y coordinate plane. The x axis ranges from 0 to beyond 1 and the y axis ranges from 0 to over 1. The line enters the second quadrant from the top, cuts the y axis at (0, 1), goes down to the right, cuts the x axis at (1, 0), and enters the fourth quadrant. The region below the line is shaded and the region is labeled R.</item>
    </list>
  </example>

title: Example 8
snippet: Example 8: Example 8 Let f\left( {x,y} \right) = 2e^{- x - 2y} be the joint probability density function for the random variables X and Y on D = \left\{ \left( {x,y} \right) \middle| x \geq 0 \right. and \left. y \geq 0 \right\} . Find the...
body_xml:
<example number="8">
    <heading level="4">Example 8</heading>
    <paragraph>Let $$f\left( {x,y} \right) = 2e^{- x - 2y}$$ be the joint probability density function for the random variables $$X$$ and $$Y$$ on $$D = \left\{ \left( {x,y} \right) \middle| x \geq 0 \right.$$ and $$\left. y \geq 0 \right\}$$ .</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>Find the probability that $$X$$ will assume a value between $$0$$ and $$1$$ and that $$Y$$ will assume a value between $$1$$ and $$2$$ .</item>
      <item>Find the probability that $$X$$ will assume a value greater than $$1$$ and that $$Y$$ will assume a value less than $$2$$ .</item>
    </list>
    <heading level="4">Solution</heading>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>The required probability is given by $$\begin{array}{l} {{P\left( {0 \leq X \leq 1;1 \leq Y \leq 2} \right)} = {\int_{1}^{2}{\int_{0}^{1}{2e^{- x - 2y}dxdy}}}} \\ {\phantom{P\left( {0 \leq X \leq 1;1 \leq Y \leq 2} \right)} = \int_{1}^{2}\left( \left. - 2e^{- x - 2y} \right|_{0}^{1} \right)dy} \\ {\phantom{P\left( {0 \leq X \leq 1;1 \leq Y \leq 2} \right)} = {\int_{1}^{2}{{({- 2e^{- 1 - 2y} + 2e^{- 2y}})}dy}}} \\ {\phantom{P\left( {0 \leq X \leq 1;1 \leq Y \leq 2} \right)} = {\int_{1}^{2}{2(1 - e^{- 1})e^{- 2y}dy}} {{Simplify the integrand}.}} \\ {\phantom{P\left( {0 \leq X \leq 1;1 \leq Y \leq 2} \right)} = {2(1 - e^{- 1})\left. \left( {- \frac{1}{2}e^{- 2y}} \right) \right|_{1}^{2}}} \\ {\phantom{P\left( {0 \leq X \leq 1;1 \leq Y \leq 2} \right)} = \left. - (1 - e^{- 1})e^{- 2y} \right|_{1}^{2}} \\ {\phantom{P\left( {0 \leq X \leq 1;1 \leq Y \leq 2} \right)} = {- (1 - e^{- 1})(e^{- 4} - e^{- 2}) \approx .0740}} \end{array}$$</item>
      <item>The required probability is given by $$\begin{array}{l} {{P(X > 1;0 \leq Y < 2)} = {\int_{0}^{2}{\int_{1}^{\infty}{2e^{- x - 2y}dxdy}}}} \\ {\phantom{P(X > 1;0 \leq Y < 2)} = {\int_{0}^{2}{\left( {\lim\limits_{b\rightarrow\infty}{\int_{1}^{b}{2e^{- x - 2y}}}dx} \right)dy}}} \\ {\phantom{P(X > 1;0 \leq Y < 2)} = {{\int_{0}^{2}\left( \left. {\lim\limits_{b\rightarrow\infty} - 2e^{- x - 2y}} \right|_{1}^{b} \right)}dy}} \\ {\phantom{P(X > 1;0 \leq Y < 2)} = {\int_{0}^{2}{\lbrack\lim\limits_{b\rightarrow\infty}( - 2e^{- b - 2y} + 2e^{- 1 - 2y})\rbrack dy}}} \\ {\phantom{P(X > 1;0 \leq Y < 2)} = {{\int_{0}^{2}{2e^{- 1 - 2y}}}dy}} \\ {\phantom{P(X > 1;0 \leq Y < 2)} = {\left. - e^{- 1 - 2y} \right|_{0}^{2} = - e^{- 5} + e^{- 1} \approx .3611}} \end{array}$$</item>
    </list>
  </example>

title: Portfolio Gary Li
snippet: Portfolio Gary Li: Portfolio Gary Li Title Associate Institution JPMorgan Chase As one of the leading financial institutions in the world, JPMorgan Chase & Co. depends on a wide range of mathematical disciplines from statistics to linear...
body_xml: Portfolio Gary Li Title Associate Institution JPMorgan Chase As one of the leading financial institutions in the world, JPMorgan Chase & Co. depends on a wide range of mathematical disciplines from statistics to linear programming to calculus. In assessing the creditworthiness of a borrower, recommending portfolio investments, or pricing an exotic derivative, quantitative understanding is a critical tool in serving the financial needs of clients. I work in the Fixed-Income Derivatives Strategy group. A derivative in finance is an instrument whose value depends on the price of some other underlying instrument. A simple type of derivative is the forward contract, in which two parties agree to a future trade at a specified price. In agriculture, for instance, farmers will often pledge their crops for sale to buyers at an agreed price before even planting the seed. Depending on the weather, demand, and other factors, the market price may turn out higher or lower. Either the buyer or seller of the forward contract benefits accordingly. The value of the contract changes one-for-one with the market price. In derivatives lingo, we borrow from calculus and say that forward contracts have a delta of $$1$$ . Nowadays, the bulk of derivatives deal with interest-rate risk rather than agricultural risk. The value of any asset with fixed payments over time varies with interest rates. With trillions of dollars in this form, especially government bonds and mortgages, fixed-income derivatives are vital to the economy. The job of our strategy group is to track and anticipate key drivers and developments in the market using, in significant part, quantitative analysis. Some of the derivatives that we look at are the forward kind such as interest-rate swaps, in which over time, you receive fixed-rate payments in exchange for paying a floating rate or vice versa. A whole other class of derivatives in which statistics and calculus are especially relevant are options. Whereas forward contracts bind both parties to a future trade, options give the holder the right but not the obligation to trade at a specified time and price. Similar to an insurance policy, the holder of the option pays an upfront premium in exchange for potential gain. Solving this pricing problem requires statistics, stochastic calculus, and enough insight to win a Nobel Prize. Fortunately for us, this was taken care of by Fischer Black, Myron Scholes, and Robert Merton in the early 1970s (the 1997 Nobel Prize in Economics went to Scholes and Merton). The Black–Scholes differential equation was the first accurate options pricing model, making possible the rapid growth of the derivatives market. Black–Scholes and the many derivatives of it continue to be used to this day.

snippet: Variance of a Random Variable X: Variance of a Random Variable X Suppose a random variable has the probability distribution x x_{1} x_{2} x_{3} \ldots x_{n} P(X = x) p_{1} p_{2} p_{3} \ldots p_{n} and expected value E(X) = \mu Then the...
body_xml:
Variance of a Random Variable X Suppose a random variable has the probability distribution $$x$$ $$x_{1}$$ $$x_{2}$$ $$x_{3}$$ $$\ldots$$ $$x_{n}$$ $$P(X = x)$$ $$p_{1}$$ $$p_{2}$$ $$p_{3}$$ $$\ldots$$ $$p_{n}$$
and expected value $$E(X) = \mu$$ Then the variance of the random variable $$X$$ is $${Var}(X) = p_{1}{(x_{1} - \mu)}^{2} + p_{2}{(x_{2} - \mu)}^{2} + \ldots + p_{n}{(x_{n} - \mu)}^{2}$$

title: Example 5
snippet: Example 5: Example 5 Find the variance of the random variable X and of the random variable Y whose probability distributions are shown in the following table. These are the probability distributions associated with the histograms shown in...
body_xml:
Example 5 Find the variance of the random variable $$X$$ and of the random variable $$Y$$ whose probability distributions are shown in the following table. These are the probability distributions associated with the histograms shown in Figure 8a–b. $$x$$ $$P(X = x)$$ $$y$$ $$P(Y = y)$$ 1 .05 1 .2 2 .075 2 .15 3 .2 3 .1 4 .375 4 .15 5 .15 5 .05 6 .1 6 .1 7 .05 7 .25
Solution The mean of the random variable $$X$$ is given by $$\begin{array}{rcl} \mu_{X} & = & {(1)(.05) + (2)(.075) + (3)(.2) + (4)(.375) + (5)(.15)} \\ & & {+ (6)(.1) + (7)(.05)} \\ & = & 4 \end{array}$$ Therefore, using Equation (4) and the data from the probability distribution of $$X$$ , we find that the variance of $$X$$ is given by $$\begin{array}{lcl} {{Var}(X)} & = & {(.05)(1 - 4)^{2} + (.075)(2 - 4)^{2} + (.2)(3 - 4)^{2}} \\ & & {+ (.375)(4 - 4)^{2} + (.15)(5 - 4)^{2}} \\ & & {+ (.1)(6 - 4)^{2} + (.05)(7 - 4)^{2}} \\ & = & 1.95 \end{array}$$ Next, we find that the mean of the random variable $$Y$$ is given by $$\begin{array}{lcl} \mu_{Y} & = & {(1)(.2) + (2)(.15) + (3)(.1) + (4)(.15) + (5)(.05)} \\ & & {+ (6)(.1) + (7)(.25)} \\ & = & 4 \end{array}$$ so the variance of $$Y$$ is given by $$\begin{array}{lcl} {{Var}(Y)} & = & {(.2)(1 - 4)^{2} + (.15)(2 - 4)^{2} + (.1)(3 - 4)^{2}} \\ & & {+ (.15)(4 - 4)^{2} + (.05)(5 - 4)^{2}} \\ & & {+ (.1)(6 - 4)^{2} + (.25)(7 - 4)^{2}} \\ & = & 5.2 \end{array}$$ Note that $${Var}(X)$$ is smaller than $${Var}(Y)$$ , which confirms our earlier observations about the spread (or dispersion) of the probability distribution of $$X$$ and $$Y$$ , respectively.

snippet: Standard Deviation of a Random Variable X: Standard Deviation of a Random Variable X The standard deviation of a random variable X denoted \sigma (pronounced “sigma”), is defined by \begin{array}{l} {\sigma = \sqrt{{Var}(X)}} \\...
body_xml:
<note type="theorem" source_type="Standard Deviation of a Random Variable X" title="Standard Deviation of a Random Variable X">
    <heading level="4">Standard Deviation of a Random Variable X</heading>
    <paragraph>The standard deviation of a random variable $$X$$ denoted $$\sigma$$ (pronounced “sigma”), is defined by</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {\sigma = \sqrt{{Var}(X)}} \\ {\phantom{\sigma} = \sqrt{p_{1}{(x_{1} - \mu)}^{2} + p_{2}{(x_{2} - \mu)}^{2} + \cdots + p_{n}{(x_{n} - \mu)}^{2}}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>where $$x_{1},x_{2},\ldots,x_{n}$$ denote the values assumed by the random variable $$X$$ and $$p_{1} = P\left( X = x_{1} \right),p_{2} = P\left( X = x_{2} \right),\ldots,p_{n} = P\left( X = x_{n} \right)$$ .</paragraph>
  </note>

<example number="6">
    <heading level="4">Example 6</heading>
    <paragraph>Find the standard deviations of the random variables $$X$$ and $$Y$$ of Example 5.</paragraph>
    <heading level="4">Solution</heading>
    <paragraph>From the results of Example 5, we have $${Var}(X) = 1.95$$ and $${Var}(Y) = 5.2$$ . Taking their respective square roots, we have</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {\sigma_{X} = \sqrt{1.95}} \\ {\phantom{\sigma_{X}} \approx 1.40} \\ {\sigma_{Y} = \sqrt{5.2}} \\ {\phantom{\sigma_{Y}} \approx 2.28} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
  </example>

snippet: Variance and Standard Deviation of a Continuous Random Variable: Variance and Standard Deviation of a Continuous Random Variable Let X be a continuous random variable with probability density function f(x) on \lbrack a,b\rbrack . Then the...

<note type="theorem" source_type="Variance and Standard Deviation of a Continuous Random Variable" title="Variance and Standard Deviation of a Continuous Random Variable">
    <heading level="4">Variance and Standard Deviation of a Continuous Random Variable</heading>
    <paragraph>Let $$X$$ be a continuous random variable with probability density function $$f(x)$$ on $$\lbrack a,b\rbrack$$ . Then the variance of $$X$$ is</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$${Var}(X) = {\int_{a}^{b}{(x - \mu)}^{2}}f(x)dx$$</paragraph>

title: Example 9
snippet: Example 9: Example 9 Find the expected value, variance, and standard deviation of the random variable X associated with the probability density function f(x) = \frac{32}{15x^{3}} on \left\lbrack {1,4} \right\rbrack . Solution Using Formula...
body_xml:
<example number="9">
    <heading level="4">Example 9</heading>
    <paragraph>Find the expected value, variance, and standard deviation of the random variable $$X$$ associated with the probability density function</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$f(x) = \frac{32}{15x^{3}}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>on $$\left\lbrack {1,4} \right\rbrack$$ .</paragraph>
    <heading level="4">Solution</heading>
    <paragraph>Using Formula (3), we find the mean of $$X$$ :</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {\mu = {\int_{a}^{b}{xf(x)dx}} = {\int_{1}^{4}{x \cdot \frac{32}{15x^{3}}dx}}} \\ {\phantom{\mu} = {\frac{32}{15}{\int_{1}^{4}{x^{- 2}dx}}} = {\frac{32}{15}\left. \left( {- \frac{1}{x}} \right) \right|_{1}^{4}}} \\ {\phantom{\mu} = {\frac{32}{15}\left( {- \frac{1}{4} + 1} \right)} = \frac{8}{5}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Next, using Formula (8), we find</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {{Var(X)} = {{\int_{a}^{b}{{({x - \mu})}^{2}f(x)dx =}}{\int_{1}^{4}{\left( {x - \frac{8}{5}} \right)^{2} \cdot \frac{32}{15x^{3}}dx}}}} \\ {\phantom{Var(X)} = {\frac{32}{15}{\int_{1}^{4}{\left( {x^{2} - \frac{16}{5}x + \frac{64}{25}} \right)\frac{1}{x^{3}}dx}}}} \\ {\phantom{Var(X)} = {\frac{32}{15}{\int_{1}^{4}{\left( {\frac{1}{x} - \frac{16}{5}x^{- 2} + \frac{64}{25}x^{- 3}} \right)dx}}}} \\ {\phantom{Var(X)} = {\frac{32}{15}\left\lbrack {\ln x + \frac{16}{5x} - \frac{32}{25x^{2}}} \right\rbrack_{1}^{4}}} \\ {\phantom{Var(X)} = {\frac{32}{15}\left\lbrack {\left( {\ln 4 + \frac{16}{5 \cdot 4} - \frac{32}{25 \cdot 16}} \right) - \left( {\ln 1 + \frac{16}{5} - \frac{32}{25}} \right)} \right\rbrack}} \\ {\phantom{Var(X)} = {\frac{32}{15}\left( {\ln 4 + \frac{4}{5} - \frac{2}{25} - \frac{16}{5} + \frac{32}{25}} \right)}} \\ {\phantom{Var(X)} = {\frac{32}{15}\left( {\ln 4 - \frac{6}{5}} \right) \approx 0.40}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>Finally, using Formula (9), we find the required standard deviation to be</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\sigma = \sqrt{{Var}(X)} \approx \sqrt{0.40} \approx 0.63$$</paragraph>
  </example>

title: Example 10
snippet: Example 10: Example 10 Use Formula (10) to calculate the variance of the random variable of Example 9. Solution Using Formula (10), we have \begin{array}{l} {{{Var}(X)} = {\int_{a}^{b}{x^{2}f(x)dx - \mu^{2} = {\int_{1}^{4}{x^{2} \cdot...
body_xml:
<example number="10">
    <heading level="4">Example 10</heading>
    <paragraph>Use Formula (10) to calculate the variance of the random variable of Example 9.</paragraph>
    <heading level="4">Solution</heading>
    <paragraph>Using Formula (10), we have</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{l} {{{Var}(X)} = {\int_{a}^{b}{x^{2}f(x)dx - \mu^{2} = {\int_{1}^{4}{x^{2} \cdot \frac{32}{15x^{3}}dx - \left( \frac{8}{5} \right)^{2}}}}}} \\ {\phantom{{Var}(X)} = \left. \frac{32}{15}\int_{1}^{4}\frac{1}{x}dx - \frac{64}{25} = \frac{32}{15}\ln x \right|_{1}^{4} - \frac{64}{25}} \\ {\phantom{{Var}(X)} = {\frac{32}{15}\ln 4 - \frac{64}{25} \approx 0.40}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>as obtained earlier.</paragraph>
  </example>

<example number="1">
    <heading level="4">Example 1</heading>
    <paragraph>Let $$Z$$ be the standard normal variable. Make a sketch of the appropriate region under the standard normal curve, and then find the values of</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>$$P(Z < 1.24)$$</item>
      <item>$$P(Z > 0.5)$$</item>
      <item>$$P(0.24 < Z < 1.48)$$</item>
      <item>$$P( - 1.65 < Z < 2.02)$$</item>
    </list>
    <heading level="4">Solution</heading>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>The region under the standard normal curve associated with the probability $$P(Z < 1.24)$$ is shown in Figure 12. To find the area of the required region using Appendix C, we first locate the number $$1.2$$ in the column and the number $$0.04$$ in the row, both headed by $$z$$ , and read off the number $$0.8925$$ appearing in the body of the table. Thus, $$P(Z < 1.24) = .8925$$ Figure 12 Details A symmetric bell shaped curve is graphed on the horizontal line. The curve enters very close and parallel to the horizontal line, rises upward to the right, concave up, after it inflects, it then goes up to the right, now concave down and reaches its high point. Then it goes down to the right, still concave down, after it reaches the inflection point, it goes down, but now concave up and runs parallel and very close to the horizontal line. A perpendicular is dropped from the high point to meet the horizontal line at the mark 0 such that it is symmetric about the curve. To the right side of 0, there is a mark 1.24 from which a vertical line rises up till it touches the curve. The region below the curve to the left of the mark 1.24 is shaded. $$P(Z < 1.24)$$</item>
      <item>The region under the standard normal curve associated with the probability $$P(Z > 0.5)$$ is shown in Figure 13a. Observe, however, that the required area is, by virtue of the symmetry of the standard normal curve, equal to the shaded area shown in Figure 13b. Thus, $$\begin{array}{l} {{P(Z > 0.5)} = {P(Z < - 0.5)}} \\ {\phantom{P(Z > 0.5)} = .3085} \end{array}$$ Figure 13 Details Two images a and b are graphed, each plot a symmetric bell shaped curve on the horizontal line. In image a, the curve enters very close and parallel to the horizontal line, rises upward to the right, concave up till it inflects, then it goes up to the right, now concave down and reaches its high point. Then it goes down to the right, still concave down, after it reaches the inflection point, it goes down, but now concave up and runs parallel and very close to the horizontal line. A perpendicular is dropped from the high point to meet the horizontal line at the mark 0 such that it is symmetric about the curve. To the right side of 0, there is a mark 0.5 from which a vertical line rises up till it touches the curve. The region below the curve to the right side of the mark 0.5 is shaded. In image b, the curve enters very close and parallel to the horizontal line, rises upward to the right, concave up till it inflects, then it goes up to the right, now concave down and reaches its high point. Then it goes down to the right, still concave down, after it reaches the inflection point, it goes down, but now concave up and runs parallel and very close to the horizontal line. A perpendicular is dropped from the high point to meet the horizontal line at the mark 0 such that it is symmetric about the curve. To the left side of 0, there is a mark negative 0.5 from which a vertical line rises up till it touches the curve. The region below the curve to the left side of the mark negative 0.5 is shaded.</item>
      <item>The probability $$P(0.24 < Z < 1.48)$$ is equal to the shaded area shown in Figure 14. This area is obtained by subtracting the area under the curve to the left of $$z = 0.24$$ from the area under the curve to the left of $$z = 1.48$$ ; that is, $$\begin{array}{l} {{P(0.24 < Z < 1.48)} = {P(Z < 1.48) - P(Z < 0.24)}} \\ {\phantom{P(0.24 < Z < 1.48)} = {.9306 - .5948}} \\ {\phantom{P(0.24 < Z < 1.48)} = .3358} \end{array}$$ Figure 14 Details A symmetric bell shaped curve is graphed on the horizontal line. The region bounded by the curve, the two vertical lines at the marks 0.24 and 1.48 and the horizontal line is shaded. $$P(0.24 < Z < 1.48)$$</item>
      <item>The probability $$P( - 1.65 < Z < 2.02)$$ is given by the shaded area shown in Figure 15. We have $$\begin{array}{l} {{P( - 1.65 < Z < 2.02)} = {P(Z < 2.02) - P(Z < - 1.65)}} \\ {\phantom{P( - 1.65 < Z < 2.02)} = {.9783 - .0495}} \\ {\phantom{P( - 1.65 < Z < 2.02)} = .9288} \end{array}$$ Figure 15 Details A symmetric bell shaped curve is graphed on the horizontal line. Similarly, to the left side of 0, there is a mark negative 1.65 from which a vertical line rises up till it touches the curve. The region bounded by the curve between the two vertical lines at the marks negative 1.65 and 2.02 and the horizontal line is shaded. $$P( - 1.65 < Z < 2.02)$$</item>

snippet: Example 2: Example 2 Let Z be the standard normal random variable. Find the value of z if z satisfies P(Z < z) = .9474 P(Z > z) = .9115 P( - z < Z < z) = .7888 Solution Refer to Figure 18. We want the value of Z such that the area of the...

<example number="2">
    <heading level="4">Example 2</heading>
    <paragraph>Let $$Z$$ be the standard normal random variable. Find the value of $$z$$ if $$z$$ satisfies</paragraph>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>$$P(Z < z) = .9474$$</item>
      <item>$$P(Z > z) = .9115$$</item>
      <item>$$P( - z < Z < z) = .7888$$</item>
    </list>
    <heading level="4">Solution</heading>
    <list type="ordered">
      <item>Refer to Figure 18. We want the value of $$Z$$ such that the area of the region under the standard normal curve and to the left of $$Z = z$$ is $$.9474$$ . Locating the number $$.9474$$ in Appendix C, and reading back, we find that $$z = 1.62$$ . Figure 18 Details A bell shaped curve is graphed on the horizontal line. The curve enters very close to the horizontal line, rises upward to the right, concave up till it inflects, then it goes up to the right, now concave down and reaches its high point. Then it goes down to the right, still concave down, after it reaches the inflection point, it goes down, but concave up and runs parallel and very close to the horizontal line. A perpendicular is dropped from the high point to meet the horizontal line at the mark 0 such that the curve is symmetric about the perpendicular. To the right side of 0, there is a mark z, from which a vertical line rises up till it touches the curve a little away from the mark 0. The region below the curve to the left of the vertical line at the mark z is shaded and the region is labeled 0.9474. $$P(Z < z) = .9474$$</item>
      <item>Since $$P(Z > Z)$$ , or equivalently, the area of the region to the right of $$z$$ is greater than $$0.5$$ , it follows that $$z$$ must be negative (Figure 19); hence, $$- z$$ is positive. Furthermore, the area of the region to the right of $$z$$ is the same as the area of the region to the left of $$- z$$ . Therefore, $$\begin{array}{l} {{P(Z > z)} = {P(Z < - z)}} \\ {\phantom{P(Z > z)} = .9115} \end{array}$$ Figure 19 Details A bell shaped curve is graphed on the horizontal line. The curve enters very close and parallel to the horizontal line, rises upward to the right, concave up till it inflects, then it goes up to the right, now concave down and reaches its high point. Then it goes down to the right, still concave down, after it reaches the inflection point, it goes down, but concave up and runs parallel and very close to the horizontal line. A perpendicular is dropped from the high point to meet the horizontal line at the mark 0 such that the curve is symmetric about the perpendicular. To the right side of 0, there is a mark negative z, and to the left side of 0, there is a mark z from which a vertical line rises up till it touches the curve. The region below the curve to the right of the vertical line at mark z is shaded and the region is labeled 0.9115. $$P(Z > z) = .9115$$ Looking up the table, we find $$- z = 1.35$$ , so $$z = - 1.35$$ .</item>
      <item>The region associated with $$P( - z < Z < z)$$ is shown in Figure 20. Observe that by symmetry, the area of this region is just double that of the area of the region between $$Z = 0$$ and $$Z = z$$ ; that is, $$P\left( {- z < Z < z} \right) = 2P\left( {0 < Z < z} \right)$$ Figure 20 Details A bell shaped curve is graphed on the horizontal line. The curve enters very close and parallel to the horizontal line, rises upward to the right, concave up till it inflects, then it goes up to the right, now concave down and reaches its high point. Then it goes down to the right, still concave down, after it reaches the inflection point, it goes down, but concave up and runs parallel and very close to the horizontal line. A perpendicular is dropped from the high point to meet the horizontal line at the mark 0 such that the curve is symmetric about the perpendicular. To the left side of 0, there is a mark negative z, and to the right side of 0, there is a mark z. From both the marks negative z and z, a vertical line rises up till it touches the curve. The region below the curve between the vertical lines at negative z and z is shaded and labeled 0.7888. $$P( - z < Z < z) = .7888$$ Furthermore, $$P\left( {0 < Z < z} \right) = P\left( {Z < z} \right) - \frac{1}{2}$$ (Figure 21). Therefore, $$\frac{1}{2}P\left( {- z < Z < z} \right) = P\left( {Z < z} \right) - \frac{1}{2}$$ or, solving for $$P(Z < z)$$ , we have $$\begin{array}{l} {{P\left( {Z < z} \right)} = {\frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{2}P\left( {- z < Z < z} \right)}} \\ {\phantom{P\left( {Z < z} \right)} = {\frac{1}{2}\left( {1 + .7888} \right)}} \\ {\phantom{P\left( {Z < z} \right)} = .8944} \end{array}$$ Figure 21 Details Three images each graph a symmetric bell shaped curve on a horizontal axis. In image a, the curve enters very close and parallel to the horizontal line, rises upward to the right, concave up till it inflects, then it goes up to the right, now concave down and reaches its high point. Then it goes down to the right, still concave down, after it reaches the inflection point, it goes down, but concave up and runs parallel and very close to the horizontal line. A perpendicular is dropped from the high point to meet the horizontal line at the mark 0 such that the curve is symmetric about the perpendicular. To the left side of 0, there is a mark negative z and similarly to the right side of 0, there is a mark z from which a vertical line rises up till it reaches the curve and the region below the curve between the two vertical lines at the marks 0 and z is shaded. In image b, the curve enters very close and parallel to the horizontal line, rises upward to the right, concave up till it inflects, then it goes up to the right, now concave down and reaches its high point. Then it goes down to the right, still concave down, after it reaches the inflection point, it goes down, but concave up and runs parallel and very close to the horizontal line. A perpendicular is dropped from the high point to meet the horizontal line at the mark 0 such that the curve is symmetric about the perpendicular. To the left side of 0, there is a mark negative z and similarly to the right side of 0, there is a mark z from which a vertical line rises up till it reaches the curve and the region below the curve to the left of the vertical line at mark z is shaded. In image c, the curve enters very close and parallel to the horizontal line, rises upward to the right, concave up till it inflects, then it goes up to the right, now concave down and reaches its high point. Then it goes down to the right, still concave down, after it reaches the inflection point, it goes down, but concave up and runs parallel and very close to the horizontal line. A perpendicular is dropped from the high point to meet the horizontal line at the mark 0 such that the curve is symmetric about the perpendicular. To the left side of 0, there is a mark negative z and similarly to the right side of 0, there is a mark z. The region below the curve to the left of the vertical line at mark 0 is shaded. Below the images, the expression P(0 < Z < z) = P(Z < z) minus ½ is written. Out of which, the expression P(0 < Z < z) appears under the first image; equals to sign appears between the first and the second graph; P(Z < z) appears under the second image; minus sign appears between the second and the third graph and the fraction ½ appears under the third image. Consulting the table, we find $$z = 1.25$$ .</item>
    </list>
  </example>

      <item>Using Equation (12) with $$\mu = 100$$ , $$\sigma = 20$$ , $$a = 75$$ , and $$b = 110$$ , we have $$P\left( {75 < X < 110} \right)$$ $$= {P\left( {\frac{75 - 100}{20} < Z < \frac{110 - 100}{20}} \right)}$$ $$= {P\left( {- 1.25 < Z < 0.5} \right)}$$ $$= {P\left( {Z < 0.5} \right) - P\left( {Z < - 1.25} \right)}$$ See Figure 23. $$= {.6915 - .1056 = .5859}$$ Figure 23 Details A bell shaped curve is graphed on the horizontal line. The curve enters very close and parallel to the horizontal line, rises upward to the right, concave up till it inflects, then it goes up to the right, now concave down and reaches its high point. Then it goes down to the right, still concave down, after it reaches the inflection point, it goes down, but concave up and runs parallel and very close to the horizontal line. The region bounded by the curve, horizontal line and two vertical lines at the marks negative 1.25 and 0.5 is shaded.</item>

body_xml:
<note type="theorem" source_type="The n th Taylor Polynomial" title="The n th Taylor Polynomial">
    <heading level="4">The n th Taylor Polynomial</heading>
    <paragraph>Suppose that the function $$f$$ and its first $$n$$ derivatives are defined at $$a$$ . Then the $$n$$ th Taylor polynomial of $$f$$ at $$a$$ is the polynomial</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$\begin{array}{lcl} {P_{n}(x)} & = & {f(a) + f^{\prime}(a)(x - a)} \\ & & {+ \frac{f^{''}(a)}{2!}(x - a)^{2} + \cdots + \frac{f^{(n)}(a)}{n!}(x - a)^{n}} \end{array}$$</paragraph>
    <paragraph>which coincides with $$f(x),f^{\prime}(x),\ldots,f^{(n)}(x)$$ at $$a$$ ; that is,</paragraph>
    <paragraph math="block">$$P_{n}(a) = f(a), {P^{\prime}}_{n}(a) = f^{\prime}(a), \ldots, P_{n}^{(n)}(a) = f^{(n)}(a)$$</paragraph>
  </note>

body_xml: Example 1 Find the Taylor polynomials $$P_{1}$$ , $$P_{2}$$ , $$P_{3}$$ , and $$P_{4}$$ of $$f(x) = e^{x}$$ at $$x = 0$$ , and sketch the graph of each polynomial superimposed upon the graph of $$f(x) = e^{x}$$ . Solution Here, $$a = 0$$ , and since $$f(x) = f^{\prime}(x) = f^{''}(x) = f^{'''}(x) = f^{(4)}(x) = e^{x}$$ we find $$f(0) = f^{\prime}(0) = f^{''}(0) = f^{'''}(0) = f^{(4)}(0) = 1$$ Using Equation (2) with $${n = 1,2,3},{and}4$$ in succession, we find that the required Taylor polynomials are $$\begin{array}{lcl} {P_{1}(x)} & = & {f(0) + f^{\prime}(0)(x - 0) = 1 + x} \\ {P_{2}(x)} & = & {f(0) + f^{\prime}(0)(x - 0) + \frac{f^{''}(0)}{2!}(x - 0)^{2} = 1 + x + \frac{1}{2}x^{2}} \\ {P_{3}(x)} & = & {f(0) + f^{\prime}(0)(x - 0) + \frac{f^{''}(0)}{2!}(x - 0)^{2} + \frac{f^{'''}(0)}{3!}(x - 0)^{3}} \\ & = & {1 + x + \frac{1}{2}x^{2} + \frac{1}{6}x^{3}} \\ {P_{4}(x)} & = & {f(0) + f^{\prime}(0)(x - 0) + \frac{f^{''}(0)}{2!}(x - 0)^{2} + \frac{f^{'''}(0)}{3!}(x - 0)^{3}} \\ & & {+ \frac{f^{(4)}(0)}{4!}(x - 0)^{4} = 1 + x + \frac{1}{2}x^{2} + \frac{1}{6}x^{3} + \frac{1}{24}x^{4}} \end{array}$$ The graphs of these polynomials are shown in Figure 2. Observe that the approximation of $$f(x)$$ near $$x = 0$$ improves as the degree of the approximating Taylor polynomial increases.
